articles.title: From ban to boundaries: how 100 high-impact journals regulate AI-generated images after the 2026 policy shift
articles.authors: Shirley Yang
articles.abstract: Generative AI can draw explanatory figures and can also fabricate research images. We asked how the 100 highest-impact journals regulate AI-generated images and how those rules changed in a year. On 30 September 2026 we captured each journal’s author instructions and the publisher policies they cite. We retrieved archived versions from September–October 2025 and coded rules for five image types. At baseline, 79 journals belonged to publishers that prohibited AI-generated images. Between May and August 2026, Taylor & Francis, Elsevier and Springer Nature replaced these bans with rules that depend on image type. By September 2026, 55 journals explicitly permitted AI-generated explanatory illustrations and 58 permitted AI-assisted data visualisations, usually with disclosure or reproducibility conditions. For 89 journals, AI-created or AI-altered primary research images were prohibited; no journal permitted them. Rules for graphical abstracts and covers varied most. The Science journals, The Lancet family and JAMA Psychiatry still restricted illustrative uses. Twenty-seven journals gave instructions that contradicted or lagged behind their publisher’s current policy, including 20 of 31 Springer Nature journals. Authors need to check journal-level instructions, and publishers need to align them.

articles.title: Polyauthorship and Proportionate Authorship Transparency in Medical Research
articles.authors: Onder Canguven
articles.abstract: Large author groups can reflect legitimate collaboration, but author counts alone reveal little about individual contributions or accountability. Three recent articles in World Journal of Men’s Health illustrate the range: an editorial on authorship accountability lists 18 authors; a systematic review and meta-analysis that included five studies lists 28; and an international survey by Shah and colleagues lists nearly 200 named authors. These figures do not establish inappropriate authorship. They do raise a question: how can readers distinguish substantive authorship from other valuable contributions? We propose proportionate reporting requirements that increase with the size and structure of a collaboration, including specific individual contribution statements and, for very large groups, an account of how final manuscript approval and accountability were secured. Greater transparency would help readers interpret academic credit without imposing arbitrary limits on author numbers.

articles.title: Everyday use of AI for emotion regulation depends on the person and the situation
articles.authors: Simon M. Li; Junkang Averi Lin; Shufang Sun; Shanshan Xu; Bin Yu; Mark S. Chen
articles.abstract: Young adults increasingly use AI to seek support and manage their feelings. Understanding when and where they use AI for emotion regulation (ER) and its effectiveness can provide evidence needed for research, practice, and policy. In a 13-day ecological momentary assessment study, 3,048 Chinese university students reported emotional situations, ER strategies, and affect four times daily. AI use for confiding, advice, or emotional support was reported on 2.0% of 134,275 prompts and by 17.3% of participants at least once. In person-level logistic regression, use was concentrated among students with greater lifetime AI use (OR up to 3.12); in multilevel logistic regression, it was more likely during digital, academic, and interpersonal situations (OR 1.22-2.56). AI use did not predict next-prompt affect overall, but was followed by lower positive affect when neither stressors nor positive events had occurred, weakening as more events co-occurred. AI has entered everyday ER as a context-dependent resource.

articles.title: Inhabiting digital ecologies: A qualitative approach to good digital practices
articles.authors: Esther Paniagua; Myriam Durán Vilches; Noemí Robles; Pepa Barral González; Manuel Armayones
articles.abstract:
The integration of digital technologies into everyday life has produced complex digital
ecologies in which platforms, algorithms, and social practices jointly shape experience,
identity, and emotional regulation. Although research on digital well-being has
increased significantly, little is known about how individuals reflect on their digital lives
and the practical criteria they develop to navigate these environments while preserving
well-being and autonomy.,This paper addresses these questions through qualitative
research conducted within a digital community of 100 adults residing in Spain whose
participation unfolded across four successive waves. Fieldwork combined individual
journals, thematic forums, and an open social space, generating a longitudinal corpus
on the everyday experience of inhabiting digital spaces. Results were interpreted
through discourse analysis to reconstruct shared patterns of meaning and discursive
positions.,Findings reveal an ambivalent relationship with digital environments: the
same tools that enable connection, communication, and access to information are also
described as sources of noise, overstimulation, attention fragmentation, and loss of
control. Alongside these discomforts, participants describe daily repertoires of
adjustment that crystallise into distinct discursive positions from which they inhabit
digital ecologies and develop good practices.,We propose that good digital practices
should not be understood as a universal list of self-regulatory norms, but as relational
competencies developed through reflection and experience. Methodologically, the
study shows that a digital community is a particularly suitable tool for examining
everyday, complex, largely automated phenomena, since it enables participants to
observe, compare, and transform their digital experience into practical criteria guiding
their relationship with digital ecologies.

articles.title: Digital Reflections of Social (Dis)connectedness: A Snapchat Data Donations Study
articles.authors: J. Loes Pouwels; Milou Tilstra; Lara Vreeswijk; Nienke Prot; Michelle Alexandra Pingel
articles.abstract: By linking self-reported psychosocial experiences to actual Snapchat interactions, the present study aims to provide a nuanced understanding of how social experiences are reflected in digital contexts. Specifically, the study investigates how adolescents’ experiences of friendship closeness, peer belongingness, loneliness, and social exclusion are related to adolescents’ online interactions with friends by combining real-time experience sampling methodology (ESM) with objective social media data from Snapchat. Participants were 123 adolescents (M age = 13.33 years; SD = 1.10; 58.50% girls). Adolescents with higher disconnectedness (i.e., greater loneliness and social inclusion) had more unanswered friendship requests and spent relatively more time on messaging. After controlling for multiple testing, social (dis)connectedness was not associated with the actual number of sent or viewed messages in the past two months, the number of friendships, Snapscore, or Snapchat AI usage. These findings do not provide clear evidence for either the social enhancement hypothesis or compensation hypothesis.

articles.title: Displacement and Compensation: How Online and In-Person Interactions Relate to Adolescents’ Social and Emotional Connectedness
articles.authors: J. Loes Pouwels; Marlies Maes; Daan Hulsmans; Maaike Verhagen
articles.abstract: By proposing that superficial online interactions displace deeper, in-person connections, displacement theory has given rise to widespread societal concerns about adolescents' use of social media. However, previous research only showed limited evidence for the displacement theory. Therefore, this study aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of how both online and in-person interactions shape adolescents' sense of connectedness. A total of 335 adolescents in Grades 7-9 participated in a 4-week Experience Sampling Methodology study. Three times a day, they reported on their in person and online interactions with friends and peer groups, as well as the quantity and quality of these interactions and their perceived connectedness to their friends and peer groups. Multilevel analyses will be used to examine how the occurrence of in-person and online contact, as well as the quantity and quality of these interactions, are related to adolescents’ social and emotional connectedness.

articles.title: Not “born that way”: Homophobic social preferences and non-essentialism of sexual orientation in childhood
articles.authors: Rebecca Peretz-Lange
articles.abstract: Although prejudice begins early in development, very few studies examine the developmental roots of homophobia. We explored the onset and developmental timecourse of homophobic social preferences as well as the cognitive and environmental factors predicting these preferences. We were particularly interested in whether children would essentialize orientation (e.g., consider it inborn and uncontrollable), since essentialism often positively correlates with prejudice but negatively correlates with adolescents’ and adults’ homophobia. As environmental predictors, we explored parents’ anti-prejudiced values and children’s LGBTQ contact. A diverse sample of participants from across the United States (n = 128 six- to nine-year-olds, 60 girls & 68 boys, 42% White & 58% of color) selected between heteroparental and homoparental peers in a Playmate Preference Task and then completed an essentialism assessment. Parents reported their anti-prejudiced values and children’s LGBTQ contact. Homophobic social preferences were present by age seven and increased across childhood. Moreover, despite children’s pervasive essentialist tendencies, participants overwhelmingly rejected the idea that being in a same-gender vs. other-gender marriage reflects any internal uncontrollable characteristic. Instead, children viewed this as a matter of choice. Essentialism was very low overall and did not predict social preferences. Instead, parents’ values and children’s LGBTQ contact predicted these preferences. In sum, children view orientation as reflecting a choice rather than an intrinsic nature, and then rely on the adults in their lives to determine how to feel toward that choice. Homophobic social preferences therefore emerge early and in the context of behavioral views of orientation. Social, cognitive, and developmental implications are discussed.

articles.title: The Not So Illusory Truth Effect: Source Credibility and the Effect of Repetition on Belief
articles.authors: Reed Orchinik; David Gertler Rand; Rahul Bhui
articles.abstract: The illusory truth effect, in which repetition increases belief, is often seen as a cognitive bias. Here, we argue that it may reflect a rational adaptation to generally high-quality information environments. A formal model shows that increasing belief in repeated statements improves accuracy when a source usually tells the truth but sometimes errs. The model captures previous findings and, unlike existing accounts, predicts that repetition should do little to increase belief when the source is not credible. In a large (N = 4,947) preregistered experiment with a quota-matched U.S. sample, the effect was substantially smaller when headlines appeared in a mostly false rather than mostly true newsfeed. In a second preregistered experiment (N = 2,484), repetition increased partisans' belief only in claims from the 2024 U.S. presidential candidate they trusted. Repeated misinformation may therefore be most persuasive when it comes from sources people trust.

articles.title: Felt but Not Detected:  Salience Versus Detectability of Affective Change in Ambulatory Assessment
articles.authors: Aleksandra Kaurin; Mario Wenzel; Paula Philippi; Jonas Dora
articles.abstract: Ambulatory assessment (AA) captures within-person fluctuations in daily life, yet not all observed change exceeds measurement error, and not all reliable change is subjectively experienced. We propose a preregistered dual-threshold framework distinguishing statistical detectability (smallest detectable change, SDC) from experiential salience (minimal important change, MIC). Adults (N = 250) completed a 14-day AA protocol with twice-daily and event-contingent assessments (5,982 observations), rating momentary stress, positive affect, and negative affect (0–4) and perceived change since the previous assessment. SDC₉₅ estimates ranged from 1.56 to 1.92 scale points, so roughly three-quarters of consecutive changes fell below reliable detection. Anchor-based MICs, in contrast, were 1 point for all constructs. Correspondence between detectable and perceived change was asymmetric: sensitivity was high (.77–.87), but specificity (.46–.56) and positive predictive values (.24–.31) were low, as participants frequently reported change without reliable change; directional reversals were rare. Reliable change strongly predicted perceived change (ORs 4.6–12.5). Event-contingent assessments, higher prior states, and person-level characteristics (e.g., impulsivity, emotion regulation) increased the general propensity to report change but did not moderate this link. Felt change thus precedes measurable change: detectability and salience are distinct thresholds that intensive longitudinal research must evaluate separately.

articles.title: Cross-Lagged Panel Analysis Using Structural Equation Modeling: Trends and Suggestions Based on a Literature Review of 111 Studies
articles.authors: Asuka Nishida; Satoshi Usami
articles.abstract:
Cross-lagged panel analysis based on structural equation modeling (SEM) has been widely used in the behavioral sciences. The present study provides a literature review based on 111 studies published in major psychology journals that conducted cross-lagged panel analysis. Through this review, we offer an overview of current trends in study design, analytical methods (e.g., estimation method, missing data handling), and model selection, and discuss practical challenges and implications for future applications. A major finding is that the use of the random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) has increased substantially (41% of the studies) over the past few years. At the same time, most studies rely on longitudinal data with a small number of measurement occasions (e.g., T = 3 − 4). Studies that employed the RI-CLPM on the grounds that it enables inference about within-person relations tended to conduct only limited comparisons with potential alternative models, and only 3% of the studies evaluated model fit from the perspective of local fit (i.e., residual correlations). Although many studies using psychological scales relied on sum scores, only 40% of the studies examined longitudinal measurement invariance, suggesting that there is
still room for improvement.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of adolescent neuroticism on short-form video overuse: A comment on Liu and Wu (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Liu and Wu, we reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking adolescent neuroticism to short-form video overuse (SVO). We demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported neuroticism, depression, anxiety, and SVO are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles.title: Stability, Asymmetric Recovery, and Sociodemographic Heterogeneity in Social Health Trajectories Across Social Disruption: A Four-Wave Hidden Markov Model
articles.authors: Karoline Huth; Lisanne Catharina Johanna Steijvers; Senne Maria Catharina Elisabeth Wijnen; Olga Schiepers; Matty Crone; Rik Crutzen; Nicole Dukers-Muijrers
articles.abstract: Social health is a key pillar of overall health, yet knowledge of distinct social health states, how these change during long-term social disruption, who is at risk of social ill-health, and how social health states affect mental and physical illness remains limited. We used Hidden Markov models to analyse prospective data from 954 adults aged 40 and over who were assessed before, during, and after the onset of the 2019–2025 pandemic. This enabled us to identify latent social health states based on network size, density, loneliness, and emotional support, and to estimate transition probabilities between states over time.  We examined the impact of sex, education, and age on state membership and trajectories, as well as the association between states and depressive symptoms and physical health. Three states were identified: socially isolated (15.9%), moderately connected (55.5%), and socially thriving (28.6%). Most participants (72.5%) remained in one state throughout the observation period; 14.4% deteriorated, 6.5% recovered, and the rest fluctuated.  Being male and having completed a practical education were associated with the socially isolated state, while being female was associated with the thriving state, as well as state deterioration. Worse states showed a graded association with depressive symptoms. Social health is characterised by three relatively stable states, even in the face of persistent social disruption. Nevertheless, many individuals exhibited persistent deterioration even after social restrictions were lifted. The differing risk across sociodemographic groups highlights the need for targeted strategies to promote resilient social health.

articles.title: The role of pragmatic context in children’s quantification of parts and wholes
articles.authors: David Barner; Hannah Bryer; Miguel Mejia; Mahesh Srinivasan
articles.abstract: Why do children sometimes include the pieces of broken things when asked to count (e.g., “Count the forks”)? In five experiments, we test two ideas: (1) that adults, but not children, exclude parts from counts by reasoning that speakers must only be interested in whole objects with functions that fulfill desired goals, and (2) that only adults exclude parts on the basis of a Gricean inference, on which it is assumed that if a speaker wanted parts to be counted, they would say so. In Experiments 1-3, we find that although children and adults are somewhat less likely to count pieces of objects when speaker goals are explicitly mentioned, large developmental differences remain unexplained. In Experiments 4-5, we provide evidence that children differ most from adults when pieces are presented in the presence of complementary parts (with which they together would form a whole), and that these pieces are significantly more likely to be conceptualized and labeled as “parts”, especially by adults. Together, these findings suggest that adults – but not children – are more likely to exclude broken parts from their counts in response to requests like “Count the forks!” when they are also able to understand that more informative requests could have been made (e.g., “Count the pieces of fork!”).

articles.title: Development and Accuracy Evaluation of an LLM-Assisted Workflow for Screening and Data Extraction in Large-Scale Syntheses
articles.authors: Vsevolod Scherrer; Franzis Preckel; Moritz Breit
articles.abstract:
Large-scale research syntheses are labor-intensive and prone to human error, and large language models (LLMs) could support their screening and data extraction. Building on current recommendations, we developed an integrated workflow for title and abstract screening (Step 1), full-text screening (Step 2), and data extraction (Step 3), and evaluated it in a preregistered proof-of-concept study.
The study updated a meta-analysis on the rank-order stability of cognitive abilities, in which records may report several nested coefficients. Every step used ensembles of five LLM-instances, and we evaluated 2,960 workflow configurations against a human gold standard of 892 records, of which 692 records with 102 coded effect sizes formed the evaluation set. Without human review, Steps 1 and 2 retained 96.72% and 100.00% of eligible records. At Step 3, the LLMs missed 35.05% of gold effect sizes in rule-based extracted text but none in text from machine-learning-based parsing, which also lowered their coding error from 10.16% to 2.61%. In the recommended configuration, human review was confined to Step 3, where checking effect sizes of 5 of 40 records and 16.43% of the cells raised specificity to 100.00% and coding accuracy from 97.39% to 99.24%.
We derive five recommendations: (1) refine criterion-specific prompts on a calibration set, (2) use machine-learning-based PDF parsing for data extraction, (3) aggregate ensemble ratings leniently at screening and strictly at data extraction, (4) focus human review on data extraction, targeted via flags and ensemble disagreement, and (5) identify nested effect sizes in a separate stage with unique identifiers.

articles.title: Changes in Single People’s Attachment Models and Co-Development with Life Satisfaction
articles.authors: Michael Dominik Krämer; R. Chris Fraley; Laura Buchinger; Julia Stern; Omri Gillath; William J. Chopik; Geoff MacDonald; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles.abstract: Attachment security (i.e., low levels of attachment anxiety and avoidance) is important for both partnered and long-term single people’s well-being. However, research gaps limit knowledge to what extent attachment processes generalize to single people. Research has often not distinguished global and relationship-specific attachment; most studies of single people were cross-sectional; and little is known about attachment change and its co-development with well-being. The present study examined selection into long-term singlehood, change in relationship-specific attachment, and co-development with life satisfaction. We used longitudinal data spanning 30 months (N = 3,542; 39,492 assessments; 82% women; M_age = 34.54) and compared consistently single, consistently partnered, and intermittently partnered people. Baseline global, romantic, and friend-specific avoidance, but not anxiety, prospectively predicted remaining single. Compared to consistently partnered people, consistently single people showed higher global and romantic attachment insecurity, and both groups decreased mostly in parallel. However, single people increased slightly more adaptively in some of the non-romantic attachment models. Intermittently partnered people were similar in romantic attachment at baseline to single people but became more secure over time. Across most attachment models, people who increased in attachment security also increased in life satisfaction. This co-development was similar between groups, except that decreasing romantic avoidance was less closely tied to increasing life satisfaction among single people. Together, persistent differences in global and romantic attachment may reflect selection into relationship status rather than distinct development. In addition, similar attachment–well-being links across groups indicate that attachment operates in similar ways in both partnered and long-term single people.

articles.title: Inhabiting digital ecologies: A qualitative approach to good digital practices

articles.title: “Puzzling, Yet So Refreshing”: Experiencing the Value of Neurodiversity Within an Inclusive Choir
articles.authors: Nicolas Petit; Géraldine Dessertenne; Fanny Aprile; Lucie Jurek
articles.abstract: The social challenges encountered by autistic people are increasingly understood as a double empathy problem: a mutual misunderstanding between autistic and non-autistic individuals, rather than an autistic deficit. This paradigm highlights a need for inclusive spaces that foster mutual understanding, yet this remains challenging. Choral singing offers a promising medium to facilitate cross-neurotype dynamics, as it is thought to have evolved as a biological mechanism to foster social bonding. Accordingly, this qualitative study explored how 12 general population choristers experienced a 6-month neurodiverse choir shared with 8 autistic adolescents and 3 autism specialists. We used a two-stage qualitative design, first capturing individual experience through an open-ended online questionnaire, and subsequently deepening our analysis through a discussion with a community stakeholder panel. The findings revealed an intrinsically demanding experience, especially emotionally and cognitively, counterbalanced by important benefits, as it was also described as joyful and powerful, encouraging personal growth among the choristers and a shift in their perceptions of autism. These findings support the neurodiversity paradigm and suggest that choral singing may be a powerful double empathy solution, facilitating intergroup contact to reduce prejudice and thereby enhance the participation of autistic voices.

articles.title: The Other-Race Effect in Implicit Memory for Face Combinations
articles.authors: Yoko Higuchi; Kiwako Shimada
articles.abstract: Other-race faces are remembered less accurately than own-race faces, a robust phenomenon known as the other-race effect or cross-race effect. However, most evidence for the other-race effect comes from tasks that require explicit encoding or recognition of individual face identities, leaving unclear whether the effect is confined to explicit memory demands. Here, we report evidence for an other-race effect not only in explicit memory, but also in implicit memory for repeated face combinations. In Experiment 1, Japanese participants intentionally encoded Asian and Caucasian faces and later performed an explicit recognition task; recognition sensitivity was higher for own-race Asian faces than for other-race Caucasian faces. In Experiment 2, Japanese participants performed an implicit memory task in which repeated face combinations were presented without awareness of the repetitions; implicit memory for repeated face combinations developed more reliably for own-race Asian faces than for other-race Caucasian faces. Taken together, these results suggest that the cognitive difficulties associated with other-race faces should be understood not only as a problem of explicit face memory, but also as a problem of implicit memory formed through repeated face exposure in everyday life.

articles.title: Facial evidence matters less for stereotype-consistent judgments: Weaker formidability-aggression associations in Black vs. White faces
articles.authors: Kirstan Brodie; Brandon Cohen; Youngki Hong
articles.abstract: Facial characteristics are reliably associated with social judgments, but these relationships may depend on whether a judgment is consistent with stereotypes of the target’s social group. Across four studies with adult participants, we tested this possibility using perceived aggression and threat in Black and White faces. Perceived dominance (Study 1, N=117) and physical strength (Study 2, N=626) predicted aggression judgments less strongly for Black than White faces. Dominance also predicted perceived threat less strongly for Black than White faces after controlling for several threat-related covariates (Study 3, N=380). Furthermore, machine learning analyses found less overlap in dominance- and threat-predictive facial information for Black faces. Finally, face morphing that matched featural variation across race while manipulating apparent race showed a weaker dominance-aggression relationship for Black-appearing faces (Study 4, N=467). Together, these findings are consistent with the possibility that facial evidence has reduced influence on judgments of stereotype-consistent traits.

articles.title: Characterizing deaf and hard-of-hearing language experiences as arousal-regulation processes
articles.authors: Christina Kim; Laurel Aichler; Onudeah Nicolarakis; Shilpa Hanumantha Lacy; Rachel Sortino; Rachel Pizzie
articles.abstract: Empirical language research with deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) groups often includes proficiency, age of acquisition, or language background measures but excludes people’s socioemotional context. Measuring socioemotional context depends on characterizing the socioemotional experiences associated with DHH language development and use. We used the biopsychosocial model of arousal regulation as a theoretical lens to explore 11 qualitative interviews with DHH participants. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we developed three characteristic themes: 1) Deafness is not a monolith, 2) Name it to tame it – Language Anxiety, and 3) Positive roots for resilient shoots. These themes show that DHH language experiences are heterogeneous, that negative experiences can represent language anxiety, and that positive experiences modulate arousal regulation. Our study highlights new socioemotional considerations for language processing research like how emotions influence language use, how motivations support language skills, and how communication strategies impact social interactions within DHH communities.

articles.title: Eye-gaze dynamics reveal the adaptive nature of real-time noisy-channel inference in speech comprehension
articles.authors: Rachel Anna Ryskin
articles.abstract: To understand spoken language, listeners must extract meaning from acoustic input that is variable and noisy. The noisy-channel framework posits that listeners overcome this uncertainty by rationally inferring the speaker's intent, combining prior expectations with a model of how the message may have been corrupted during transmission. However, the exact nature of this noise model and its sensitivity to context (e.g., speaker or acoustic environment) remain unknown. Here, I use eye-tracking to measure human speech processing as it unfolds on the millisecond timescale, and I use the representational geometry of a self-supervised speech model (HuBERT) to estimate the noise model. I show that spoken word comprehension is well captured as real-time Bayesian belief updating. Further, listeners flexibly tune their expectation of noise to the specific acoustic environment. These results extend the noisy-channel framework to the moment-by-moment comprehension of speech. More broadly, these findings demonstrate that the human language system continuously adapts its internal model to the statistical structure of the communicative environment. By linking noisy-channel inference with real-time perceptual dynamics, this work highlights the remarkable flexibility of human cognition in navigating uncertainty and opens the door to investigating internal representations in human and artificial speech recognition systems through their fine-grained temporal dynamics.

articles.title: Towards the Social Microstructure of Human Movement as a Topic of Psychological Inquiry
articles.authors: Mark Jaime
articles.abstract: Human action unfolds through movement, and how that movement is organized can itself reveal psychological information about the person producing it. I use social microstructure to refer specifically to patterned organization within unfolding movement that bears systematically on socially relevant characteristics or processes of the person producing it. The purpose of this paper is to develop social microstructure as a perspective for expanding the psychological questions we ask through the examination of movement. Doing so means treating social microstructure as a topic of inquiry and asking what psychological questions become possible when the organization within movement is related systematically to the person producing it. Advances in computer vision, machine learning, and related computational methods now make increasingly rich representations of unfolding human movement available for such analysis. I pursue several questions opened by this perspective, including how different representations derived from recorded movement preserve psychologically relevant organization, how social microstructure may change across development, and what organization within self-generated and socially relevant movement might contribute to our understanding of the self and social functioning. Across these directions is a common question: what can be learned about the person from variation within the unfolding of an action itself?

articles.title: Perceptual Cues Can Influence Curiosity, Metamemory, and Memory Processes
articles.authors: Ashley Chen; Matthew Rhodes; Alan Castel
articles.abstract: Important information is often presented in large fonts, a tactic used to direct individuals’ attention and emphasize relevance. In a series of experiments, we tested whether font size, a perceptual cue that may communicate relative importance, may influence one’s curiosity, judgments of learning (JOLs), and recall. Participants were presented with lists of word pairs consisting of rare English words and their more commonly known synonyms. After being shown the rare word in small (12-point) or large (48-point) font, they rated how curious they were to learn its synonym, studied the synonym, and judged how likely they were to remember it at a later time before completing an immediate cued-recall test. We found that individuals exhibited greater curiosity towards large versus small items (Experiments 1a and 1b), but JOLs were unaffected by font size (Experiments 1a and 1c), perhaps due to a reliance on other perceptual cues (e.g., word structure, mental imagery) during encoding (Experiment 1c) or opportunities for pretesting attenuating the font-size JOL effect (Experiment 1d). Moreover, although large items were rated as more important to learn (Experiment 2), the positive relationship between font size and recall (Experiments 1 and 2) was only mediated by curiosity and not perceived importance (Experiment 2). Overall, our findings provide insight into how perceptual cues may influence how individuals select, process, and remember information, contributing to our understanding of how curiosity and memory are shaped by perceptual processes.

articles.title: Characterizing deaf and hard-of-hearing language experiences as arousal-regulation processes
articles.authors: Christina Kim; Laurel Aichler; Onudeah Nicolarakis; Shilpa Hanumantha Lacy; Rachel Sortino; Rachel Pizzie
articles.abstract: Empirical language research with deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) groups often includes proficiency, age of acquisition, or language background measures but excludes people’s socioemotional context. Measuring socioemotional context depends on characterizing the socioemotional experiences associated with DHH language development and use. We used the biopsychosocial model of arousal regulation as a theoretical lens to explore 11 qualitative interviews with DHH participants. articles.title: Gaze semantics: A scoping review of how gaze conveys and constrains meaning in social contexts
articles.authors: Nikol Figalová; Anne Böckler; Lynn Huestegge
articles.abstract: Humans rely on gaze to encode information and signal to others. Gaze may indicate where someone is attending, but its contribution extends beyond spatial orientation. Evidence is scattered across different research traditions. This scoping review synthesises 361 publications on gaze as a meaningful social cue. Gaze semantics describes the systematic contribution of gaze to conveying and constraining social meaning. A cross-domain synthesis identified four recurrent operations: gaze orients by making objects, people, or locations socially relevant; addresses by positioning people as recipients or interaction partners; qualifies by modifying how other cues are interpreted; and coordinates by organising participation and unfolding action. These functional contributions can co-occur within a single gaze event. Gaze interpretation is inferential, shaped by five categories of contextual factors: signal properties; interactional availability; multimodal and sequential embedding; cultural, social and activity frame; and gazer and observer states and interactional history. We propose a Gazer-Observer Model of Gaze Understanding that integrates these findings to describe the dynamic relation between gaze production and interpretation. The same gaze pattern may support different interpretations across situations yet allow a relatively specific interpretation within a particular encounter. Gaze can therefore systematically affect social interpretation while remaining semantically underdetermined to varying degrees.

articles.title: Neural Racing Accumulator Model Estimation With Lightweight Monotonic Flows
articles.authors: Malte Lüken; Stefan T. Radev; Lourens Waldorp; Andrew Heathcote
articles.abstract: Race models describe speeded decision-making as a race between competing runners that accumulate evidence in favor of available choice options. Their parameters can be estimated through the model likelihood that combines the probability and cumulative density functions of each runner. However, estimating parameters of complex race models whose runners have intractable densities with (hierarchical) Bayesian inference has been challenging: Numerical density approximations tend to be slow and amortized neural posterior estimation methods require complex network architectures that can be expensive to train and, in classical settings, tie the trained estimator to a specific prior distribution and generative model. We propose a flexible neural estimation method that decouples training from the choice of prior distribution or model parameterization. We train a small neural network together with a monotonic neural spline flow to simultaneously learn the runners' conditional probability density and cumulative density functions. We then combine both functions to efficiently estimate race model likelihoods that can be used in combination with modern samplers. We demonstrate the utility of our approach on both tractable and intractable versions of the popular racing diffusion model. Based on our results, we argue that, when flexibility in choosing prior distributions or model parameterizations is needed, learning the model likelihood with lightweight neural density estimators is advantageous.

articles.title: Weak Distributive Inference in Language Acquisition
articles.authors: David Barner; Dimitrios Skordos; Elena Pagliarini; Alan Clinton Bale
articles.abstract: We find that children compute distributive inferences, and thus that they are capable pragmatic reasoners when alternatives can be derived without lexical substitution. This provides further evidence that they are not limited by other factors like working memory or pragmatic tolerance. In addition, we find evidence that children consistently computed weak distributive inferences. In the spirit of Fox’s (2007) grammatical account, such inferences require double application of Exh, one scoping above the universal quantifier and another below. Thus, not only do children compute implicatures, but they appear to adopt the more complex parse—embedding one operator inside another—rather than relying on the simpler, global option that generates a strong distributive inference.

articles.title: Problematic Internet Use and Anxiety in Adolescents: A Scoping Review of Mechanisms and Contextual Influences
articles.authors: Cleo Albertus; Freda Scheffler; Sibeko; Dan J. Stein; Christine Lochner; Nynke A. Groenewold
articles.abstract: Problematic internet use (PIU) and anxiety are prevalent, co-occurring difficulties during adolescence, yet their shared psychological mechanisms remain insufficiently mapped. This scoping review investigated evidence on the PIU-anxiety relationship in adolescents aged 13-18 years, following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, EBSCOhost, and Web of Science were searched from January 2014 to December 2025, supplemented by hand-searching of reference lists. Ninety-six studies from 20 countries were included. Across all modalities, PIU was associated with elevated anxiety. Longitudinal studies indicated suggestive but not definitive bidirectional associations with symptoms of anxiety. Avoidance-based coping and cognitive-emotional dysregulation emerged as primary mechanism clusters, with emotion dysregulation as a central transdiagnostic process. Co-occurring internalising phenomena including depressive symptoms and loneliness were included where they provided relevant context for interpreting the association between PIU and anxiety in adolescents. Family functioning, social support, and environmental stressors moderated associations. These findings indicate that PIU and anxiety should be assessed concurrently. Interventions may benefit from targeting shared transdiagnostic mechanisms, particularly emotion dysregulation, while taking family and environmental contexts into account.

articles.title: Return-to-office (RTO) is multidimensional: Attendance level and trajectory predict different employee outcomes
articles.authors: Yingyue Luan; Yeun Joon Kim; Pengzhao Lyu; Soo Min Toh
articles.abstract: Organizations increasingly require employees to return to the office, yet evidence on the consequences of return-to-office (RTO) policies remains limited and typically treats RTO as a binary change. We propose a multidimensional perspective of RTO that distinguishes attendance-level— the proportion of time employees spend in the office over a given period—from attendance-trajectory—changes in attendance over time. Analyzing 13,956 employee-month observations from badge-swipe records for 1,163 employees whose attendance remained stable or increased at a multinational financial services organization over 12 months, we examined how these two dimensions related to ten subsequent outcomes: job performance, stress and burnout, three perceptions of organizational culture, and four forms of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and utilization. Attendance-level and attendance-trajectory showed distinct patterns of association across outcome domains. For job performance, overall attendance-level was unrelated to subsequent performance; instead, a faster increase in attendance predicted lower performance. Well-being showed the opposite pattern: higher overall and initial attendance-level predicted greater stress and burnout, while trajectory was unrelated to either outcome. Culture perceptions and AI adoption showed more complex patterns involving both dimensions, with higher or increasing attendance generally linked to more positive culture perceptions and deeper AI engagement, though the relevant dimension differed by outcome. These findings indicate that attendance-level and attendance-trajectory are not interchangeable and carry benefits in some domains while imposing costs in others. RTO policies should be designed and evaluated according to both how much and how quickly attendance increases, rather than being assumed uniformly beneficial or harmful.

articles.title: Parental ethnic-racial socialization in Europe: A scoping review
articles.authors: Ymke de Bruijn; Jana Vietze
articles.abstract: Objectives: Children in Europe grow up in societies with high ethnic-racial diversity. It is therefore imperative to understand how they learn about ethnicity and race (ethnic-racial socialization). Knowledge on parental ethnic-racial socialization, however, is very heavily based on U.S. research, and sociohistorical and -political differences limit generalizability. Therefore, the aim of the present study is to create an overview and synthesis of research on parental ethnic-racial socialization in the European context. Methods: A preregistered scoping review was conducted following the PRIMSA-ScR guidelines. Three electronic databases (PsychInfo, ERIC, Web of Science) were searched for papers published up and till 2024. After two rounds of screening, 32 out of 1431 papers were deemed eligible and included for data extraction and synthesis. Results: The findings display an overrepresentation of Northern/Western European countries, families of immigrant or minoritized backgrounds and quantitative research on adolescence. Cultural socialization by families or immigrant or minoritized backgrounds has received the most attention. Qualitative study results furthermore describe how parental ethnic-racial socialization is shaped by developmental timing, reactive and reciprocal processes, intersecting identities, and selective engagement with cultural “others. Conclusions: The findings of this scoping review underscore both the promise and current limitations of research on parental ethnic-racial socialization in Europe. To further this research agenda, we need more systematic inclusion of underrepresented populations, greater investments in qualitative and mixed-methods designs, openness to diverse and self-identified ingroup boundaries and identity meanings, and the development of conceptualizations and measures that reflect Europe’s distinctive sociohistorical trajectories, demographic diversity, and linguistic practices.

articles.title: Epistemic Stances in Humanoid Robot Evaluation: Evidence from the Frankenstein Syndrome Questionnaire and Morph-Based Perceptual Judgements
articles.authors: Ilaria Maria Antonietta Benzi; Francesca Ciardo
articles.abstract: Humanoid robots occupy an ambiguous position between social partners and artefacts, and people differ markedly in how they evaluate them. Research on individual differences in human–robot interaction has focused on personality, anthropomorphic tendencies and technology acceptance, leaving largely unexamined the processes by which people decide whether an artificial agent can be treated as a credible source of social information. The present study introduces epistemic stances, as conceptualised within the mentalizing tradition, to this literature. Seventy adults completed the Epistemic Trust, Mistrust and Credulity Questionnaire, along with measures of generalized attitudes toward robots (Frankenstein Syndrome Questionnaire, Negative Attitudes toward Robots Scale, Robotic Social Attributes Scale), and a morph-based task in which robot faces varying in human likeness were rated for likeability, eeriness and human likeness. Epistemic stances were selectively associated with generalized social evaluations: Epistemic Trust predicted higher Robot Anxiety and lower attributed Warmth, whereas Credulity predicted higher attributed Warmth, with no associations for perceived Competence. At the stimulus level, morph condition strongly shaped all three judgements, whereas epistemic stances added little. Rather than a failure to extend person-level effects, this dissociation follows from the claim that epistemic stances operate on socially communicated information rather than on perceptual appraisal. Epistemic functioning may therefore shape the social meaning attributed to artificial agents, offering a testable framework for the design of robot communication.

articles.title: An inverted U-shape association between mind health and generative AI-use frequency
articles.authors: Jerzy Bala; Tara Thiagarajan
articles.abstract: Generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude have rapidly become part of how we work and live, yet there is little systematic understanding of what they do to the human mind. Here we use a global Internet-enabled sample of 176,198 adults aged 18+, collected in 2025-2026, to examine how frequency and type of generative AI use relate to mind health. Respondents completed a 47-item assessment of emotional, social, cognitive, and physical capacities and problems, aggregated into an overall mind health score, the MHQ, alongside questions on AI use, lifestyle, and life context. Mind health rises with low to moderate GenAI use and then falls sharply with daily use, an inverted U most pronounced among adults aged 18-34. The pattern holds for both cognitive and emotional purposes, although those using GenAI for emotional support or companionship have markedly lower MHQ at every frequency, reflecting higher levels of suicidal thoughts, confused or slow thinking, hallucinations and other problems linked to psychosis. These associations are cross-sectional and cannot be considered causal, but they persist after adjustment for education, trauma, exercise, nature exposure, and sleep. As GenAI becomes part of daily life, these results suggest a downward trajectory of collective global mind health.

articles.title: Peer Transmission of Mental Health Information Increases ADHD Self-Diagnosis
articles.authors: Tanay Katiyar; George Gillett; Adam Hunt; Amanda M Ferguson; Alessia Pascale; Alberto Acerbi; Nikhil Chaudhary; Amy Orben
articles.abstract: Increased sharing of mental health information online has intensified public concern that social media may amplify mental health self-diagnosis rates. While much work has examined the types of mental health information available online, little attention is paid to the mechanisms governing how this information is created and consumed. Taking a cultural evolutionary perspective, we posit that social media facilitates peer-to-peer transmission of psychiatric information in novel formats and provides new motivations to transmit such information; this alters the information people see and their reactions to it. We investigate this through an adapted transmission chain paradigm where participants sequentially modify and transmit Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) explanations amongst each other, allowing us to examine how self-diagnostic tendencies evolve during this process. Across four studies, we find that such transmission increases participants’ tendency to diagnose themselves, and another individual with subclinical traits, with ADHD. Participants’ tendency to recommend this other individual to seek professional help also increases. Transmission format (i.e. generating an example list versus narrative summary) and motivation (i.e. making an explanation for maximising likes versus accuracy) moderate some effects. These results indicate that peer-to-peer transmission may play a key role in determining psychiatric diagnostic trends and shaping the public understanding of mental health.

articles.title: Multimodal Dynamics in Learning and Explaining Abstract and Concrete Concepts: A Triadic Interactive Task with Families
articles.authors: Chiara De Livio; Claudia Mazzuca; Francesca Bellagamba; Alessandro Gennaro; Giuliana Mazzoni; Silvia Mazzoni; Julian Zubek; Anna M. Borghi
articles.abstract: Studies have shown that learning abstract concepts (e.g., freedom compared to table) may be particularly challenging. To address concept learning, most studies use paradigms involving a single participant, such as lexical decision, match to sample, induction, and rating tasks. Here, we use an interactive task involving three family members—mother, father, and a 5-year-old child—and examine how concepts differing in abstractness are explained by the parents, either individually or together, and how the child learns and employs them. We investigate multimodal dynamics in interaction, studying gestures, movements of bodily parts, and movement coordination among interactors, in an effort to capture different embodied signatures characterizing concepts differing in abstractness. Results reveal that people gesture differently with abstract and concrete concepts, but in both cases tend to instantiate the conceptual referent, either metaphorically or iconically. Subtle differences in head movements and social touch suggest that people struggle more to understand the meanings of abstract concepts than concrete ones. Finally, with abstract concepts, coordination episodes are longer. Overall, the results provide support for the view that, with abstract concepts, people use more communicative signals and tend to converge more than with concrete concepts.

articles.title: Childhood Instability Predicts Educational Attainment
articles.authors: Andrew Caplin; Nora Harhen; Catherine A. Hartley; Ida Maria Hartmann; Søren Leth-Petersen; Johan Sæverud
articles.abstract: Educational attainment is a major determinant of health, wealth, and relationship quality, making it key for human flourishing. A diverse set of major childhood disruptions are known to predict poorer academic performance. Here we propose that childhood unpredictability constitutes a latent dimension of early-life environments underpinning these effects, suggesting everyday instability, in addition to major disruptions, should determine educational success. To test this hypothesis, we link population-wide Danish administrative records with a validated survey measure to quantify individuals' life disruptions, both major and minor. Among 2,793 respondents, greater unpredictability is associated with lower grade point averages and reduced high school completion, even after accounting for parental socioeconomic status and observed major life disruptions. Our finding that childhood unpredictability alters educational success, suggests a pathway through which disadvantage may be transmitted across generations and highlights everyday unpredictability as a potential target for interventions aimed at improving social mobility.

articles.title: The structure and degree of social connection is associated with the structure and idiosyncrasy of emotion perception
articles.authors: David Dodell-Feder; Tamar Galvin; Tara Augenstein
articles.abstract: Social connection is associated with broad aspects of social cognition. Here, we probe the nature of this association in two studies (Ns=305, 759) with college-aged samples in which we measured different aspects of social (dis)connection (e.g., loneliness) and performance on a measure of emotion perception. We find that intersubject differences in social connection mirrored intersubject differences in emotion perception, suggesting a shared fingerprint between the experience of one’s social relationships and the perception of emotion information. Further, greater levels of social disconnection were associated with greater idiosyncrasy in emotion perception, which was largely driven by task inaccuracy. This finding suggests that social disconnection may distort internal models of affective states in a way that pulls individuals from a canonical understanding of how emotions are expressed in faces. Although findings were specific to Study 2, these results provide important context to how social connection relates to emotion perception and highlights emotion perception as a potential intervention target for social disconnection.

articles.title: Using Large Language Models to Contextualize Smiling in Psychotherapy Research
articles.authors: Martin Lund Trinhammer; Stella Grasshof; Jana Volkert; Pia Rasche; Anna-Maria Weiland; Sami Sebastian Brandt; Uwe Altmann
articles.abstract:
The meaning of a smile during conversation depends on what is being
said, yet psychotherapy research has historically analyzed facial movements independently of
context. We introduce a methodology that links both partners’ smiling in a dyadic setting to
the sentiment of a speech turn (positive, neutral, negative). Using open-weight models on local
hardware only, we transcribed and diarized attachment interviews, annotated the sentiment of
the participant’s speech turns with a large language model (LLM), and analyzed individual smiling
 and smile synchrony as a function of that sentiment. We applied linear mixed models to
test for differences in smiling according to sentiment. Across 70 interviews and 1,294 speech
turns, only the interviewer’s smiling differed significantly according to the sentiment of what
the participant was saying (interviewer d = .51, q < .001; participant d = .05, q = .165); the
pair smiled simultaneously more often during positive than negative turns (d = .21, p < .001).
By conditioning smiling on what is being said — sentiment annotated from the conversation
as it unfolds rather than created by experimental instruction — our method enables the kind of
context-sensitive analysis contemporary theories call for. The pipeline is open and reproducible,
runs entirely on local hardware so that no data leave the site, and can be easily modified for any
annotation scheme or clinical setting.

articles.title: Abstract concepts map differently onto the body in humans and generative AI
articles.authors: Kyoshiro Sasaki; Yuki Yamada
articles.abstract: Abstract concepts are systematically associated with body-centered space, yet it remains unclear how they are represented across the body itself. Here, we used Body Mapping to characterize the bodily organization of four conceptual dimensions—time, length, quantity, and physical size—in humans and generative artificial intelligence (AI). In Experiment 1, human participants reported significant increases in bodily activity for “future”, “long”, “more”, and “large”, whereas no significant activation or deactivation survived correction for their conceptual opposites. “Future”, “more”, and “large” were primarily associated with the head and central torso, whereas long showed a distinct limb-centered pattern. In Experiment 2, six image-generation models were tested; five produced sufficient valid samples for the main comparison and yielded statistically reliable body maps whose organization differed markedly from the human pattern and across model families. GPT Image models showed either strongly lateralized or widespread activation patterns, whereas Nano Banana models more clearly expressed conceptual opposition through complementary activation and deactivation. These findings show that bodily organization of abstract concepts cannot be inferred directly from conventional spatial compatibility effects and that sensitivity to conceptual polarity does not imply human-like bodily organization. More broadly, Body Mapping provides a common representational framework for comparing conceptual organization across human and artificial systems, opening a route from behavioral comparison toward representation-level comparison—and potentially training—using human-derived bodily data.

articles.title: Growing Up With Conversational AI: A Developmental Framework for Adolescent Agency Over Conversational AI Use
articles.authors: shanting chen; Mary Kate Koch; Renkai Ma; Cindy Liu; Natalie C. Ebner
articles.abstract: Conversational generative AI has rapidly reached majority adoption among U.S. adolescents. These systems now provide advice, emotional support, academic assistance, simulated social interaction, and opportunities for identity exploration at a critical phase in development when mental health needs are rising and capacities for self-regulation, autonomy, and social competence are still developing. Scholars and clinicians have raised urgent questions about what these systems do to adolescents, and early findings point to both benefits and risks. In this article, we ask what adolescents do with AI and introduce the concept of adolescent agency over conversational AI use: the degree to which adolescents purposefully direct, critically evaluate, and set limits on their engagement with conversational AI. Existing constructs such as AI literacy and AI self-efficacy describe what young people know or believe about AI and the risks associated with its use, but they do not capture how adolescents exercise agency across areas of their lives. We identify nine processes that arise at the intersection of conversational AI’s features and key developmental tasks during the period of adolescence, which we label AI-ERA: autonomy, identity, emotion regulation, relationships, and achievement. We distinguish this agency from existing constructs, including agentic engagement with AI and AI overreliance, and then propose how it is shaped by adolescents’ developing capacities, adult scaffolding, and peer influence. We conclude with implications for families, schools, clinicians, and researchers, as well as considerations regarding the design, regulation, and ethics of AI systems.

articles.title: Emotional and Well-being Consequences of Discrimination and Collective Action Engagement
articles.authors: Shahrzad Goudarzi; Riana M. Brown; Ashley L Berkebile-Weinberg; Maureen A. Craig
articles.abstract: Inequality and collective struggles against it are psychologically taxing. Yet to be successful, social movements must persist through sustained action despite their toll on the participants, and many do. While the negative affective determinants of collective action, particularly outrage, are extensively studied, less is known about the accompanying positive psychological states. Using cross-sectional and experience-sampling methodologies, we find that engaging (and intending to engage) in collective action is marked by heightened subjective well-being and a range of positive feelings. Nonetheless, the positive consequences of engagement (but not mere intention) may only emerge when action is coupled with experiences of discrimination targeting outgroups (but not the self, personally, or ingroups) or in the absence of discrimination. This suggests that some psychological distance from discrimination supports the psychological benefits of collective action in grappling with inequality. Overall, this work can provide insight into a psychological mechanism contributing to sustained mobilization.

articles.title: Questions about Generative Language Models for Human Resources Decision Making
articles.authors: Dev K. Dalal; Gaurav Malhotra; Gregory Edward Cox; Adam T. Weber
articles.abstract: In this chapter, we discuss the gaps in the current understanding of how generative large language models (LLMs) make person judgments. Person judgments refer to inferences about someone's standing on a psychological construct, particularly when the judgment is made under uncertainty. We extend this concern to the application of LLMs to inform human resources (HR) decision making. We consider the ethical and legal implications of using LLMs to make person judgments to inform HR decision making. Finally, we outline a set of general research questions centered on  unstudied and understudied questions as it pertains to the use of LLMs in HR decision making.

articles.title: People With Lower Well-Being Show Longer and Less Stable Smartphone Use: A Large-Scale Analysis of 12 Datasets
articles.authors: Anna M Langener; Philip Chow; Aurelio Fernández; Nicholas C. Jacobson; Martien Kas; Anne Milek; Rüdiger Pryss; Theda Radtke; Ramona Schoedel; David de Segovia Vicente
articles.abstract: Debate over whether smartphone use relates to poorer well-being is limited by self-reports, small single-country samples, and a focus on average use. We harmonized objective app-use from 12 studies  (2,945 participants; 37,229 person-days; 851,865 person-hours) across five countries to examine associations of well-being with smartphone use and its variability. Additionally, we examined variations in smartphone use across age, gender identity, and time-of-day and day-of-week. Daily, participants averaged 3.27 hours of use (SD = 2.28), accessed 15.9 apps (SD = 6.16), and were unstable (40.6% of the total variation accounted for by within-person changes). Poorer well-being was associated with longer, more variable use; a depressive symptom increase of 10% of the scale range corresponded to 7 additional minutes of daily use and 7.5% higher within-person variance. Overall, younger persons and women used their phones more frequently, and higher wellbeing was related to consistently lower smartphone usage.

articles.title: Remembering how events unfold: Emotion and memory consolidation for naturalistic events
articles.authors: Charline Colson; Arnaud D'Argembeau
articles.abstract: Although emotional content is known to strengthen memory consolidation, its influence on how the unfolding of events is retained over time has received little attention. Building on the finding that negative events are remembered with less temporal compression and richer detail than neutral events, this study examined whether this emotional advantage changes over time, as would be expected if consolidation contributes to it. Participants viewed a series of negative and neutral videos and, either immediately or after a 24-hour or 72-hour delay, mentally replayed each event and verbally described it. Temporal compression was indexed by the ratio of video duration to replay duration, memory richness by narrative length and linguistic measures of episodic detail, and the preservation of event content by embedding-based similarity to descriptions produced during viewing. At immediate recall, negative events were replayed with less compression and described with more words and episodic detail than neutral events, replicating prior findings. After a delay, the emotional advantage in narrative length and episodic detail increased, and similarity to the video descriptions declined for neutral but not for negative events, whereas evidence for a corresponding increase in the emotion effect on temporal compression was less conclusive. These findings show that the emotional advantage in memory content for naturalistic, dynamic events is not fixed at encoding but increases over time, pointing to a role for consolidation.

articles.title: How AI chatbots shape political attitudes when they are not prompted to persuade
articles.authors: Sayeh Yousefi; Jens Koed Madsen
articles.abstract: People increasingly turn to AI chatbots to find information, including information about politicians and political issues. Given evidence that Large Language Models (LLMs) have high persuasive capacities, this has raised concerns about their potential to have undue influence on political attitudes. However, most existing research on AI persuasion explicitly prompts the LLM to persuade the user, which is not representative of how people typically engage with LLMs. Whether undirected political conversations with LLMs shift political attitudes, and whether personalisation amplifies any such effect, remains unclear. We address these questions across two studies. First, in a quota-matched survey of UK adults (N = 2,137), we find that political use of AI is already widespread and its outputs are generally perceived as being politically neutral. Second, in a pre-registered randomised controlled trial (N = 2,081), participants conversed with an LLM about either a politician or political issue, with the LLM not being prompted to persuade. We find that conversations about politicians increased favourability toward them, while conversations about policies modestly reduced support. Conversation personalisation did not amplify these effects. Our findings show that AI chatbots are already a meaningful source of political information in the UK, and that undirected chatbot conversations can influence political attitudes.

articles.title: Battling Bots and Combating Fraud in Digitally Mediated Social Science Research: A Typological Toolbox of Countermeasures
articles.authors: Bradley E. Cox; Yilun Jiang; Brett Ranon Nachman; Karly Ball Isaacson
articles.abstract: As social science researchers increasingly use online mechanisms to recruit participants and collect data, they must also defend against the growing threat of fraudulent submissions from autonomous bots and bad-faith human respondents. This paper describes such threats and outlines conditions that make some studies particularly vulnerable. It also provides explicit guidance for researchers by introducing a typology of 30 protective countermeasures designed to deter, prevent, track, and detect fraudulent responses.

articles.title: Moving beyond single-shot studies  toward cumulative research
articles.authors: Balazs Aczel; Eiko I Fried; Sabine Hoffmann
articles.abstract: In this perspective, we argue that single-design, single-analysis studies leave too much uncertainty unresolved to provide sufficiently informative answers to research questions. Such single-shot studies remain common across many disciplines, yet they reflect numerous explicit and implicit design and analytical decisions. Yet without systematically examining the consequences of these choices, researchers cannot determine the extent to which empirical findings depend on them. We contend that uncertainties arising from variability in research design and analysis are an unavoidable feature of empirical inquiry and a major source of the persistent replication problems, conflicting and seemingly irreconcilable findings, and limited cumulative knowledge observed across many fields. To address this challenge, we present a unifying framework for existing methodologies that allow researchers to systematically explore, reduce, and integrate these often-overlooked uncertainties underlying empirical claims. We argue that many of the necessary methods already exist across disciplines, but their broader impact has been limited by a lack of a shared conceptual framework and interdisciplinary integration. By balancing hypothesis testing with exploration and theory building, and by systematically incorporating Space Analysis tools into research practice, scientific fields can move beyond isolated single-shot studies toward systematic research programmes capable of producing more reliable, robust, and cumulative scientific knowledge.

articles.title: Beyond Turing Equivalence:  The Human Premium in Human–AI Interaction
articles.authors: Ophelia Deroy
articles.abstract: Asking whether we can know whether a given text or output is coming from a machine or a human, which was at the core of the Turing test, is being progressively retired. This opens a new and no less interesting question: what happens when we know? This paper reviews evidence that when humans encounter exactly the same content, presented here as coming from a human and there from an AI, they do not behave similarly. The evidence across different kinds of interaction, advice giving, compliance, reciprocal interaction, and preferential choice, is that humans respect other humans more than they respect machines. This difference is often described as a 'machine penalty' where we distrust machines or lack familiarity with them, and predicted to decrease as AI becomes more prevalent. The paper offers a different interpretation, showing that we treat humans better for good reasons, including utility calculations, and that this human premium is likely to stay.

articles.title: Rethinking a “core moral concept” in infancy: A relationship account of infants’ responses to resource distributions
articles.authors: Alex Mackiel; Amanda Woodward
articles.abstract: Infants’ responses to resource distributions are commonly interpreted as evidence of early fairness expectations and evaluations. We systematically review and meta-analyze this literature and propose an alternative, the relationship account: infants may use allocations to infer how distributors are connected to recipients and whether they are available as potential social partners. Our meta-analyses of the reviewed literature identify an overall reliable tendency for infants to look longer at unequal outcomes and preferentially engage with equal distributors. However, we argue that the current body of evidence does not uniquely establish fairness reasoning. Instead, infants’ responses may stem from preferences, expectations, and predictions grounded in reasoning about relationships. We propose that infants treat a distributor’s allocation as evidence about their relationships with recipients and use this information to assess the potential for themselves seeking relationships with the distributors. We outline experiments that could distinguish between fairness and relationship interpretations of infants’ responses and conclude by highlighting the generative potential of a relationship-focused framework for understanding infant social cognition.

articles.title: A database of subjective evaluation ratings for decision-making research
articles.authors: Kianté Fernandez; Sumedha Goyal; Ian Krajbich
articles.abstract: Subjective value ratings guide everyday choices, and value-based decision-making research collects them in many experiments. Yet the field has no common method for eliciting them. Studies use different response scales, instructions, and stimulus sets, and their ratings are rarely shared in a form that allows them to be used together. We present the Liking Initiative, a curated database of 759,399 individual ratings from 38 studies (59 datasets) covering 2,217 items, rated by 5,377 participants summed across datasets. Each rating is provided along with dataset-level metadata documenting the response scale, the question asked, and the source publication. The database is available through a web application, versioned releases on Zenodo, and R and Python packages. Because many items were rated in more than one dataset, item-level ratings can be compared across samples, response scales, and laboratories.

articles.title: AI or Human Support for Suicide Prevention?  Examining Help-Seeking Intention in Suicidal Crisis
articles.authors: Daisuke Nakamura; Hajime Sueki; Jiro Ito
articles.abstract:
This preprint has now been published in the peer-reviewed journal Suicide Policy Research. Please read and cite the published version:

Nakamura, D., Sueki, H., & Ito, J. (2026). AI or human support for suicide prevention? Examining help-seeking intention in suicidal crisis. Suicide Policy Research, 5(1), 1–12.

The published article is freely available at:
https://jscp.or.jp/assets/img/SPR_5-1_1_Nakamura.pdf


Background:
Chat-based crisis support is a common strategy for suicide prevention, and artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots have the potential to improve the low response rates to such support. Although AI chatbots are technically feasible for crisis support, it remains unclear whether individuals experiencing suicidal ideation intend to use them.

Aims:
To examine the intentions of adults with depressive symptoms experiencing suicidal ideation to use chat-based crisis support (human vs AI) and explore how these intentions relate to their background characteristics.

Methods:
A cross-sectional web-based survey was performed, recruiting participants aged 18–69 with a Kessler-6 score ≥13 from an internet research company’s database in Japan. Participants completed a questionnaire assessing their intention to use chat-based crisis support when feeling suicidal, sociodemographic factors, and suicide-related characteristics. Subsequently, participants were categorized into four groups: (1) those intending to use both human and AI-based chats, (2) AI chat only, (3) human chat only, and (4) neither. We calculated the proportions of each group and used the chi-square, Kruskal–Wallis, and Fisher’s exact tests to compare group differences.

Results:
Overall, 1,024 participants completed the survey, and we determined that 19.5% intended to use AI chat support and 21.3% intended to use human chat. The proportions of participants who intended to use both human- and AI-based chat, AI chat only, human chat only, and neither option were 15.6 %, 3.9 %, 5.7 %, and 74.8 %, respectively. Significant differences were observed in gender (p = 0.028), history of crisis support use (p <0.001), and current issues (financial problems [p = 0.002)] and sexuality-related concerns (p = 0.006) across the groups.

Conclusion:
In this web-based survey, approximately 20% of individuals with depressive symptoms feeling suicidal were willing to seek help, even if it was provided by AI.

articles.title: What Fifty Years of Research on the Misinformation Effect Can Tell Us: A Meta-Analytic Review
articles.authors: Björn Alfons Edmar; Nathalie Shekila Anna Enquist; Timothy John Luke
articles.abstract: This meta-analysis examines the impact of misleading or incorrect information on subsequent reports of witnessed events, with the aim of identifying key moderators of the misinformation effect – defined as reduced accuracy following exposure to misinformation. We synthesized experimental studies using the three-phase misinformation paradigm published between 1975 and 2025. A three-level mixed-effects meta-regression model was used to account for effect size non-independence and to examine moderators, including retention interval, warnings, overall test performance, and study characteristics. Across 480 studies and 1,998 effect sizes (N = 59,079), the average misinformation effect was substantial (g = 0.694, 95% CI [0.259, 1.128]) and highly heterogeneous (σ2 = 0.697, I2 = 92.21%). Control condition accuracy was positively associated with the magnitude of the effect, and post-misinformation warnings significantly reduced it. In contrast to prior findings, post-event testing did not significantly moderate the effect. These findings support the robustness of the misinformation effect and suggest that it reflects a combination of memory-related and strategic processes. Given the substantial heterogeneity observed, the misinformation effect may be better conceptualized as a constellation of related phenomena rather than a single unified effect, with important implications for theory and applied settings such as eyewitness testimony.

articles.title: Development and Preliminary Psychometric Validation of the Guna-Based Social Media Consumption Questionnaire: Associations with Social Networking Addiction and Nomophobia
articles.authors: Divyansh Pandey; Arnav Bhavsar; Alok Bajpai
articles.abstract:
Objective: This study aimed to develop and conduct preliminary psychometric validation of the Guna-Based Social Media Consumption Questionnaire (G-SMCQ) and examine its associations with social networking addiction (SNA) and nomophobia (NMP) using the Triguna framework from Indian psychology.
Method: Participants were 106 Indian undergraduate students (86 males, 20 females; aged 16–20 years, M = 18.05, SD = 0.72). A cross-sectional design evaluated the preliminary psychometric properties of the G-SMCQ and its relationships with the Social Networking Addiction Scale and the Nomophobia Questionnaire.
Results: MCA provided some preliminary evidence that the G-SMCQ response patterns were characterised by a multidimensional structure. Mean scores for the three Gunas indicated that Sattvic consumption was 9.86 (SD = 4.24), Rajasic consumption was 5.97 (SD = 3.66), and Tamasic consumption was 1.17 (SD = 1.75). Internal consistency reliability coefficients for the three Gunas were reported to be .840, .776, and .697, respectively. The relationship between Sattvic consumption and social networking addiction and nomophobia was negative (SNA: ρ = −.530, p < .001; NMP: ρ = −.295, p = .002), while Rajasic consumption was positively correlated to both constructs (SNA: ρ = .463, p < .001; NMP: ρ = .284, p = .003). However, Tamasic consumption was correlated to SNA (ρ = .270, p = .005) only, but not with nomophobia (ρ = .157, p = .109).
Conclusion: The results provided some preliminary psychometric evidence that suggests the potential of the G-SMCQ as a culturally-grounded measure of the Triguna-based social media consumption patterns.
Keywords: Social Media Consumption; Social Networking Addiction; Nomophobia;
