Triguna Theory; Digital behavior

articles.title: The Cultural Evolution of Analytic and Holistic Thought: How Informational Ecologies shape Bayesian Reasoning
articles.authors: Tian Chen Zeng; Ivan Kroupin; Rahul Bhui; Joseph Henrich
articles.abstract: A growing body of evidence suggests that human cognition is shaped by culture, affecting processes from attention and memory to causal inference and concept representation. Such psychological differences are often described in terms of the analytic-holistic spectrum of cognitive styles. However, a unified mechanistic account of this variation remains elusive. In this paper, drawing on concepts from computational cognitive science and cultural evolution, we propose that the analytic-holistic spectrum reflects cognitive adaptations to different information ecologies. Cultural traits such as social organization, communication norms and prevalent learning modalities determine how observations are sampled, thereby affecting how much people should weigh parsimony when building mental models. We propose that information ecologies associated with holistic thought produce observations that more loosely reflect underlying structure (``weak sampling''), whereas those associated with analytic thought produce more diagnostic observations (``strong sampling''). These regimes license weaker and stronger applications of Bayesian Occam's Razor, respectively, which we show can provide a unified mechanism for cognitive differences along the analytic-holistic spectrum. By offering a computational lens on one of the most prominent empirical patterns in cultural psychology, we pave the way toward further informational-ecological accounts of how culture shapes cognition.

articles.title: Explicit affective inferences enhance behavioral sensitivity to naturalistic expressions
articles.authors: Doron Atias; Maria Gendron
articles.abstract: Emotion theories highlight the fundamental function of emotional expressions in regulating social behavior. Yet, this basic premise relies mostly on studies using posed expressions that may fail to capture the diversity of real-life emotional signals and invite explicit affective inferences due to their salient symbolic nature. Across three studies (N=1,529), we tested how naturalistic emotional expressions differentially shape affective judgments and prosocial behavior. Participants watched videos of distressed individuals expressing typical crying, atypical crying, typical laughter, or no vocalization, and either inferred the targets’ affect (Study 1) or donated real money to help them from a provided budget (Study 2). Perceivers were sensitive to the vocal crying variation when explicitly inferring affect, but not when making donation decisions. Importantly, when perceivers explicitly inferred affect before donating (Study 3), they donated nearly 40% more and showed increased sensitivity to vocal cue variation. These findings suggest that inferring other people’s affect when making behavioral decisions is not routine and can facilitate helping behavior and the sensitivity to others’ emotional signals. This also highlight the important role of explicit inferential processes in linking real-life emotional expressions to prosocial behavior in everyday life.

articles.title: Old Test, New Tricks: Using Large Language Models to Generate New Divergent Thinking Test Items
articles.authors: Averie Elizabeth Linnell; Simone A Luchini; Austin Swanson; Roni Reiter-Palmon; Roger Beaty; Antonio Laverghetta
articles.abstract: Automated item generation (AIG) using large language models (LLMs) is emerging as a promising solution for scalable creativity assessments, yet the potential of AIG to create psychometrically rigorous creativity items has thus far received little attention. In the present study, we evaluated the psychometric properties of LLM-generated items for the classic Consequences task of divergent thinking, comparing them to human-written items. A sample of 192 undergraduates completed six Consequences tasks—two human-written, two standard LLM-generated, and two genre-inspired LLM-generated, drawing on sci-fi and fantasy themes—along with measures of personality, cognitive ability, and creative behavior. We found that LLM-generated items elicited significantly higher fluency and flexibility. Genre-inspired items (fantasy and sci-fi) additionally elicited higher originality, enjoyment, and positive valence ratings; LLM-generated items were similar to human-written items. Genre-inspired items did not unfairly advantage participants with more exposure to genre content, demonstrating measurement invariance. Together, these findings suggest that LLMs can generate consequences items with psychometric properties comparable to those of human-written items. We discuss the implications for creativity assessment, item bank development, and best practices for AIG in creativity research, and we provide the prompts we used for item generation to enable researchers to generate new Consequences items at scale.

articles.title: Shared and Divergent Multisensory Emotion Perception Deficits across Mild Cognitive Impairment, Alzheimer’s Disease, and Frontotemporal Dementia: A Systematic Review and Hierarchical Bayesian Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Yi Lin; Yangfan Lu; Enze Tang; Yang Zhang
articles.abstract: The ability to decode others’ emotions from multisensory cues is central to social functioning. However, findings remain inconsistent regarding the extent to which this capacity is compromised in neurodegenerative diseases, leaving the underlying mechanisms unclear. This study aimed to delineate the shared and divergent patterns of multisensory emotion perception (MEP) deficits among clinically distinct populations of individuals with Alzheimer’s disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and mild cognitive impairment (MCI). We conducted a systematic review on 51 studies identified from Web of Science, MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO and PsycARTICLES to synthesize research trends in this field between 2001 and 2025. We applied a hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis (1,511 patients and 1,151 healthy controls) to quantify the deficits and their moderators. Meta-analytic results demonstrated a differential magnitude of MEP impairment across groups (FTD > AD > MCI), reflecting distinct socio-emotional vulnerabilities rather than a single disease continuum. Moderator analyses of 15 participant- and study-related factors showed that impairment magnitude was more strongly associated with age, sex, education, global cognitive functioning, publication year, and emotion category, and less strongly with region, paradigm, language, and modality. Sensitivity analyses indicated that these patterns remained robust to potential publication bias, though the results were less stable within the FTD cohort. We propose a Hierarchical Socio-Emotional Disintegration and Compensation Framework to explain the dynamic interplay between neurodegeneration-driven deficits and compensatory mechanisms. This framework advances mechanistic insight into the relationship between emotion and cognition, informing future clinical efforts to support the interpersonal well-being of aging populations.

articles.title: Dynamic Semantic–Prosodic Integration in Emotional Speech Perception: From Channel Dominance to Precision-Weighted Predictive Coding
articles.authors: Yi Lin; Yang Zhang
articles.abstract: Emotional speech is an important carrier of affective information in spoken communication. Its perception depends on the joint processing of emotional semantics and prosody, yet the relative contribution of these two information sources varies across individuals and contexts. However, a unified account is still lacking of why their processing weights change and how the brain dynamically adjusts them according to the reliability of incoming information. This review synthesizes evidence on emotional semantics and prosody, from relatively independent processing to interactive integration, and argues that their relationship is best understood in terms of dynamic weight allocation. On this basis, we propose a Precision-Weighted Predictive Coding Model (PW-PC), which integrates Bayesian inference, cue precision, and prediction error within a unified framework. The model assumes that semantic and prosodic information are continuously reweighted according to current evidence and its estimated precision, while incorporating sensory reliability, experience-based expectations, contextual diagnosticity, and reweighting flexibility. This framework shifts the focus of emotional speech research from identifying which channel dominates to explaining when, why, and how the brain dynamically reallocates weight across multiple affective information sources, thereby providing a unified theoretical perspective linking behavioral performance, neural dynamics, and computational mechanisms.

articles.title: Functional Neuroanatomy of Sign Language Production: An ALE Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Lydia Wiernik; Angela D. Friederici; Karen Emmorey; Patrick C. Trettenbrein
articles.abstract: Sign languages are natural languages expressed by a distinct set of linguistic articulators: the hands, face, and body. Several neuroimaging studies of the neural substrates underlying sign production have observed the recruitment of brain regions previously identified as being involved in speech production, despite the difference in production channels. However, no prior work has provided a statistical synthesis of this available literature. Here, we report a pre-registered meta-analysis of the published positron emission tomography (PET) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) literature on sign language production (N experiments = 15, N participants = 168). Combining an Activation Likelihood Estimation (ALE) approach with jackknife re-sampling to validate the robustness of our findings, we identify four clusters consistently associated with the production of single signs across studies in the literature located in (1) left inferior frontal gyrus including BA 45 and extending into (2) left anterior insula, (3) the left superior frontal gyrus, and (4) the medial and right cerebellum. Meta-analytic connectivity modelling using data from a large-scale database of neuroimaging studies confirmed that the IFG, insula, and SFG clusters observed for sign language production are also recruited for spoken language production and comprehension. Moreover, our results also highlight the importance of the cerebellum during sign production and indicate modality-dependent convergence patterns in cerebellar subregions. In sum, our findings complement prior work on sign language comprehension and spoken language production, suggesting substantial overlap in the neural substrates of language processing and production-related mechanisms between sign and spoken language.

articles.title: How should fillers be selected for lineups? Comparing the match-to-description and match-to-suspect methods via a systematic review and meta-analysis
articles.authors: Courtlyn Elkins; Myat Aung; Edwin James Burns; Ruth Horry
articles.abstract: Lineups should contain known-innocent individuals (fillers) who resemble the suspect. Two common filler selection methods are: the match-to-suspect method, where fillers are selected based on perceived similarity to the suspect; and the match-to-description method, where fillers are selected based on how closely they match the culprit description. This systematic review sought to examine how the match-to-description method has been implemented since it was first proposed and revealed the match-to-description method has been operationalised in various ways. Meta-analytic techniques were used to investigate how filler selection method impacts lineup outcomes. Results revealed the odds of making a suspect identification, both guilty and innocent suspect, are higher in lineups created using the match-to-description method than the match-to-suspect method. Results also revealed lineup construction method did not impact discriminability. However, the small number of studies directly comparing the methods limits our ability to draw conclusions. Thus, highlighting the need for high-powered, pre-registered research.

articles.title: Repetition increases belief more for trivia statements than news headlines
articles.authors: Raunak M Pillai; Steven Yang; Qiwenjing Jiang; Lisa Fazio
articles.abstract: Repetition increases belief in true and false statements. This “illusory truth effect,” has been documented across dozens of experiments using materials ranging from trivia statements to claims about consumer products to political news. Further, current theories of the effect focus on low-level psychological cues like processing fluency that arise spontaneously and that should affect judgements of truth uniformly for all such types of statements. In contrast to this picture, we find that the size of the illusory truth effect varies for different types of statements, with larger effects occurring when people see banal trivia statements as opposed to political or viral, health-related news headlines. We report six studies (total N = 1,749 US MTurkers) demonstrating this effect or testing potential explanations. We find that these differences appear to be driven by the overall context of the type of statements participants encounter rather than features of each individual statement. These findings speak to the malleable nature of the link between repetition and belief, with repetition being more a more impactful contributor to beliefs in contexts where people are saying some kinds of statements (e.g., trivia statements) than others (e.g., political or health-related news).

articles.title: Making Sense of Sensory Differences: Identifying Sensory Processing Phenotypes and Their Relationship to Social and Executive Functioning in Neurotypical Children.
articles.authors: Adrianna M Molenaar; Natalia Van Esch; Nichole Scheerer
articles.abstract: Sensory processing varies substantially across individuals, yet research on distinct sensory phenotypes has focused primarily on neurodivergent populations. We examined whether comparable sensory phenotypes could be identified in 200 children aged 4-12 years with no known neurodevelopmental or psychiatric diagnoses, and whether phenotype membership was associated with executive functioning, social competence, mental health, alexithymia, and neurodivergent traits. K-means clustering of parent-reported sensory processing identified four sensory phenotypes: Sensory Adaptive, Generalized Sensory Differences, Under-responsive/Filtering Differences, and Sensory Sensitive. Children in the Sensory Adaptive group showed fewer executive functioning difficulties than children in all other groups and higher social competence than those in the Generalized Sensory Differences and Sensory Sensitive groups. In contrast, phenotypes did not differ significantly in autistic or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder traits, alexithymia, anxiety, or depression. These findings demonstrate substantial heterogeneity in sensory processing among children without diagnosed conditions and suggest that sensory phenotypes may be meaningfully related to everyday cognitive and social functioning. Future transdiagnostic work should directly examine the extent to which these phenotypes are shared across neurotypical and neurodivergent children.

articles.title: No evidence of phonosymbolic effects in Polish echoic reduplications with sr-
articles.authors: Antonio Benítez-Burraco; Mingshan Xu; Monika Lisowska
articles.abstract: Expressives (i.e. linguistic items used for conveying emotions) can be phonosymbolic in nature or culturally-motivated. In Polish, echoic reduplicated sequences with the formant sr- are frequently used to convey contempt. We conducted an online survey to determine whether sr- is universally associated with this emotion. We tested speakers of Polish, but also of 2 other Indo-European languages (English and Spanish), and 3 non-Indo-European languages (Hungarian, Turkish and Indonesian). Findings suggest that only Polish speakers associate sr- with contempt, but less than expected. This suggests that this association does not result from any phonosymbolic effect or is typical of Indo-European languages generally. But is confined instead to Polish language, seemingly because sr- is the onset of one derogatory term in this language (srać). Still, the effect is stronger when concerning real words compared to pseudowords.

articles.title: Real-Time Associations Between Emotional Responses to Social Media and Mood Differ By Adolescent: Implications For Risk and Resilience
articles.authors: Melissa J Dreier; Jennifer Susan Silk; Evan Kleiman; Jessica L. Hamilton
articles.abstract: Adolescents differ in their vulnerability to social media’s mental health effects. Some may experience stronger links between emotional reactions to social media (ERSM) and mood, increasing risk for subsequent mental health problems. In the current study, 131 adolescents (ages 14–17) completed baseline assessments and eight weeks of ecological momentary assessment (3x/day). A dynamic structural equation model tested group-level and person-specific relationships between negative ERSM and depressed mood, controlling for prior mood. Adolescents showed substantial heterogeneity in ERSM-mood relationships. Stronger coupling was associated with baseline depression, anxiety, suicidal thoughts, and nonsuicidal self-injury, but not suicide attempts. Throughout the study, stronger coupling was associated with higher depressed mood, suicidal thoughts, and mood volatility. It was not associated with the frequency or intensity of negative ERSM or in-person experiences or emotion regulation strategies. Taken together, adolescents whose mood is more strongly tied to ERSM may be at heightened risk for mental health problems.

articles.title: What beliefs are most debunkable?
articles.authors: Esther Boissin; Thomas H Costello; David Gertler Rand; Gordon Pennycook
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can persuade people to revise their beliefs, but it is unclear which beliefs are most "debunkable," and why. Across three pooled studies, participants (N = 3,341 online U.S. adults) discussed a self-reported conspiracy or other epistemically suspect belief with GPT-4, instructed to debunk it using facts and evidence. An LLM classified each belief by content domain (i.e., conspiratorial, paranormal/supernatural, pseudoscience, political, religious, other) and evidential status, from strong counterevidence to supported by evidence. Confidence decreased in every domain, but belief updating tracked evidential status rather than domain: reductions were substantial wherever the belief was open to counterevidence — strong, weak, or uninvestigated — and small for non-falsifiable and supported beliefs. Domain no longer predicted change once evidential status was accounted for, and the counterevidence the LLM deployed partially mediated the gradient. AI debunking appears most effective for falsifiable beliefs resting on weak evidence.

articles.title: Comparing the efficacy of virtual reality and flat screen delivery of breath control training for anxiety management
articles.authors: Grace Yat Sum Leung; Naresh Subramaniam; Benjamin Cook; Lucie Daniel-Watanabe; Johanna Finnemann; Toby Woolley; Craig Powell; Sergey Sitnikov; Paul Fletcher
articles.abstract: Game-based biofeedback offers a promising approach for learning and practising breath control techniques to manage anxiety and stress. Traditionally known as a response-modulation emotion regulation strategy, biofeedback operates through a closed-loop system that measures and feeds back real-time physiological information for users to monitor and subsequently manage their bodily responses. Few studies, however, have directly compared breath control training integrated with game-based biofeedback across two-dimensional flat screen display and three-dimensional immersive environment. It remains unclear whether differences in realism and immersiveness might influence the efficacy of breath control training. The present study investigated training effectiveness and user evaluation of a novel biofeedback-based breath control game among forty-five healthy adolescents. The breath control training was delivered in both virtual reality (VR) and flat screen modalities in a randomised and counterbalanced order using a within-subject study design. Consistent with hypotheses, the biofeedback game significantly improved both subjective and physiological (standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals (SDNN) and heart rate) markers of anxiety. While the two modalities indicated comparable intervention efficacy, the VR biofeedback game contributed added benefits in increasing SDNN, a physiological indicator of stress that reflects overall autonomic nervous system activity, as well as facilitating greater levels of interest and enjoyment, as indicated by ratings of intrinsic motivation to engage in the self-regulation training. These findings suggest that VR-based breath control training may enhance engagement and specific physiological responses, with implications for the design, development and evaluation of VR games for improving anxiety and stress.

articles.title: Redundancy Protects Human Collaborations from Failure
articles.authors: Elizabeth Mieczkowski; Rachit Dubey; Natalia Vélez; Thomas L. Griffiths
articles.abstract: In the name of efficiency, organizations and governments around the world are increasingly trimming redundancy---personnel or overlapping capabilities beyond what routine operations require. Drawing on distributed computing and cognitive science, we challenge this view. Using queueing simulations and a preregistered multiplayer experiment (N = 832 in 187 teams of 3–6), we show that redundancy improves performance through two distinct routes. Adding collaborators to a team improves resilience, with larger teams completing more tasks when members became temporarily unable to contribute. Giving team members overlapping capabilities also improved efficiency, with teams in which collaborators could perform multiple roles completing substantially more work. These findings suggest that efforts to improve short-term efficiency by reducing redundancy may come at a cost, quietly eroding a team’s capacity to withstand unexpected failures.

articles.title: Nonverbal Cognition is Associated with Discourse Production in Persons with Aphasia: Evidence from Expository and Picture Description Tasks
articles.authors: Hana Kim; Manaswita Dutta
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Spoken discourse analysis has gained empirical and clinical attention, yet current practice predominantly relies on picture-based tasks which may not fully capture the language impairments experienced by persons with aphasia (PWA) in more complex contexts. Expository discourse, though more cognitively demanding and structurally complex, remains under-researched in aphasia despite its ecological relevance. This study aimed to (1) compare nonverbal cognitive abilities in PWA and neurologically healthy adults (NHA); (2) examine the effects of discourse task by comparing expository and picture description performance in PWA; and (3) investigate associations between nonverbal cognitive abilities and discourse outcomes. 
Method: Participants (PWA = 24; NHA = 13) completed nonverbal cognitive tasks that assess processing speed, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility. They also completed expository discourse tasks (expressing opinions on the healthcare system and homeschooling). Discourse samples were analyzed using six variables (MATTR, Percent CIU, Verbs per utterance, syntactic complexity, local and global coherence) selected to represent linguistic, propositional, and macrostructural domains in discourse.
Results: Significant group differences were found in cognitive flexibility task accuracy, and response times on tasks measuring cognitive flexibility and processing speed. In expository discourse, PWA performed worse than NHA across the linguistic, propositional, and macrostructural domains. Notably, task comparisons revealed that expository discourse elicited greater performance in syntactic complexity but poorer coherence than the picture description task in PWA. Cognitive influences on discourse differed by tasks and groups: in PWA, cognitive flexibility generally showed strong associations with all discourse domains across both tasks, with fewer correlations for the picture description task. Also, the pattern of associations varied across cognitive tasks and discourse measures for the picture description task. No significant associations were observed among controls. 
Conclusion: Findings highlight the unique interplay between cognitive and linguistic skills in the expository task. This finding supports the potential use of expository discourse in aphasia assessment.

articles.title: Comprehenders’ Error Correction Mechanisms are Finely Calibrated to Language Production Statistics
articles.authors: Peng Qian; Roger Philip Levy
articles.abstract: An essential feature of human communication is robustness to errors: even when speakers and writers make mistakes, listeners and readers can usually determine the intended meaning. A leading hypothesis is that comprehenders achieve robust error correction by internally deploying a "noisy-channel" model of the language production process. Crucially, to best achieve error robustness, a comprehender's noisy-channel model should be finely calibrated to the environmental statistics of language production, incorporating not only prior expectations about communicative intents but also structure-sensitive likelihoods of different types of speaker error. This environmentally-calibrated noisy-channel hypothesis has been difficult to test, because the rates of most types of language production errors are hard to estimate. Here we test this hypothesis by experimentally investigating comprehenders' interpretations of subject-verb agreement errors, for which context-contingent language production error rates are feasible to estimate. In a novel free-form error correction task,  participants edited sentences with subject-verb agreement mismatches to indicate what they think was intended. Bayesian analysis of the resulting data shows that comprehenders' interpretations reflect both item-specific prior expectations and structure-sensitive error likelihoods that closely correspond to error rates in language production. These results provide quantitative evidence that humans closely track prior statistics over linguistic forms and deploy a noisy-channel model finely calibrated to statistics of the linguistic environment to achieve robust language understanding.

articles.title: What is it like for matter to matter?
articles.authors: David Vandenheever
articles.abstract: Consciousness research often asks where, when, or under what conditions neural processing becomes conscious. Here I introduce the Distributed Architecture of Valenced Evaluation (DAVE), which starts from a different premise. Nervous systems continuously represent states in terms of what those states imply for the organism, and these evaluations are physically instantiated in dispositions that bias bodily, attentional, predictive, and action systems. DAVE proposes that, where such organism-relative evaluation is embedded in the embodied dynamics through which a represented state can alter the organism, its evaluative character is already minimally phenomenal. Each such evaluative event constitutes a micro-quale: not a miniature conscious subject or an independently experienced percept, but a local phenomenal contribution to the experience of the organism. Recurrent interaction among many micro-qualia forms the richly differentiated, context-sensitive, and apparently unified phenomenal tapestry familiar in human experience. Attention, task demands, working memory, and self-representation selectively amplify, stabilize, and organize parts of this tapestry, producing increasingly integrated, accessible, and self-related forms of experience. Because introspection presents the integrated tapestry rather than its constituent evaluative events, phenomenal character may appear to be an additional property beyond the physical organization that constitutes it. This conception of phenomenal character makes the explanatory gap seem inevitable. DAVE does not solve the hard problem by discovering a mechanism that converts nonphenomenal processing into phenomenality; it attempts to dissolve the need for such a conversion by identifying minimal phenomenal character with organism-relative evaluative disposition itself.

articles.title: Green Against the Machine: Natural Environment Exposure Attenuates Subjective and Physiological Responses to Technostress Across Levels of Agency
articles.authors: Simone Di Plinio; Claudia Greco; David Perpetuini; Massimo De Acetis; Miriam D'Ignazio; Arcangelo Merla; Daniela Cardone; Sjoerd Ebisch
articles.abstract: Urban living often limits routine contact with nature, while digital technologies have become deeply embedded in everyday life and cognition. Yet technological malfunctions, intrusions, and diminished user agency can elicit technostress, raising the question of whether exposure to natural environments can buffer its effects. This study examined whether exposure to a natural (green) environment, compared with a built urban (gray) environment, attenuates psychophysiological responses to technostress. Fifty-two healthy adults were assigned to either a green (garden-like) or gray (built urban) environment. Before and after two outdoor walking sessions in the assigned environment, participants completed a word-selection task manipulating technology-induced stress and sense of agency. High-resolution infrared thermal imaging was used as a contact-free method to monitor facial temperature dynamics, providing indirect indices of peripheral autonomic regulation during task performance, while heart rate variability (HRV) was monitored as an index of cardiac autonomic activity during task performance. High technostress reduced task accuracy and increased perceived stress. Under the condition combining high technostress and reduced agency, perceived stress decreased following green, but not gray, exposure. Facial thermal responses, particularly in the nose-tip and perioral regions, also differed between the green and gray groups under stressful task conditions, indicating that environmental exposure modulated peripheral physiological responses associated with technostress. No effects were observed for HRV. After gray, but not green, environmental exposure, an increase in self-report agency measures under high technostress was accompanied by an increase in perioral temperature, indicating a relationship between subjective experience and peripheral activation. These findings suggest that even brief exposures to natural green environments may reduce vulnerability to technostress by attenuating subjective stress and modulating peripheral physiological responses. The results contribute to the growing literature on restorative environments, human–technology interaction, and psychophysiological resilience.

articles.title: Eye Movements Reflect Listening Effort and Visualizable Speech
articles.authors: Geneva Mariotti; Bjorn Herrmann; Jennifer D. Ryan
articles.abstract: Eye movements can index the recruitment of cognitive resources. During listening, increased effort is associated with reduced eye movements. However, eye movements also support mental imagery, suggesting that reduced eye movements during effortful listening may reflect the difficulty of creating mental images to support speech comprehension. Here, we examined how speech content and listening difficulty interact to shape eye movements during listening and later recall. Young adults listened to, and subsequently recalled, descriptions for which rich, visual details were (i.e., concrete descriptions) or were not (i.e., abstract described) spoken in different levels of background noise (easy vs hard) while eye movements were recorded. During listening, fixation rate, saccade amplitude, and gaze dispersion decreased under difficult listening conditions and for concrete descriptions. Gaze dispersion timecourses tracked spatial-relational words, but not other relational content, in concrete descriptions. During recall, eye movements were lower for concrete descriptions, particularly when encoded under hard listening conditions. Notably, gaze dispersion peaked before the recall of spatial-relational details, especially in participants with higher recall accuracy. Together, these findings suggest that listening effort shapes eye movements, while visualizable speech content elicits distinct patterns in which eye movements may be co-opted to represent imagined space and support memory accuracy.

articles.title: Temporal associations between short-form video use and affective dynamics: A 14-day ecological momentary assessment among Chinese university students
articles.authors: Yu Gu; Wen Zheng; Johannes Thrul
articles.abstract: Short-form video use is associated with poor emotional well-being, yet its short-term temporal relationship with affect in daily life remains unclear. We conducted a 14-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA) study to examine bidirectional associations between reported short-form video use (SV) and affective states, seperate within-person fluctuations from between-person differences, and assess whether the daily SV use rate was associated with affective inertia and innovation variability. A total of 134 Chinese university students contributed 17,514 valid EMA responses, yielding 14,899 complete same-day lag-1 transitions. Using Bayesian dynamic structural equation modeling, we identified several associations at the momentary timescale: 1) SV use during the preceding survey interval was associated with lower positive affect at the subsequent assessment; 2) SV use and above-zero negative affect intensity were positively associated in both directions, whereas no credible association was observed between SV use and the all-zero negative affect state. At the daily timescale: 1) Daily SV use rate was not associated with mean levels of either positive or negative affect; 2) Higher daily SV use was associated with weaker inertia in both positive affect and above-zero negative affect, as well as lower innovation variability in positive affect. In conclusion, our findings highlight the dynamic associations between SV use and affect across multiple timescales. These findings motivate further research using objective use logs and designs capable of supporting causal inference.

articles.title: Mere co-presence and evaluative observation differentially shape motor response execution and inhibition: Behavioral, signal-detection, and ERP evidence
articles.authors: Cuihong Liu; Guoliang Chen; Yi Wei; Yansong Li
articles.abstract: This study examined how mere co-presence and evaluative observation shape motor response execution and inhibition in a Go/NoGo (GNG) task. In Experiment 1, 199 participants were randomly assigned to mere co-presence, evaluative observation, or control. Mere co-presence slowed Go responses and reduced self-reported concentration relative to both other groups without affecting Go accuracy or the NoGo commission error rate relative to control. Only in this group was slower responding associated with greater perceptual sensitivity (d′), suggesting compensatory slowing. By contrast, evaluative observation reduced the NoGo commission error rate and increased d′ relative to both other groups without affecting Go performance relative to control. Experiment 2 used a within-subject event-related potential (ERP) design (N = 44) and replicated the lower NoGo commission error rate and higher d′ under evaluative observation without affecting Go performance. Additionally, evaluative observation produced evaluation-related affective costs—increased evaluative pressure and anxiety—that predicted smaller d′ gains and attenuated its benefit in mediation analyses. Eletrophysiologically, evaluative observation attenuated NoGo-N2 and NoGo-P3 amplitudes without affecting Go components, suggesting that enhanced Go–NoGo discrimination facilitated inhibition by reducing early conflict-monitoring and later reactive-control demands. These findings suggest two dissociable pathways through which distinct forms of social presence shapes motor control.

articles.title: Parsing structured semantic knowledge from arbitrary text with GenAI
articles.authors: A.T. Lopes Rego; Joshua Snell; Martijn Meeter
articles.abstract: Frame Semantics offers a compelling framework for representing meaning as structured conceptual scenarios (frames). FrameNet operationalizes this theory as a lexical resource linking words to frames and their conceptual roles (frame elements, FEs). However, applying Frame Semantics to arbitrary text has historically required either laborious manual annotation or complex, task-specific classification pipelines that presuppose known targets and/or frames. Here we present an open-source method that leverages Generative AI (GenAI) to automatically parse semantic frames and their FEs from any input text, without requiring pre-specification of frames or target spans, or task-specific model training. The tool combines a retrieval step, in which candidate frames are identified via embedding-based semantic similarity, with a selection step, in which a Large Language Model (LLM) is prompted, using zero- or few-shot examples, to determine which frames are evoked, which spans trigger them, and which spans fill their FEs, returning a structured, machine-readable output. We detail installation, execution, and output interpretation, and provide a built-in evaluation module supporting exact, semantic, and graph-based matching against FrameNet's human-annotated data. This freely available tool lowers the barrier to frame-semantic analysis for researchers across linguistics, who wish to explore structured semantic content in naturalistic text, including in relation to behavioral and neural measures of language comprehension.

articles.title: Repurposing, redefining, and reimagining: A paradigm shift towards person-driven neuroscience in the digital age
articles.authors: Becky Inkster; Mark Sheppard
articles.abstract: The focus of neuroscience has traditionally hinged on collecting quantifiable physiological data that are often distanced from the lived experiences of people. In contrast, qualitative, subjective, and situational information provides rich context, but lacks the empirical precision needed to map to neural processes. To reconcile this gap, we established ‘The Lαβ’ as an interdisciplinary initiative that fuses person-driven experiences, personal reflection, and empirical neuroscience. People engage with their chosen experiences in their chosen settings while wearing a portable EEG headset. Timestamped information is then collected from a variety of sources. We introduce our novel neurotriangulation approach: A person‑driven synthesis of quantitative electrophysiological signals, qualitative observations, and subjective and situational information into a single analytic stream. Our aim is to provide people with opportunities for neuro-self-reflection. We use an ethics-first approach to preserve data sovereignty, privacy, autonomy, and agency for the individual. In this paper, we present real-world case studies to demonstrate our data collection, real-time field analysis, and co-interpretation methodologies. These case studies also underscore the neurotriangulation model as an approach to move beyond reductive, data-centric models toward a person‑driven paradigm. This shift allows neurodata to be more accessible, inclusive, and personally meaningful, while prioritising safety and subjectivity. This has the potential to reshape how we think about neuroscientific applications in fields such as education and training, anthropology, creative arts, wellbeing, and mental health. By repurposing and redefining the use of extant neurotechnology, we are reimagining a future in which our understanding of ourselves is person-driven, reality-based, and ethically sound.

articles.title: Art Therapy for Recovery from Childhood Trauma in a Vietnamese Adolescent: A Case Study
articles.authors: THANH TU NGUYEN
articles.abstract: Childhood trauma is associated with self-injury and suicidal behaviour, yet traumatised young people often cannot put their experiences into words, particularly where family hierarchies limit emotional disclosure between children and parents, as in Vietnam. This case study describes a 17-year-old Vietnamese girl ("Lily") who presented with severe non-suicidal self-injury and previously undisclosed suicide attempts rooted in childhood adversity. She received a 12-session, three-phase intervention comprising House-Tree-Person (HTP) art therapy, prosocial community action and structured family sessions. Session records, journal entries, field notes and parent interviews were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, and pre- and post-intervention drawings using compositional and iconographic visual analysis. Three themes were generated: art as a bridge to concealed trauma; consolidation of gains through prosocial agency; and relational repair within the family. The final drawing was interpreted as reflecting psychological integration and post-traumatic growth. Art therapy, supported by family engagement, the young person's active cooperation and a compassionate therapeutic relationship, may offer a culturally responsive pathway to recovery. Findings from a single, clinician-interpreted case without long-term follow-up are illustrative and require further study.

articles.title: Short-term Cultural Evolution in Response to COVID-19:  Integrating Quantitative Analysis with AI-Assisted Thematic Analysis
articles.authors: Aiya Wang; Patricia M. Greenfield
articles.abstract: Using Greenfield’s Theory of Social Change, Cultural Evolution, and Human Development as a framework, we examine psychological, cultural, and behavioral shifts in China during the first 70 days of COVID-19. We focus on three levels—mortality salience at the psychological level, collectivism at the cultural level, and subsistence activities at behavioral level. Our big-data sample consists of over 200,000 social media posts. Quantitatively, we found a significant increase in mentions of mortality salience, collectivism, and subsistence activities, consistent with prior results established in the U.S., Mexico, Indonesia, and Japan, suggesting a universal response to existential threat. Qualitatively, AI-assisted thematic analysis, an innovation of the present study, identified the most frequent recurring themes across three levels, which complemented the quantitative analysis by providing in-depth insight into the COVID experience. A methodological strength was to compare expert human coder to AI coding, establishing both the reliability and validity of AI coding.

articles.title: Embodied mirroring increases interpersonal synchrony of movement and positive experience in subsequent conversations
articles.authors: Yasemin Abra; Christine Falter-Wagner; Irene Sophia Plank
articles.abstract: Interpersonal synchrony, the alignment of behaviours between individuals, plays a key role in social interactions. The degree of synchrony depends on many factors, including interaction partners, context, and goals. Brief playful warm‑ups may prime synchrony and improve subsequent conversations between strangers. We used the Mirror Game, a fundamental exercise from theatre where two players nonverbally imitate each other’s movements, to examine whether instructed interpersonal synchrony of movement would carry over to spontaneous interpersonal synchrony. We used recordings of facial expressions, gaze patterns, movement, and speech to capture multi-modal conversational behaviour. In line with our preregistered hypothesis, dyads who played the Mirror Game before conversing exhibited greater interpersonal synchrony of movement than those who performed a non-social movement exercise. Furthermore, playing the Mirror Game prior to the conversation also increased positive social experience and rapport. Exploratory analyses also revealed that conversational behaviour capturing interpersonal adaptation of the individual predicted social experience in the conversation. While these effects may not be specific to the Mirror Game, we argue that the embodied, collaborative and improvising nature of the Mirror Game make it a promising tool for fostering positive social interactions. These findings may inform interventions for populations with reduced interpersonal synchrony, such as individuals with autism.

articles.title: From “Person = Me” to “Person = Man,” New Evidence from Eastern Matrilineal and Patriarchal Societies
articles.authors: Jialin Zhou; Xi Cheng; Yinyin Zang; April Hope Bailey; Yin Wang
articles.abstract: How do people imagine a generic “person”? Who comes to mind by default shapes downstream decisions, with harmful consequences when one gender stands in for everyone. Existing work finds that people often imagine a “person” as a man more than a woman. However, prior research is limited almost exclusively to Western adults, leaving the origins and development of these representations unknown. We examined two novel cultures with very different gender structures. In the unique and hard-to-reach matrilineal Mosuo society, both men and women showed a stable tendency to imagine a “person” as someone of their own gender. In a mainstream Chinese sample, boys and men imagined a “person” as a man, whereas for girls and women representations shifted across age groups and increasingly towards a male default. These results show that male defaults are not a given: Initial own-gender biases are reshaped to a male-generic model through culturally-specific factors.

articles.title: Decomposing attentional differences between willingness-to-pay and choice: Evidence from gaze and computational modeling
articles.authors: Yiming Wang; Anderson K. Fitch; Konstantina Sokratous; Peter D. Kvam
articles.abstract: Different preference-elicitation formats can induce different attentional patterns and yield conflicting apparent preference orders for the same options; a classic example is preference reversals between choice and willingness-to-pay (WTP) judgments. Reversals may be attributed to multiple different attentional features between choice and WTP, including initial attentional orientation, sustained attentional allocation, information search patterns, and information integration structures. To identify the mechanisms that underlie reversals, we combined experimental and computational modeling approaches to examine responses, response times, and gaze from participants who evaluated matched risky and/or delayed payoffs (prospects) through WTP and Choice. In WTP, payoff was more likely to be viewed first and most overall, and gaze transitions were organized around payoff, whereas Choice showed more variable first gaze orientation and attribute-wise transitions across prospects. Preference reversals were associated with a larger WTP-relative increase in payoff-directed gaze proportion (sustained attention) but not in the probability of payoff taking the first gaze (initial attention), indicating that anchoring may not be solely responsible for reversals. To connect these overt attentional patterns to latent decision processes, we extended the attention-guided evidence accumulation framework to continuous valuation and fit parallel WTP and Choice models with distinct information integration architectures. The fitted models’ generative predictions suggested that differential overall attribute weighting be not necessary for reversals to emerge, given model-specific information integration architectures. Behavioral data indicate a correspondence between reversals and greater overt attention (gaze) to payoff in WTP relative to choice, but model-based findings favor architectural differences between elicitation procedures—particularly, attribute-wise comparison in choice versus alternative-wise integration in WTP—as the most plausible explanation for reversals.

articles.title: Delegating Knowledge: Belief in AI Sufficiency and its Consequences for How People Process Information
articles.authors: Sangwon Lee; Sebastián Valenzuela
articles.abstract: Generative AI produces information on demand, raising the question of why one would ever learn something that a chatbot can always retrieve. In this paper, we introduce Belief in AI Sufficiency (BAS): the belief that acquiring and retaining knowledge is less valuable because AI can provide it when needed. BAS represents a qualitatively distinct conceptual domain from the Google effect, cognitive offloading, and the “News Finds Me” perception. Using four preregistered studies in the United States (development, N = 307; validation, N = 903; experiment, N = 767; test-retest, N = 298), we present evidence for a 12-item BAS measure with a strong general factor structure. In the validation survey, higher BAS was associated with greater reliance on heuristic and less systematic processing, and with reduced factual knowledge. In the experiment, BAS strongly predicted the likelihood to delegate a learning task to AI. The relationship between BAS and the gap between self-reported and measured knowledge was smaller, reflecting reduced accuracy rather than an illusion of knowledge. Finally, BAS scores were approximately equal in mean level and showed moderate rank-order stability across a 3-month period. BAS is one way to measure how far AI is becoming central to the study of how people learn.

articles.title: Fact-Checking Using AI
articles.authors: Thomas Renault; Mohsen Mosleh; Hause Lin; Gordon Pennycook; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can both correct inaccurate beliefs (1, 2, 3) and manipulate attitudes (4, 5, 6). As LLMs are increasingly deployed as fact-checkers on social media, their impact depends not only on the models’ technical capability, but also on the choices of their designers and the attitudes and behaviors of platform users. Here, we shed light on all three dimensions of this sociotechnical system. We analyze an exhaustive sample of 1,555,281 English-language fact-check requests sent to Grok and Perplexity bots on X from February through September 2025 and a random sample of 184,124 fact-checks from Grok from September 2025 to August 2026. We also benchmark 19 frontier LLMs against professional fact-checkers’ evaluations of hundreds of news headlines, and conduct a preregistered survey experiment (N=1,592) to evaluate correction efficacy. On the user side, Grok requesters skew heavily Republican; familiarity with and trust in specific LLMs vary substantially, such that trust in AI is no longer a unitary construct; and revealing that a fact-check comes from Grok reduces belief updating among Democrats while increasing belief updating among Republicans. Examining LLM outputs, we find that from a technical perspective, LLM fact-checks can match or exceed agreement among professional fact-checkers. Yet we also show that this capacity is readily undermined by designers’ choices: for example, restricting sources (e.g. Truth Social AI) or disabling search can degrade accuracy. Designers and users, more so than technical capability, are now the primary binding constraints.

articles.title: Mesmer’s error: Beliefs reverse the rubber hand illusion (a Registered Report)
articles.authors: Peter Lush; Zoltan Dienes
articles.abstract: In the rubber hand illusion (RHI), participants report ownership of a fake hand which is stroked in synchrony with their own concealed hand, with lower ownership ratings for asynchronous stroking. This effect has been historically attributed to multisensory integration. However, such a pattern of results is consistent with experimental demand characteristics, and an alternative theory proposes that the RHI is an effect of phenomenological control (the trait ability to change experience to satisfy goals). To date, support for a phenomenological control theory of the RHI has been limited to correlational evidence. Here we conduct a pre-registered causal test of the relative contribution of these two proposed mechanisms in RHI effects. 25 high phenomenological control participants (top 15%) were tested in an RHI procedure and the classic effects of greater response for synchrony than asynchrony were replicated. The procedure was then repeated following imaginative suggestions for a reversal of the classic effect (i.e. greater synchrony than asynchrony effects). Ratings of ownership and proprioceptive drift were modulated by suggestion. Effects for ownership and drift were reversed. Exploratory analysis showed the same pattern of results for referred touch ratings. Participant beliefs arising from demand characteristics dominated over multisensory mechanisms in RHI ownership of a fake hand and proprioceptive drift. Multisensory synchrony was not necessary to produce the classic effects, falsifying the theory that the illusion requires multisensory integration. Claims of an illusion beyond that attributable to demand characteristics and phenomenological control require experimental evidence from controlled experiments.

articles.title: The Dual-Level Dynamics of Moral Incongruence:  A Multilevel Analysis of Problematic Pornography Use
articles.authors: Joshua B. Grubbs; Christopher Floyd; Kristiana Carrasquillo; Shane Winfield Kraus
articles.abstract: Research regarding Compulsive Sexual Behavior Disorder (CSBD) has expanded rapidly, yet controversy remains concerning the role of moral evaluations in shaping perceptions of behavioral addiction. This study evaluated the longitudinal relationships between moral disapproval of pornography, pornography use frequency, and problematic pornography use (PPU) at both between-person and within-person levels. Data were collected over five waves (two years) from a large community sample of American adults (N = 4,363); analyses were restricted to those who contributed at least one active-use wave (N = 7,512 person-waves from 2,903 individuals). Using a Multi-Level Modeling approach, results at the between-person level indicated that moral disapproval was negatively associated with use frequency but positively associated with PPU, and that the interaction of disapproval and frequency was a significant predictor of PPU. At the within person level, we did not find evidence for a purely within-person effect of moral incongruence (e.g., state pornography viewing frequency and disapproval did not interact to predict PPU), but we did find clear evidence for a cross-level interaction.  Trait moral disapproval interacts with within-person, within-timepoint deviations in pornography use frequency to predict greater levels of PPU. Collectively, these findings suggest that while moral disapproval may serve as a population-level barrier to pornography use, it functions as a specific risk factor for self-reported feelings of addiction among individuals who use pornography, particularly during periods when they experience relatively higher levels of use. Our results also underscore that behavioral frequency is an insufficient metric for assessing sexual dysregulation and must be interpreted within the context of an individual’s moral evaluations. Clinically, these findings emphasize the necessity of diagnostic precision to differentiate moral incongruence from genuine behavioral dysregulation in the assessment and treatment of CSBD and PPU.

articles.title: The Moral Mechanism of Norms and Political Polarization
articles.authors: Julie Maria Ejby Pedersen; Adam Moore
articles.abstract: Political polarization continues to divide people across the world, threatening the safety of individuals and of democracy. We propose a theoretical account of the emergence and maintenance of political polarization as a social identity phenomenon, driven by moral values as an ingroup norm representation. Norms play a crucial role in intergroup processes as a representation, both supporting signaling and inference of ingroup membership, and approximating a shared concept of the group that needs to be inferred and updated itself. Yet, little work on political polarization has addressed the role of norms, despite a large literature on its social identity mechanisms. Here, we argue that moral values are highly suitable as an ingroup norm representation and implement this as a formalized computational account of echo chamber formation. In this model, we also account for the cyclical interaction between these social identity pressures on moral values and moral cognitive processes such as moral disengagement and moral drift. When simulating this model under different conditions (Study 1 and 2), we find systematic differences in how liberals and conservatives form groups, corresponding to empirical investigations of interactions with people and news online. We discuss how the resulting polarization emerges as an interaction between the structure of liberal and conservative moral values, observed in empirical data, and their role as an ingroup norm representation. Finally, we consider how this moral mechanism of political polarization influences how we study political polarization, and we posit that liberals and conservatives may have different pathways to political polarization.

articles.title: Communication Profiles in School-Age Children with Congenital Blindness: A Matched Comparison Study
articles.authors: Tremaine Love; Allison Gladfelter; Lindsay N. Harris; Rebecca Treiman
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Previous research on communication development in school-age children with visual impairment identified structural language as an area of relative strength and pragmatic language as an area of relative weakness. However, these studies included children who had some visual experience and predated the COVID-19 pandemic and pervasive child screen use, both of which affected communication development in sighted children. The present study examined whether past communication patterns in congenitally blind children are evident today by assessing all five domains of language using caregiver report and spontaneous conversation.

Method: A cross-sectional matched case-control design was used. Ten children with total congenital blindness, ages 5–14 years, were individually matched with 10 sighted children. The Children’s Communication Checklist–Second Edition (CCC-2) assessed communication skills in everyday contexts, and conversational language samples elicited during an online research session were assessed using Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts (SALT).

Results: Children with congenital blindness had lower overall CCC-2 communication scores than sighted peers, with differences concentrated in Initiation, Scripted Language, and Nonverbal Communication, all aspects of pragmatic language. The remaining CCC-2 subscales did not reliably differ between groups. No significant group differences during conversation were identified using the standard measures in SALT.

Conclusions: The pattern reported in earlier research was partially evident. Structural language was comparable between groups, while caregiver reports identified differences in pragmatic communication that were not observed during spontaneous conversation. Thus, strengths and weaknesses across the five language domains differed by assessment method.

articles.title: Cognitive-Affective Factors Associated with Psychological Distress in Young Adults: A Cross-Sectional Structural Equation Modelling Study
articles.authors: Rose Seneviratne; Matt Garner; Emma Claire Palmer-Cooper
articles.abstract:
Objectives: To examine concurrent associations among cognitive-affective factors associated with psychological distress in young adults. 
Methods: Cross-sectional structural equation modelling was conducted in a community sample of 841 young adults aged 18 to 30 years. Psychological distress was specified as a latent factor indicated by depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), anxious symptoms (GAD-7), and perceived stress (PSS-10). Mindfulness facets (FFMQ), metacognition (MSAS-18), resilience (ER89), and creativity (RDCA) were entered into two models with alternative structural orderings. Model fit was evaluated using the CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR, AIC, and BIC.
Results: Model 1 showed acceptable-to-good fit (CFI = .98, TLI = .94, RMSEA = .07, SRMR = .03) and better comparative fit than Model 2 (CFI = .97, TLI = .90, RMSEA = .09, SRMR = .06). Model 1 statistically accounted for 53.9% of the variance in latent psychological distress. Acting with awareness (β = -.29), nonjudging (β = -.39), and nonreactivity (β = -.20) showed unique negative associations with distress, whereas observing showed a small positive association (β = .08). Resilience showed a direct negative association and negative indirect associations in configurations involving acting with awareness, nonjudging, and nonreactivity. Metacognition showed negative indirect associations involving acting with awareness and nonreactivity. Creativity showed a bivalent pattern: a positive indirect association involving observing and a negative indirect association involving nonreactivity.
Conclusions: Acting with awareness, nonjudging, and nonreactivity showed the clearest unique associations with lower psychological distress in young adults. These findings identify candidate self-regulatory capacities for prospective testing in preventive and therapeutic intervention research.

articles.title: “It’s not that I don’t have a life, it’s that I choose to have many”: A Qualitative Exploration of Video Gamers’ Perceived Motivations for Gaming and their Impact on Psychological Health.
articles.authors: George Farmer; Tom Buchanan; Nina Smyth; Tina Cartwright
articles.abstract: While several factors have been highlighted as either facilitators or inhibitors of basic psychological needs in video gaming, there is little evidence to identify the specific mechanisms by which these effects operate. Using qualitative semi-structured online interviews with 15 video game players (MAge = 38.28, SD = 12.65) and analysed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis, this study explored experiences in video games and gaming culture that provided either a source of need satisfaction or need frustration. Participants discussed experiences that provided a sense of competence, mood management, social connection, and positive disengagement, as well as experiences that could be unfair, unpleasant, toxic, or generally stress-inducing. This study highlights specific factors that promote positive well-being and contribute to negative well-being in players and illustrates less-explored experiential factors that are vital to video gaming as a psychologically restorative activity.

articles.title: The Language of Trauma: A Comparative Analysis Using Natural Language Processing and Traditional Text Analysis Methods
articles.authors: Giuliano Groer; Laurin Plank; Armin Zlomuzica
articles.abstract:
Post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is associated with alterations in the recall of
autobiographical memories (AMs) regarding the traumatic event, but methodology of studies investigating traumatic and non-traumatic narratives in the context of PTSD vary. There is little consensus regarding the linguistic differences between different narrative 
valences and the influence of PTSD-symptomatology outside of clinical populations. We collected 450 narratives regarding traumatic, negative non-traumatic and neutral AMs of 150 healthy participants and their post-traumatic stress measured by the PTSD checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5). For a comprehensive analysis of differences in linguistic patterns, we examined syntactic, lexical, semantic, and discourse-level features of the narratives. Compared to neutral narratives, traumatic narratives were linguistically richer, more PTSD-congruent in semantic content, less coherent, and were subjectively experienced as more emotionally intense and vivid. Trauma and negative narratives were largely similar in their linguistic and structural features, with differences confined to word count, death-related language, coherence, and semantic alignment with hyperarousal and intrusion symptom domains. Post-traumatic stress did not moderate any of the association between narrative categories and linguistic features, but higher PCL-5 scores predicted use of death-related words and how temporarily close participants felt to the traumatic event.
Although future research should replicate these findings in clinical comparison samples, the present study provides a comprehensive attempt to characterize the language of trauma narratives.

articles.title: The Association Between Family-Related Variables and Cross-Cultural Adaptation: A Meta-Analytical Review and Migrant Family Adaptation Framework
articles.authors: Kinga Bierwiaczonek; Aisha Vogel; Dinh-Hung Vu; Colleen Ward; Rongtian Tong; Mike W.-L. Cheung; Nora C. G. Benningstad; Evita Willemiek van Duin; Karine Lindholm; Jonas R. Kunst
articles.abstract: With global migration at an all-time high, understanding the role of family-related factors in cross-cultural adaptation is crucial yet underexplored. This paper proposes a new Migrant Family Adaptation Framework and reports a meta-analysis of the association between a large set of family-related variables and cross-cultural adaptation with data from 449 studies (Nparticipants = 308,335; neffects = 1,174) conducted between 1988 and 2022. Specifically, we tested nine broad categories of family-related variables underpinning key processes of family resilience (family cross-cultural adjustment, family functioning, lack of family-work conflict, family support, contact with family, presence of family, relationship status, family characteristics, and family attitudes towards living abroad) and three adaptation outcomes (overall, psychological, socio-cultural). Three-level models showed that family cross-cultural adjustment was the strongest and most consistent predictor of migrants’ overall, psychological, and socio-cultural adaptation. In terms of more nuanced sub-indicators, family satisfaction, spousal support, low family conflict, and positive family attitudes towards living abroad showed robust effects. Effects were comparable across migrant, refugee, student, and expatriate samples, except that the effect of family support was stronger for expatriates than migrants, whereas family presence mattered more for migrants than expatriates. Comprehensive sensitivity checks (excluding studies at risk of bias, unpublished reports, and statistical outliers) left the pattern and magnitude of effects virtually unchanged. No evidence of small-study or publication bias was observed. Theoretical implications in light of the new theoretical framework, directions for future research, and policy implications are discussed.

articles.title: Fifteen Years of Child-Centered Long-Form Recordings: Promises, Resources, and Remaining Challenges to Validity
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Loann Peurey; Marvin Lavechin; Tarek Kunze; Manel Khentout; Lucas Gautheron; Emmanuel Dupoux; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract: Audio-recordings collected with a child-worn device are a fundamental tool in child language research. Long-form recordings collected over whole days promise to capture children’s input and production with minimal observer bias, and therefore high validity. The sheer volume of resulting data necessitates automated analysis to extract relevant metrics for researchers and clinicians. This paper summarizes collective knowledge on this technique, providing entry points to existing resources. We also highlight various sources of error that threaten the accuracy of automated annotations and the interpretation of resulting metrics. To address this, we propose potential troubleshooting metrics to help users assess data quality. While a fully automated quality control system is not feasible, we outline practical strategies for researchers to improve data collection and contextualize their analyses.

articles.title: Do we hear and read the same? Attention to detail in narrative storytelling while reading and listening with reduced distraction
articles.authors: David Berga; Benan Demir; Anita Dieckhoff; Monica Moreno-Dionis
articles.abstract: Most research agrees that reading and listening are equally efficient. But research on multimedia learning searched for modality specific processes that could improve learning efficiency, this is relevant considering the current panorama and worldwide usage of intelligent text-based agents. Our brief study compares the audio-verbal channel with the visual-verbal channel, facilitating exact wording identification after a reading or a listening task. We focus on comparing reading and listening overall performance, but also category specific performance by modality. Twenty-six native Spanish speakers read one text and listened to another one. Each text had five instances of each word category (color, feeling, object and person) and there were 3 questions per category. Each question framed 3 possible answers and the participants had to recognize which one was correct. We tested if the correct answers were recognized and whether abstract or concrete concepts or specific word categories affected encoding. We minimized distraction for both modalities and standardized the word rate, to avoid text backtracking. Results have shown that for non-demanding material, there isn't a significant difference in regard to input modality. Both reading and listening modalities are not effectively different, and processing of category-specific wording is not either.

articles.title: TAIL: A Test of AI Literacy for Adolescents and Teachers
articles.authors: Tomas Lintner; Ivan Ropovik; Lukas Plch; Adam Klocek; Libor Juhaňák
articles.abstract: Most instruments that claim to measure AI literacy inquire how competent people feel rather than test what they know, and almost none has been validated for both students and teachers. We developed the Test of AI Literacy (TAIL), a multiple-choice test of AI literacy built on an established four-aspect framework and piloted with cognitive interviews and item analysis. We evaluated it among Czech secondary-school students tested in fall 2025 (n = 2,441) and six months later (n = 1,669; 897 linked across the two measurement waves), and among teachers (n = 564). In every sample the items fitted a one-factor model, whereas the four content aspects could not be distinguished as separate factors. Three weakly discriminating items were removed after the first wave, leaving a 17-item form with internal consistency of .79 to .87 and item response theory reliability of .80 to .84. Item parameters were almost identical across waves. Six-month test-retest reliability was .63, with a standard error of measurement of 2.4 points. Teachers scored .41 standard deviations above students, and teachers of information and communication technologies, grammar-school teachers, and students with a university-educated parent scored higher, as predicted. Teachers' self-rated AI self-efficacy was practically unrelated to their tested knowledge, and students who used and relied on AI more knew less about it. TAIL is a short, knowledge-based measure that places adolescents and their teachers on one scale.

articles.title: The Perception and Metacognition of Time Within and Between Stimulus Modalities
articles.authors: Aris Yiu; Daniel R. Little; Simon James Cropper
articles.abstract: Time perception depends not only on judging duration but also on evaluating how accurate that judgement was. Our previous work compared visual, auditory, and audiovisual intervals separately and observed a modality asymmetry at short durations. The present study examined whether pairing them within a trial reproduces this pattern, and whether order matters. Eleven participants completed a modified temporal bisection task, bisecting two consecutive intervals then choosing the more accurate. Intervals were both audiovisual (AV), auditory followed by visual (A+V), or visual followed by auditory (V+A), tested at 1500 and 3000 msec. The AV condition ran twice, showing no reliable repetition difference. The modality asymmetry did not reappear once the two modalities were directly paired. Neither Modality nor Duration reliably affected the metacognitively-selected estimate. However, this stability did not extend to metacognitive accuracy, indexed by our Metacognitive Index (MCI), which was higher for V+A at the shorter duration, though only anecdotally (BF10 = 1.43). A hierarchical Bayesian model tracked the observed data closely, with individual consistency explaining much of the between-participant variability. In summary, perceiving a duration and judging one’s own performance may not be the same computation, with the latter more sensitive to modality-induced distortion.

articles.title: ­­­Neural markers of implicit metric processing in 6-to-10-year-old children
articles.authors: Katerina Drakoulaki; Mara Breen
articles.abstract: Introduction. Auditory processing is guided by exogenous and endogenous processes: neural responses adapt to hierarchically organized structures and task-specific conditions across development. Here, we investigated the endogenous selective attention mechanisms influencing subjective metric tracking of an isochronous sequence of identical tones in children 6-10-years-old. Methods. We adapted an adult imagined meter paradigm to map the developmental neural trajectories of implicit metric coding. High-density electroencephalography data were recorded from 112 children listening to undifferentiated tones grouped subjectively into quaternary or ternary meters in fast (450ms SOA) and slow (625 SOA) tempi. We predicted that mature metric encoding would manifest as adult-like N1 and late metric negativity (LMN) amplitudes to metrically strong beats. Results. Across four age cohorts, we replicated established findings on cortical auditory evoked potential morphological development. Behavioral accuracy on the task reflected more mature neural responses to imagined strong beats. High-scorers reliably showed negative responses in the N1 and LMN time windows for strong beats across hierarchies. Low scorers showed positive responses in the N1 and LMN time windows for strong beats, similar to other selective attention paradigms in this age range. Discussion. Metric tracking was modulated by tempo and meter: we suggest that fast tempo facilitated tracking by aligning with children's faster endogenous temporal preferences, while slower tracking was more difficult; similarly, tracking ternary meter was more challenging than quaternary, likely due to familiarity.

articles.title: Sex and gender differences in functional and participation experiences of students with developmental coordination disorder in higher education
articles.authors: Clare Copley; Kimberly Petersen; Madeleine Pownall; Lucy H Eddy
articles.abstract:
Background: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) is a common neurodevelopmental condition characterised by persistent motor coordination difficulties that negatively impacts daily functioning and participation across the lifespan. Despite a high prevalence (5-6%), DCD remains under recognised in adulthood, creating particular challenges in contexts requiring high levels of independent participation, such as higher education. Sex and gender are also important to examine, given their potential to influence the recognition, presentation and lived experience of DCD. However, there is a notable lack of research exploring how sex and gender identity may impact these experiences. 
Aims: This exploratory study aimed to investigate whether functional challenges and participation experiences differed according to sex and gender identity among higher education students with DCD.
Methods: Data were collected via an online self-report questionnaire completed by 77 higher education students with DCD/dyspraxia across the UK and Ireland.
Results: Findings indicate high levels of functional difficulty and participation restriction across the sample, with fatigue often reported as a consequence. Females with DCD were significantly more likely than males to report challenges related to gross motor skills (p<.05, d=.60) and executive function skills (p<.05, d =.60). Participants who identified as a gender minority reported a higher incidence of difficulty with fine motor skills (p<.05, d=–.63) and executive function (p<.05, d =–.60) compared to cisgender participants. 
Conclusions: Findings indicate that students with DCD experience persistent functional challenges that restrict participation in higher education.  Experiences and support needs may also differ based on sex and gender identity.

articles.title: Her Canvas, Her City: Gender, Gaze, and Empowerment in Art Engagement Among Women Artists and Viewers in Pune, India
articles.authors: Sakina Bharmal; Samrddhee Pathare; Tanvi Raghuram; Esha Phadke; Prafull Botre; Nishkala Reddy; Tithi Roy; Madhura Deshmukh; Sanjana Edwankar; Raju Sutar
articles.abstract: Feminist visual theory holds that the devaluation of women’s art is reproduced not only by institutions but by how people look. We report a preregistered, mixed-methods study in Pune, India, connecting women artists’ lived experience with viewers’ perceptual responses. In an online experiment, 49 viewers (30 women, 18 men, 1 non-binary person) rated 12 artworks (7 by women, 5 by men) without knowing the artist’s gender, on liking, objectification, empowerment, immersion, and emotion. Neither artist gender nor viewer gender significantly predicted objectification, empowerment, or liking, although descriptive trends favoured works by women. Art experience was the most consistent predictor of engagement. Viewers who reported immersed rather than detached enjoyment perceived depicted subjects as more empowered (p < .001), consistent with feminist critiques of disinterested spectatorship. Exploratory analyses showed that closer alignment between artists’ stated intentions and viewers’ interpretations predicted transcendence-related responses, resonating with the rasa concept of the attuned viewer (sahṛdaya). Thematic analysis of interviews with 37 women artists showed that becoming, remaining, and being recognised as an artist depends on unequally distributed access, the continual negotiation of gendered expectations, and audiences and markets that confer legitimacy unevenly. Implications for feminist psychology, empirical aesthetics, and arts practice are discussed.

articles.title: When You See Is Not Always When You Move: Preview Availability Influences Movement Control and Visual Search in Human Multi-Target Foraging
articles.authors: Danilo A. Kuhn; Jan Tünnermann; Anna Schubö
articles.abstract: In real-world tasks, such as picking berries from a bush or assembling a LEGO® set, actors frequently search for multiple targets while also planning and executing movements. We investigated how a preview, that is, the availability of visual information during trial instructions, influenced target selection behavior. We hypothesized that preview availability would improve movement planning and execution compared to no preview.
