Participants were asked to pick LEGO® bricks of a specific color and place them into predefined areas, with the placing precision varying between trials (collect, sort, pile). We assumed that higher precision requirements would delay movement onset, especially without a preview. Interestingly, results showed a consistent impact of preview availability only for those participants who first performed the task without a preview: These participants initiated their movements faster without a preview but also reached less directly and took longer to complete a trial, suggesting greater reliance on feed-back control rather than feedforward planning. Overall, participants preferred selecting a large, more easily graspable target first when a preview was available, indicating that preview availability aided target selection. Finally, the longest delay in movement onset was observed in the pile condition regardless of preview availability. This suggests that participants considered placing precision requirements already when preparing a search-and-place sequence. In sum, we found no evidence for a general benefit of preview availability for movement preparation or execution in a real-world selection task. Instead, preview benefits emerged mainly when a preview followed prior experience without one.

articles.title: Joint (versus individual) task representations are activated spontaneously and preferentially: evidence from switch cost asymmetry
articles.authors: Shaheed Azaad; Kassandra Friebe; Günther Knoblich; Natalie Sebanz
articles.abstract: We routinely face the decision to act either alone or with another person. Research has found that humans exhibit a joint action preference, choosing to coordinate even when it is unnecessary and inefficient. Here, we tested one mechanism that might contribute to this preference: that joint task representations are activated spontaneously and preferentially to individual task representations. To this end, we conducted a secondary (meta)analysis of seven experiments (total N = 288) in which dyads completed a stimulus-response task requiring switching between individual and joint responses. Switch-cost asymmetry between the two trial types revealed that joint task representations were represented preferentially to individual task representations. This held even though participants did not coordinate intentionally, responding together only incidentally when a stimulus cued responses from both. In other words, the task was represented jointly and preferentially activated, spontaneously. Our results add to a body of joint action research indicating that a suite of spontaneous perceptual and cognitive processes automatically prepare us to coordinate with others.

articles.title: Embodied Copresence Confers No Advantage Over Screen-Based Delivery in Robot-Facilitated Language Learning
articles.authors: Nathan Caruana; Aitor Miguel Blanco; Emily S. Cross
articles.abstract: The past decade has seen growing interest in deploying social robots as assistive technologies in educational settings. Key unresolved questions concern the extent to which, and possibly when, the embodied copresence of a robot confers benefits over screen-based alternatives. This is an issue with applied significance given the logistical and cost constraints of deploying physical robots at scale. In a preregistered between-subjects experiment, 40 adults completed a Spanish language learning task alongside a Pepper humanoid robot that was either physically co-located next to participants (Embodied, n = 20) or presented via live video feed on a large screen next to participants (Screen, n = 20). Contrary to our predictions, conditions did not differ on any objective measure of task engagement (accuracy, completion time, voluntary continuation), self-report indices (enjoyment, difficulty), attention allocation to the robot or task (subjectively coded gaze orientation), or validated measures of robot perception and affiliation (Godspeed questionnaire; Self-in-Other scale), with the exception of greater perceived task difficulty and robot awareness in the Embodied than Screen condition. Reflexive thematic analysis of post-task interviews identified three cross-condition themes: robot learning companions (1) create experiences of invigilation; (2) are expected to fulfil multiple social roles (motivational coach, tutor, and companion); and (3) are expected to interact in a human-like, intelligent, and adaptive manner. These findings suggest that, for adult learners engaged in short-duration tasks, such as the simple language-learning task explored here, screen-based delivery may be functionally equivalent to physical co-presence, with implications for the scalable deployment of social robots in educational contexts.

articles.title: Liberal paternalism: Weak-victim narratives facilitate the disempowering treatment of refugees and low-income individuals
articles.authors: Christina Bauer; Steve Rathje; Gregory M Walton
articles.abstract: Refugees, low-income individuals, and other groups that are systemically disadvantaged often show substantial strength and agency, including in contending with the adversity they face. Yet, media, politicians, and other stakeholders sometimes portray these individuals as weak and passive victims. In eight studies (Ntotal=226 newspaper articles & 1,895 participants in the UK, US, & Australia) focused primarily on refugees (Studies 1-4), and secondarily on low-income individuals (Studies 5a-b), we show that i) weak-victim narratives are common in both media portrayals and mental representations, especially in liberal (vs. conservative) media and minds (Studies 1-2c & 5a), and ii) that weak-victim narratives facilitate functionally disempowering behaviors among liberals (Studies 3, 4, & 5b).

articles.title: Adolescent anxiety and gaming: a case study of stability loops
articles.authors: Tiina Auranen; Roope Holopainen; Veli-Matti Karhulahti
articles.abstract:
This research presents two longitudinal case studies of intensively gaming adolescents who 
express clinically significant anxiety symptoms in the Finnish cultural context. By means of 
Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis, two shared themes were constructed based on in-depth 
qualitative data from both participants: self-reinforcing loop between interpersonal problems and 
gaming, and self-reinforcing loop between lacking affordances and gaming. Collectively, the themes 
point at a developmental mechanism that we call stability loops: anxiety-gaming interactions that 
minimise changes over time in socioecological systems. These exploratory findings highlight how 
individual experiences of circumstances create potentially different loop trajectories, which can both 
complicate and support age-relevant development depending on the social context. As such, the study 
offers an alternative to diagnostic gaming frameworks by modelling the activity as a part of 
psychological development in a world where technology is rapidly evolving and ubiquitous.

articles.title: From what they hear to what they say: The distribution of word classes in the output of young English-speaking children and their caregivers
articles.authors: Antje Endesfelder Quick; Karsten Schmidtke-Bode
articles.abstract: Usage-based approaches propose that children assimilate the statistical regularities of their input. While prior studies have documented such input–output correlations for specific constructions, more systemic properties like word-class distributions have received less attention. The present study examines twelve English-speaking children aged two to three from the Manchester Corpus, comparing their part-of-speech (POS) distributions with their mothers' at three time points. Maternal distributions remain highly stable; children's speech is initially noun-heavy but approaches maternal patterns by age 2;9. These findings suggest that, even at more abstract levels of grammatical organization, children's developing grammars reflect the distributional properties of their input.

articles.title: Metacognitive Ownership in Human–AI Regulation: Construct Definition, Boundaries, and a Research Agenda
articles.authors: Michael Pin-Chuan Lin; Daniel H. Chang
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools can suggest criteria, evaluate learners’ work, and recommend or carry out revisions, yet it is often unclear how learners direct these decisions when they study with AI. In this conceptual paper, we introduce metacognitive ownership: learners’ governance of standards, evaluative judgments, and actions within a learning episode in which AI or another external source contributes to at least one of these functions. Here, governance refers to how learners direct the use of that contribution. Drawing on self-regulated learning, human–AI regulation, agency, and evaluative judgment, we define three components: standards appropriation, monitoring-judgment governance, and control authorization. These components address the criterion a learner uses, how the learner reaches an evaluation, and what guides the next action. Control authorization also requires a realistic opportunity to act differently. A hypothetical example illustrates how a learner can evaluate AI advice and reach an incorrect conclusion, or accept correct advice without examining it. After distinguishing metacognitive ownership from related constructs, we set out four principles for interpreting evidence about each component. We then offer two tentative propositions about later advice decisions and continued learner regulation when support is reduced. The research agenda asks whether these interpretations are reproducible, add to existing explanations, and withstand evidence that challenges them. The framework provides a basis for examining learner-governed assistance; its relationships with learning require empirical evaluation.

articles.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Psychotherapy: Understanding How Therapy Supports Brain-Based Change
articles.authors: Marc L. Copersino; Jamie Berry
articles.abstract: Psychotherapy can be conceptualized as a structured, experience-dependent process of learning supported by neuroplasticity. Although psychotherapies differ in theory, technique, and therapeutic entry points, they may engage overlapping functional domains of therapeutic learning and change. This chapter presents a transdiagnostic, domain-based framework in which neuroplasticity provides the biological capacity for change and learning serves as the overarching therapeutic process. Five interacting domains organize the framework: emotion regulation and threat learning; cognitive control and belief updating; memory updating and integration; motivation, reinforcement, and habit learning; and social and relational learning and co-regulation. These domains are conceptual organizers rather than discrete mechanisms common to all psychotherapies. Repeated and emotionally meaningful experiences may support changes in expectations, emotional responses, memories, behavior, self-understanding, and interpersonal functioning. The framework also provides a practical structure for neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE). Connecting therapeutic activities with accessible explanations of relevant neuroscience may clarify the treatment rationale, reduce self-blame, support engagement, and foster realistic expectations about change. Consistent with a biopsychosocial perspective, the framework integrates neurobiological processes with meaning, agency, relationships, and environmental context rather than treating them as competing explanations. Domain-based NIPE may help bridge neuroscience and psychotherapy, although its effects on treatment engagement, therapeutic alliance, persistence, and clinical outcomes require empirical evaluation.

articles.title: Rethinking empathy in the age of AI
articles.authors: Joshua D Wenger; Daryl Cameron; Madeline G. Reinecke
articles.abstract: People increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) for empathic support, often reporting feelings of being cared for and supported. Longstanding models of empathy, however, center the empathizer’s embodied emotional experience, which AI fundamentally lacks. This tension between human experience and traditional researcher-imposed empathy definitions raises important scientific questions as to what it truly means for AI to “empathize.” In the present paper, we propose an alternative definition and approach to studying empathy which eases this tension, emphasizing the multiple dissociable functions that empathy serves within various relational schemas. Taking a functional-relational approach redefines the study of empathy by centering practical meta-scientific concerns (e.g., surrounding the exploration of empathy within study contexts, foregrounding lived experience). In doing so, we seek to future-proof empathy as a construct, ensuring that our science remains relevant, generalizable across time, and responsive to lived human experience as technology advances and new forms of relationships emerge.

articles.title: Assessing Parent and Youth Perceptions of Attachment:  Validation of the Adolescent Attachment Anxiety and Avoidance Inventory (AAAAI)
articles.authors: Jason W. Payne; Sebastian Dys; Sherene Balanji; Marlene Moretti
articles.abstract:
Objective: Attachment is a robust protective factor for youth mental health. This study examined the factor structure and validity of the Adolescent Attachment Anxiety and Avoidance Inventory (AAAAI), a 16-item measure of youth (8–18 years) attachment in parent and other caregiving relationships. Structural validity was assessed using parallel youth and parent report formats among over 2,000 respondents from both clinical and community samples.
Method: Participants were caregivers in three independent clinical samples and one community sample (N = 571, 407, 220, and 551) and youth self-reporting in the first clinical sample (N = 571). Youth were 7.5 to 18 years old (sample means 13.4 to 14.6), 51% to 61% female, and 61% to 78% White. Caregivers were predominantly mothers (80% to 96%). Confirmatory factor analyses were followed by multi- informant models and tests of associations with caregiver-reported internalizing and externalizing problems.
Results: A two-factor structure replicated across all samples under a single specification, whereas a one- factor model fit poorly. Differential associations with youth internalizing and externalizing problems supported the discriminant validity of each subscale. Multi-method analyses confirmed that anxiety and avoidance were distinguishable across informants, while moderate parent-youth convergence suggested complementary rather than interchangeable perspectives.
Conclusions: The findings support the AAAAI as a measure of attachment anxiety and avoidance in both parent and youth report. For research and clinical practice, the two subscales capture distinct attachment patterns, and parent and youth forms together show where caregivers and youth see the relationship similarly and where they differ.

articles.title: Individual differences in eye movements dynamics of free viewing conscious and unconscious naturalistic scenes
articles.authors: Shaked Lublinsky; Yoni Pertzov lab; Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg; Liad Mudrik
articles.abstract: Different individuals produce different gaze patterns while exploring the world. Here we examined whether these differences occur also when viewing a scene unconsciously. We reanalyzed the data collected in Lublinsky et al., 2025, looking for two types of individual differences; content-based individual differences, which depend on the visual stimulus presented, and content-free individual differences, which do not relate to the observed stimuli. In two experiments, 52 participants viewed scenes consciously and unconsciously, rendered invisible via Continuous Flash Suppression (CFS). We found reliable content-based individual differences in the conscious condition only, suggesting that unconscious processing of scenes does not evoke consistent patterns within individuals. On the other hand, we found consistent content-free individual differences in both visibility conditions. In the unconscious condition, these most likely reflect consistent gazing patterns on the CFS stimulation (i.e., the changing color patches). Yet these content-free measures showed differential strength for seen vs. unseen trials, thereby validating participants' subjective reports. These findings provides novel means to support a dissociation between conscious and unconscious processing under CFS, which is notoriously difficult due to methodological challenges.

articles.title: Orthography Shapes L2 Stress PerceptionAcross Development: Evidence from L1 Mandarin Learners of Portuguese
articles.authors: Chao Zhou; Guilherme D. Garcia
articles.abstract: Despite growing evidence that written input shapes second-language speech learning, its role in suprasegmental acquisition remains underexplored. This study examines whether orthography facilitates lexical stress identification through syllable weight. Portuguese is well suited for this question because stress placement is strongly conditioned by syllable weight, which is transparently encoded in the writing system. A total of 186 L1 Mandarin speakers identified stress location in Portuguese pseudowords presented either auditorily or with accompanying written forms. Naïve listeners used syllable weight as a stress cue only when orthographic information was available, whereas experienced learners showed weight sensitivity from auditory input alone. For experienced learners, however, orthography did not further enhance weight sensitivity; instead, it biased responses toward the default penultimate- stress pattern. These findings suggest that orthographic effects change over L2 development, interacting with auditory cue weighting and distributional regularities in L2 stress perception.

articles.title: Is it Difficult to be a People Pleaser? An Item Response-Theoretical Examination of the People Pleasing Scale
articles.authors: Christian Blötner; Johanna Werner
articles.abstract: The phenomenon of people-pleasing—meaning the tendency to sacrifice one’s own needs and obligations to help others—has gained a lot of interest in lay psychology. Only recently have scientific endeavors been devoted to the development and validation of suitable measurement tools such as the People Pleasing Scale (Blötner, 2026; https://doi.org/10.1007/s12144-026-09519-2). The measure provides desirable psychometric properties from the perspective of Classical Test Theory, but in this framework, several statistical assumptions about item and scale characteristics remain untested. To address this gap, we subjected the People Pleasing Scale to item response-theoretical examinations as per the polytomous graded response model (N = 2,538). Its three subscales (Responsibility, Neglect of Own Needs, and Others’ Expectations) provided favorable item discrimination, widely dispersed item thresholds (even though the thresholds to obtain high scores were located at best at moderate levels), and ample levels of item information and reliability across the three latent trait spectra. These findings underscore that people-pleasing, as measured with the People Pleasing Scale, refers to an everyday rather than a clinical construct. As such, it is apt to be used to assess people-pleasing in studies across diverse areas of academic psychology and for applied contexts alike.

articles.title: Gender Differences in Self-reported Emotional Sharing in Social Interaction: A Meta Analysis
articles.authors: X. Jia; Karen Holtmaat; Y. Mo; ZIHAO Zeng; M. Kaneva; Annet Kleiboer; Sander L. Koole
articles.abstract: Through emotional sharing, individuals can make their emotional experiences available to others, creating opportunities for interpersonal emotion regulation. Although gender differences in these behaviours have been documented across various domains, findings regarding their magnitude and consistency remain inconclusive. This meta-analysis examined gender differences in emotional sharing among adults. A systematic search identified 32 articles comprising 37 independent samples, 155 effect sizes, and 13,147 participants, including 8,504 women and 4,643 men. Overall, women reported higher levels of emotional sharing than men, g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.18, 0.44]. This effect was not significantly moderated by (1) functions (emotional expression, emotional disclosure, emotional expression as coping), (2) temporal level (dispositional, situational), (3) emotional valence (negative, positive or unspecified), (4) specific negative emotion (anger, sadness, fear/anxiety, shame/guilt, and unspecified negative emotions), and (5) the interpersonal target (romantic partner, friend, other, or no partner specified). Despite the absence of significant moderation effects, pooled estimates within most subgroups remained significantly positive, indicating higher levels of expression and disclosure among women than men across a wide range of emotional contexts and interpersonal relations.

articles.title: Manipulating Temporal Expectations to Accelerate Recovery After Cataract Surgery:  A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles.authors: Peter J Aungle; Juliette Bross; Viknesh Nagarathinam; Daniel L. Chen; Peter Rapoza; Ethan Brass; Sophie Cate; Ellen Langer
articles.abstract: Perceived time can objectively influence physiological outcomes, but such effects have been produced using false temporal feedback in laboratory settings, which is difficult to extend clinically. Drawing on the Embodied Models of Health (EMH) framework, in which beliefs shape health by orienting attention and expectation, the present study tested whether shifting patients' temporal expectations could influence post-surgical recovery. Patients undergoing bilateral cataract surgery (N = 147) were randomly assigned to a fast healing condition, comprising a preoperative video emphasizing faster recovery timelines and daily surveys directing attention toward healing variability, or a standard healing condition, comprising conventional information and surveys unrelated to healing. Visual acuity was assessed at baseline and at 1-day, 1-to-2-week, and 3-month follow-ups. Group-level differences across conditions were directionally consistent but modest. The theoretically motivated analyses, however, revealed an Attention × Sensitivity interaction consistent with the framework's core prediction: among patients who absorbed the faster expected healing times, greater daily attention to healing variability predicted faster recovery; among those who did not, attention had little effect. By the morning after surgery, and at every follow-up through three months, high-attention patients with strong healing expectations or high sensitivity to the faster-healing message held an acuity advantage over belief-matched controls equivalent to reading print roughly 10% smaller at the same distance, and reported at least 50% greater improvement in self-reported visual function. These findings provide the first clinical evidence that attention functions as a belief-weighted mediator between psychological and physiological processes, extending laboratory demonstrations of mind-body unity to clinical practice.

articles.title: Low-certainty modals not future tenses cause increased psychological discounting
articles.authors: Cole Robertson; Sean Roberts; Asifa Majid; Tammy Lu; Phillip Wolff; R. I. M. Dunbar
articles.abstract: Speaking a language that obliges the future tense for linguistic Future Time Reference (FTR) has been hypothesised to cause speakers to perceive delayed outcomes as temporally distal and therefore less valuable (“temporal discounting”). Conversely, we hypothesise that the obligation to use low-certainty modal verbs, e.g. may, causes speakers to construe risky and delayed outcomes as riskier and therefore less valuable (“combined discounting”). We experimentally elicited free-text FTR responses and measured construals of future temporal distance and discounting of (risky) delayed rewards in speakers of Dutch (which does not oblige FTR marking) and English (which does). We used statistical mediation models, which parse out an indirect effect of a predictor on an outcome via a mediating variable, a direct effect of a predictor on an outcome, and a total effect—the other two combined. English speakers construed future events as temporally proximal, which in turn caused less (rather than more) temporal discounting (indirect effect). The direct effect went in the opposite direction, meaning there was no population-level difference in temporal discounting (no total effect, Study 1). When we measured combined discounting, English speakers discounted more (a total effect, Study 2). Further, English speakers used more low-certainty language and this caused increased combined discounting (an indirect effect). Future tense use did not impact construals of temporal distance, meaning future tense use did not mediate an effect on combined discounting (Study 2). We addressed possible cultural confounds by testing Dutch-English bilinguals (Study 3). When bilinguals were tested in English, they used more low-certainty modal verbs, which in turn caused increased combined discounting (an indirect effect). This was moderated by self-reported English proficiency, indicating language, not culture, is responsible for effects. Results suggest effects of FTR grammar are not driven by obligatory future tenses affecting temporal discounting, but by obligatory low-certainty modals affecting combined discounting.

articles.title: The When, Who, Why, and How of Crocodile Tears: Manipulative Crying is Associated with Specific Situations, Traits, Motivations, and Expressive Behaviors
articles.authors: Janis Zickfeld; Monika Wróbel; Paweł Ciesielski
articles.abstract: The notion of crocodile tears suggests that crying can be used strategically to manipulate others. However, systematic evidence on manipulative crying remains limited. Here, we addressed this gap by examining the prevalence of crocodile tears, along with the contexts, motivations, individual traits, and expressive behaviors associated with this phenomenon across seven studies. In the first three studies (N = 2,036), participants from seven regions reported real-life experiences of being manipulated with crying or using crying to manipulate others. Results indicated that crocodile tears are a widespread yet relatively infrequent manipulative strategy, primarily occurring in close relationships and typically intended to evoke compassion or induce guilt. Women, younger participants, individuals scoring higher on Machiavellianism and psychopathy, and participants from lower-trust countries reported more frequent use of crocodile tears. Manipulative crying was also associated with intense expressive behaviors, including exaggerated facial expressions, face-touching, and loud vocalizations. Another set of four studies (N = 4,514), conducted across five regions, experimentally manipulated crying-related behaviors to examine how expressive cues shape perceptions of crying. Machine learning analyses revealed that crying was perceived as most “crocodile” when it involved high-intensity behaviors but no tears. Moreover, intense expressive behaviors combined with the absence of tears improved participants’ accuracy in detecting fake crying. Together, these findings provide a comprehensive empirical account of crocodile tears, highlighting how multimodal expressive cues, as well as social, individual, and cultural factors, shape the strategic use and perception of crying.

articles.title: Psychopathology-AI-interaction (PAII) framework: Disorder-specific dynamics in conversational AI
articles.authors: Alexander Diel; Niels Weber; Martin Teufel; Alexander Bäuerle
articles.abstract: Chatbots based on large language models (LLM-CBs) are increasingly used for mental health support by both individuals with and without mental health conditions. Simultaneously, potential risks and harms of LLM-CB use for mental health are widely discussed, typically in disorder-unspecific terms, evaluated through single-turn benchmark and vignette designs, and rarely linked to established models of psychopathology. The current work presents the Psychopathology-AI-interaction (PAII) framework, which conceptualizes harmful human-chatbot interaction as arising from three interacting components: human factors (disorder-specific pathology, individual vulnerabilities, and personality dispositions), chatbot factors (model-specific safety failures and design principles), and interaction factors. Drawing on established models of technology-associated psychopathology, LLM-CBs are presented as a new domain in which disorder-specific maladaptive patterns emerge. A roadmap for future research is presented, focusing on psychopathology-based multi-turn benchmarks, experimental induction of vulnerabilities and manipulation of chatbot risk factors, and analysis of naturalistic conversation logs.

articles.title: A puzzling situation: How cooperation and social observation influence visuospatial problem-solving
articles.authors: Federico Cassioli; Nellia Bellaert; Mandy Rossignol; Clay B. Holroyd; Rudi De Raedt
articles.abstract: Human problem-solving rarely occurs in social isolation. Yet how cognitive performance and subjective experiences vary across social situations, and whether these effects depend on individual differences in social anxiety (SA), remains underexplored. In this preregistered, within-subject experiment, 101 healthy young adults completed a visuospatial problem-solving task, involving tangram puzzles of different difficulty levels (1,818 trials total) across three social conditions: alone or joined by an experimental confederate acting as either a scrutinizing observer or an active cooperator. Using hierarchical Bayesian modeling, we modeled task performance and post-trial self-reported experiences, and tested whether SA, measured with the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale, moderated the effects of social condition. Both performance and self-report ratings were modulated by task difficulty and social condition. Relative to performing alone, being observed was associated with a decrease in the probability of success and higher post-trial anxiety. Cooperation facilitated performance and reduced perceived difficulty. Crucially, SA moderated the effect of cooperation on post-trial anxiety: cooperation produced the largest reduction in post-trial anxiety among participants with greater fear of being observed. This buffering effect was specific to social-evaluative fear rather than general trait anxiety or task performance. Our findings reinforce the view that cognitive performance and participants’ experiences are jointly shaped by the social context in which they occur.

articles.title: Contact first, protocols second: How to establish a therapeutic alliance in team-based care for severe mental illness according to mental health professionals?
articles.authors: Melina Tetzlaff; Jojanneke Bruins; Kurt van Houten; Stynke Castelein
articles.abstract: Intro: The therapeutic alliance (TA) is a well-established predictor of treatment outcomes, yet traditional conceptualizations are usually dyadic. For individuals with severe mental illness (SMI), contemporary care is primarily delivered in multidisciplinary teams, raising questions about how the TA is established when responsibility is shared across providers. Qualitative research on this topic remains scarce. Methods: We aimed to: 1) conceptualize the modern TA; 2) identify factors that facilitate TA development; 3) provide an initial exploration of a treatment team alliance; and 4) formulate practice-oriented recommendations for TA development. N=13 mental health professionals (MHPs), including peer support workers (PSWs), participated in in-depth, semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed using inductive thematic analysis, supported by iterative coding, researcher triangulation, member-checking, and peer-debriefing. Results: Participants described the TA as dynamic, reciprocal, and context-dependent and identified the relational component as its foundation. Key facilitators included genuine listening, authenticity, transparency, reliability, balanced professional boundaries, and collaborative decision-making. Protocolization, time constraints, and authority were identified as barriers. In team-based care, participants emphasized consistency, effective communication, and self-reflection among MHPs, and a designated point of contact for service users. Conclusion: Our findings emphasize the importance of establishing a connection before starting protocol-centric treatment.

articles.title: Perceived and evidenced benefits of videogame play amongst neurodivergent populations: A scoping review
articles.authors: Emily J Smith; Jonathan Farnell; Lacey-ann Carter; Roshan Rai; Benjamin Gibson
articles.abstract: There are meaningful concerns that videogame play is harmful for neurodivergent populations, including people with autism spectrum disorders. However, there is a disproportionate focus in the literature on dangers, and there are fewer efforts to consider why such populations may be more likely to play videogames in the first place. In considering benefits to play, this scoping review attempts to map out a more balanced view of videogame engagement amongst a range of neurodivergent populations. A search of academic databases identified 9 articles comprising a mix of qualitative and quantitative studies. Using a narrative synthesis, we found that benefits to play included (1) friendship and belonging, (2) immersion, escapism, and emotional regulation, and (3) development, growth, and autonomy. In the future, we recommend a pivot away from a deficit-focused approach to investigations, and a larger investment in research that considers motivations, attitudes, and consequences of play from a lived-experience perspective.

articles.title: Psychological inoculation against deepfakes
articles.authors: Cambridge Social Decision-Making Lab; Liana Cheetham; Kelly Wong Kar Yee; Sander van der Linden
articles.abstract: Despite growing interest in countering the threat of deepfake misinformation, most interventions aimed at enhancing human detection have thus far proven unsuccessful. In the current study we explore the potential of a popular psychological intervention: cognitive inoculation—which to our knowledge—has not been tested in the context of deepfakes. In a pre-registered between-subjects experiment (N = 297), we evaluate whether an inoculation-based video intervention improves people’s deepfake detection skills compared to a control intervention. The inoculation intervention forewarned participants they may be manipulated by deepfake content and prebunked it by deconstructing deepfake misinformation in weakened form. Following the intervention, participants were asked to classify a series of 10 videos as either real or deepfaked. We find that mean detection accuracy of deepfakes was significantly higher in the inoculation compared to the control group (d = 0.625, 95% CI [0.39, 0.86]) without shifting response bias, indicating that the inoculation intervention substantially improved deepfake discernment. Further investigation of the mechanisms behind the inoculation process finds that both motivation to resist deepfakes and self-reported ability to recognize them increased following the intervention. Overall, our findings highlight the potential of inoculation interventions to build resistance to deepfake misinformation.

articles.title: Cross-cultural and Indigenous perspectives on music and social bonding
articles.authors: Danya Vivianne Pavlovich; Patricia Opondo; Juan David Leongómez; Yuto Ozaki; Zixuan Jia; Suzanne Purdy; Patrick E. Savage
articles.abstract: Experimental studies of primarily Western participants have suggested that musical synchrony facilitates social bonding. Critics question the validity and cross-cultural generality of synchrony-bonding relationships, as well as the causal role of music. Drawing on new data from large-scale Registered Reports co-designed and implemented with over 100 collaborators (“Many Voices”), we show that group singing enhances social bonding significantly more than speaking, across 901 participants speaking 30 languages. We share lessons from this collaboration regarding evolutionary hypotheses about the origins of music and language, as well as the importance of collaborating with Indigenous and non-Western researchers. By making the psychology of music research more inclusive, we may broaden our understanding of music and social bonding in humans and beyond. Indigenous knowledge does not oppose science: it improves science.

articles.title: Assistive AI in Counseling Psychology for Dyslexia (AAIC-D): A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing the Therapeutic Alliance
articles.authors: KHAIRUL KORAI
articles.abstract:
Individual with dyslexia frequently experience persistent reading difficulties that extend far beyond academic environments, contributing to heightened anxiety, low self-esteem, and chronic psychological distress. In traditional mental health counseling, literacy-heavy tools such as written intake questionnaires, thought journals, and dense psychoeducational handouts impose a heavy extraneous cognitive load. This load exhausts working memory and triggers reading anxiety, effectively diverting mental bandwidth away from core therapeutic processing. To address this barrier, this paper introduces a conceptual framework: Assistive AI in Counseling Psychology for Dyslexia (AAIC-D). Grounded in a narrative synthesis of existing literature, this model positions artificial intelligence not as a replacement for human clinicians, but as an accessible cognitive scaffold managed under ethical oversight. The framework synthesizes Cognitive Load Theory, the Triadic Therapeutic Alliance model (Client, Therapist, and AI), and Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles. By leveraging Generative AI summaries, speech-to-text journaling, and multimodal text-to-speech presentation, AAIC-D offloads reading and writing effort, restoring the client's emotional capacity for therapeutic engagement. Finally, we address critical counseling practice governance concerns including algorithmic bias, data privacy under HIPAA/GDPR, and client over-reliance offering actionable guidelines to humanize and democratize psychological care. 

Keywords: Dyslexia, Assistive AI, Therapeutic Alliance, Cognitive Load Theory, Universal Design for Learning, Counseling Psychology, Cyberpsychology

articles_hidden.title: Learning to Enumerate Reorganizes Magnitude Representations
articles_hidden.authors: Lauren S Aulet
articles_hidden.abstract: Human adults show a number bias in magnitude perception, weighting numerical information more heavily than continuous magnitudes like area. However, developmental research suggests this bias is not innate: young children show an area bias that reverses to a number bias only later in development. What drives this shift? Here we use deep neural networks as a tool for testing computational sufficiency, asking whether learning to estimate number is by itself enough to reorganize how a visual system weights magnitude. We trained ResNeXt-50 networks on an enumeration task (labeling the number of dots in an image, an operationalization of a functional outcome of counting) and measured representational bias by linearly decoding number versus cumulative area from penultimate-layer features, with the two dimensions decorrelated by design. Untrained networks showed a robust area bias, with area more decodable than number. Critically, networks trained to estimate number showed a reversal, with number becoming substantially more decodable than area, and this shift emerged after a single epoch of training. The effect was not a trivial consequence of training on a dimension: a matched control trained to estimate area did not produce the mirror-image effect, because enumeration training actively suppressed area information rather than merely amplifying number. Principal component analysis confirmed a reorganization of representational geometry, with numerosity becoming the dominant axis of variation (r² = 0.95) and area variance strongly reduced. These findings provide a computational proof-of-concept that learning to enumerate can restructure magnitude representations, suggesting that the perceptual primacy of number in adults may be partly a consequence, rather than a precondition, of symbolic number acquisition.

articles_hidden.title: The Genesis of Grievance: Examining the Formation of Grievances and their Impact Upon Violent Extremist Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Bettina Rottweiler; Paul Gill
articles_hidden.abstract: The causal role of grievances, personal and political, is commonly attributed to the development of violent extremist outcomes. However, our conceptual and empirical understandings of how grievances develop and why only a minority with grievances go on to become radicalised remain underdeveloped. This paper uses structural equation modelling to examine the effects of perceived victimhood, personal grievances, and anger rumination on attitudes and intentions to engage in violent extremism via revenge motivation and reduced self-control capacity. We further analyse the protective effects of trait forgiveness on anger rumination and revenge motivation as well as self-control. The findings demonstrate that the experience of personal grievances mediates the effects of individuals’ tendency for interpersonal victimhood on anger rumination. The findings further highlight the mediating effects of revenge motivation and low-self-control on individuals’ attitudes and intentions to engage in extremist violence. We also demonstrate the indirect protective effects of trait forgiveness on support for and intentions to engage in extremist violence via its negative relationship with anger rumination, revenge motivation and low self-control. Our findings have important practical implications. Anger rumination may serve as a warning sign that an individuals’ perceived victimhood and personal grievances are translating into an increased vulnerability and potential escalation towards engagement in violent extremism, and thus may be a crucial point of intervention. During this rumination phase, there may be opportunities to intervene in the case by sign-posting critical information or warning signs about the consequences of going further than simply ruminating. Collectively, this suggests ways to inform programmatic approaches to prevent and counter violent extremism, while suggesting future avenues for joint risk assessment and management efforts tackling violent extremism.

articles_hidden.title: Bounding Causal Effects in Pretest-Posttest Designs with a Control Group
articles_hidden.authors: Muwon Kwon; Peter M. Steiner
articles_hidden.abstract: With data from a pretest-posttest design with a nonequivalent control group, researchers have two main options for identifying the causal impact of a treatment: covariate adjustment (CA) or difference-in-differences (DID). Each strategy rests on strong assumptions: the adjustment criterion (unconfoundedness) for CA and the common trend assumption for DID. In practice, neither of these assumptions is typically fully satisfied, resulting in biased effect estimates. To address uncertainty about potential assumption violations, we propose reliability-based bounds for the average treatment effect (ATE) that rely on a linear structural causal model and the reliability of the outcome's pretest measure with respect to an unobserved confounder. Unlike existing bracketing approaches, the reliability-based bounds do not require the stationarity assumption and remain valid even when the pretest and posttest measures are on different scales. Using simulated data, we demonstrate that the proposed bounds outperform existing methods by covering the true ATE even when stationarity is violated, while often producing narrower bounds when stationarity holds. The bounds also remain informative under moderate violations of linearity and the single-unobserved-confounder assumption. An empirical example illustrates how the bounds are established based on subject-matter knowledge and that they tend to cover the benchmark effect estimate from a corresponding randomized experiment.

articles_hidden.title: Does Parent-Rated Neurocognitive Functioning of Children with ADHD Moderate the Effects of Different Behavioral Parent Training Techniques?  A Randomized Controlled Microtrial
articles_hidden.authors: Dominique Petra Amadee Doffer; Barbara van den Hoofdakker; Tycho Dekkers; Rianne Hornstra; Marjolein Luman; Saskia van der Oord
articles_hidden.abstract: The effectiveness of behavioral parent training (BPT) techniques for children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may vary across individuals. Using a microtrial, we studied whether parent-ratings of child “hot” and “cool” executive functions moderated effects of stimulus-control (antecedent-based) versus contingency-management (consequent-based) techniques on child behavioral difficulties. Parents of 92 children with ADHD were randomly assigned to antecedent-based training, consequent-based training or waitlist. Results indicated that consequent-based techniques were particularly effective for children with lower arousal regulation and higher reward responsivity, while antecedent-based techniques were most effective for children with lower sensitivity to aversive stimuli. Possible explanations for these findings are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: The other side of social dance for mental health: What needs to be addressed before it can be offered to vulnerable populations?
articles_hidden.authors: Brennan Delattre
articles_hidden.abstract: A growing body of research suggests that social dance can be good for mental health, especially for individuals with depression, anxiety, and loneliness. However, less work has been conducted investigating for whom and in what circumstances social dance is beneficial, what safety considerations should be in place, and who might not yet be included in social dance spaces. In light of ongoing research investigating whether salsa dancing should be offered as an option to patients seeking care for depression and anxiety through the United Kingdom’s National Health Service (NHS) Talking Therapies as a social prescribing initiative and on a larger scale, and given the growing interest in social dance as a mental health solution more broadly, this Perspective piece highlights key issues that need to be addressed in community-based social dance spaces before social dance can be offered safely and equitably for vulnerable populations through public healthcare prescribing channels.

articles_hidden.title: Canine-Assisted Interventions and Symptoms Associated with Borderline Personality Disorder: A Scoping Review
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Pestell; Richard Gorman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background:
Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is associated with symptoms including self-harm, suicidality, impulsivity, anger, and mood disturbance. Although psychotherapeutic approaches are commonly used in treatment, there remains interest in alternative and complementary approaches for managing BPD-related symptoms. Canine-assisted interventions (CAI) have been investigated across a range of mental health settings, though their relevance to BPD-related symptoms has not previously been described.

Aims:
This scoping review aimed to map the available research on CAI addressing symptoms associated with BPD, describing study populations, intervention characteristics, outcome measures, and gaps in the evidence.

Methods:
A systematic search was conducted across 5 databases. Studies were considered eligible if they examined the effects of CAI on predefined BPD-related symptoms, involved CAI interventions, and reported primary empirical data. Study populations, intervention characteristics, outcome measures, and reported findings were tabulated and summarised descriptively.

Results:
Eleven studies met the inclusion criteria. Studies varied in their populations, intervention formats and outcome measures, and coverage of the selected symptoms was uneven. Most studies reported reductions in at least some BPD-related symptoms following CAI. However, several studies demonstrated important methodological limitations, including small sample sizes, non-randomised designs, and limited control for confounding. Most included studies did not recruit participants with a formal diagnosis of BPD specifically.

Conclusion:
Existing research on CAI does address several symptoms associated with BPD, but spans diverse populations, interventions and outcome measures. There are, however, gaps in symptom coverage and research involving populations specifically diagnosed with BPD, providing priorities for future investigation.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Standardized Affirmation: Transgender and Nonbinary Youths’ Experiences and Recommendations for Flexible Crisis Care
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Pablo Zapata; Alyssa N Gorkin; Aileen Kangavary; Amanda Smock
articles_hidden.abstract: Suicide rates are particularly high among transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) youth. Although gender-affirming care is increasingly incorporated into crisis services, little is known about how its delivery across crisis-care touchpoints may support or undermine safety and affirmation. This study used a youth-centered, iterative, qualitative design to examine practices shaping TGD youths’ experiences of gender-affirming care across crisis encounters. The study included 12 TGD youth aged 13–17 years (M = 16.3), all of whom reported suicidal-related thoughts and behaviors within the past month. Participants completed 22 semi-structured interviews across two iterative waves. Wave 1 explored experiences across crisis-care touchpoints and informed prototypes of gender-affirming practices, which participants reviewed and refined in Wave 2. Data underwent two-phase inductive-deductive analysis, with Wave 1 interviews coded to identify themes, and Wave 2 interviews coded to examine responses to emerging findings and practices. Across in-person acute care and virtual touchpoints, three themes described a mismatch between crisis response and gender affirmation: (1) standardized gender-affirming practiced could feel scripted; (2) agency and control over disclosure and decisions about care, shaped whether encounters felt affirming; and (3) direct and indirect experiences shaped trust and future use of crisis-care resources. A fourth theme focused on proposed improvements to gender-affirming care; across waves, participants favored approaches that adapted affirmation to individual identities, knowledge, and preferences rather than applying standardized practices uniformly. Findings highlight the need for crisis care that addresses immediate safety while tailoring gender-affirming practices to youths’ identities, knowledge, preferences, and disclosure control.

articles_hidden.title: Forging ahead, pulling back, and acting strategically: Climate activists’ responses to criminalisation and repression in the UK
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Gardner; Sunniva Davies-Rommetveit; Jenny Douch; Anna Aretha Sach
articles_hidden.abstract: In response to the post-2018 rise in climate protest, many liberal democratic countries have witnessed the criminalisation and repression of environmental activists. Instead of assessing macro-level effects of repression on activism, this paper explores the micro-level responses to surveillance, arrest, fines, and imprisonment. Drawing on socio-legal scholarship that understands the law as socially constructed rather than objective and external, this paper delves into the black box of political repression, offering an examination of how climate activists respond to state sanctions. Analysing a survey of 1,375 Extinction Rebellion UK activists through thematic analysis and quantitative coding, we demonstrate that individual biography and narrativisations of the law lead activists to forge ahead, pull back, or act strategically in response to repression.

articles_hidden.title: Attachment-Informed Leadership (AIL):  A New Leadership Framework based on Attachment Theory and Social Neuroscience
articles_hidden.authors: Pascal Vrticka; Jonathan Wolf-Phillips
articles_hidden.abstract: Leadership research has catalogued many styles, among them transformational, authentic and servant leadership, but has offered few accounts of the regulatory mechanisms through which leader-follower relationships operate. We propose that attachment, understood through social neuroscience, supplies one such mechanism. Humans regulate environmental demands relationally, and attachment organises this social regulation of a finite bioenergetic budget under challenge. When followers face threat, dependence or uncertainty, this relationship can come to serve attachment functions, and the leader's reliability as a security provider bears on how much of followers' regulatory resources remains available for work. Building on the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt), we develop an attachment-informed leadership (AIL) framework spanning social allostasis, attachment and caregiving, predictive regulation and biobehavioural synchrony. We position AIL relative to evolutionary accounts of leadership and derive nine propositions that distinguish attachment processes from exchange, trust and identification, measurable from self-report to physiology and brain activity.

articles_hidden.title: To replicate or not to replicate? My nine failures to publish a successful replication
articles_hidden.authors: Sharon Gilaie-Dotan
articles_hidden.abstract: Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011) proposed disclosure-based practices — a priori power analyses, full reporting of conditions and exclusions, results reported with and without exclusions applied — as a remedy for the replication crisis. Following these practices explicitly, our lab attempted to publish an online replication and extension of our earlier PNAS findings on image size and memory, expecting that doing so would make publication straightforward. It did not. The manuscript was rejected nine times over 2.5 years, largely on the grounds that a transparent, successful replication lacked sufficient theoretical novelty to warrant publication on its own; it was accepted only after this framing was substantially minimized in favor of additional analyses and an alternative theoretical framework. Here, I reflect on this experience and raise open questions about whether the field's evaluation of replications has kept pace with its stated commitment to them.

articles_hidden.title: Rethinking Spaced Practice Under Limited Instructional Time: The Benefits of Repetition Depend on Spacing
articles_hidden.authors: Meng Cao; Paulo F. Carvalho
articles_hidden.abstract: Spacing and repetition are two fundamental principles of learning, yet under limited instructional time, increasing repetitions necessarily shortens the intervals between encounters. Prior research found that more repetitions with shorter spacing produced better learning than fewer repetitions with longer spacing, but the respective contributions of spacing and repetition remained unclear. The present study sought to disentangle these contributions and replicate prior findings. Data were collected in 2026 from 120 English-speaking U.S. adults. Participants learned Indonesian-English word pairs three or six times under both massed and spaced schedules within a fixed instructional time. Retention was assessed immediately, one day, and three days later, and forgetting curves were used to estimate initial memory strength and forgetting rate. We replicated the advantage of more repetitions with shorter spacing. Spaced practice produced greater initial memory strength and slower forgetting than massed practice, whereas additional repetitions increased initial memory strength only when practice was spaced. These findings suggest that, under time constraints, additional repetitions benefit learning primarily when spaced, indicating that the advantage of repeated practice depends on the accumulation of learning across spaced encounters.

articles_hidden.title: The Meta-Awareness – Equanimity Framework of Self for Psychiatry: Phenomenological Insights from Psychosis and Mindfulness
articles_hidden.authors: Saampras Ganesan; Antoine Lutz; Andrew Zalesky; Vanessa Cropley; Barnaby Nelson
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychiatric disorders remain a major global health challenge, yet research does not adequately incorporate first-person lived experience. A central component of lived experience is the sense of self, which is often profoundly altered in psychiatric conditions and can serve as a prognostic phenomenological marker, particularly in psychosis. In psychiatry, the most minimal form of self, i.e., the basic-self, is conventionally conceptualized as an enduring, individuated subjectivity defined by perspectival ownership and a clear boundary between self and world. Conversely, some contemplative frameworks, including mindfulness and certain non-dual perspectives, view the basic-self as a dynamic, conditioned process, such that experience need not be fundamentally structured by a self–world distinction or a fixed perspective. Drawing on phenomenological evidence from published first-person reports, we argue that the contemplative view can illuminate previously unexplored mechanisms underlying basic-self disturbances in psychosis-spectrum disorders. We formalize this view in a testable meta-awareness - equanimity (MA–E) framework of self that maps key phenomenological overlaps and distinctions across mindfulness, psychosis, and psychedelic experiences. Finally, we outline future research directions for validating and operationalizing the MA–E framework with implications for intervention design in psychosis.

articles_hidden.title: On Color and Emotion: What Can Vision Science Learn from the Rorschach?
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: For a century, clinicians have recorded how people use color when they interpret inkblots, rank colored cards, or draw. They believed that how a person handles color reveals how that person handles feeling. Vision science has rarely read this literature, and the most complete modern review of color and emotion research excluded it. This paper introduces the projective color literature to vision scientists in plain language. Three conclusions follow. First, the tradition’s central belief, that chromatic color stirs emotion directly, was tested from the 1940s onward and largely failed. Second, narrower findings survived. The degree to which a person lets color lead over form in an ambiguous image is modestly related to several independently assessed clinical, behavioral, and biological outcomes. Some indices that set color in balance with other responses, such as coping versus overload, are also supported. What these scores measure is disputed. Third, the findings concern how color is weighted against form, which vision science already studies, yet only one study has linked that weighting to an object-recognition task, and none has used calibrated stimuli. I then read both literatures through a constructivist model of color in which the percept and the wider event it belongs to determine each other reciprocally. On this reading, the question is not only whether color influences emotion but also whether emotion influences color. The projective tradition raised the second question. Modern color-emotion science has mostly set it aside. Five studies are proposed that would join the two fields.

articles_hidden.title: Theories of Symbolic Number Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Hillary Mastarciyan; H Moriah Sokolowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding numerical symbols (e.g., the verbal number word ‘six’ or the Arabic digit ‘6’) is fundamental to the development of mathematical knowledge, yet how humans acquire meaningful representations of numerical symbols remains an ongoing theoretical question. In this review, we examine major theoretical accounts of symbolic number learning and consider how these perspectives explain the emergence and development of symbolic numerical knowledge. We focus particularly on the processes through which children establish meaningful connections between numerical symbols and their referents, addressing the longstanding symbol-grounding problem in numerical cognition. By synthesizing perspectives across developmental psychology and cognitive neuroscience, we identify areas of convergence and divergence among existing theoretical accounts and highlight key unresolved questions. Building on this synthesis, we propose the Grounded-to-Abstraction Theory, in which symbolic number knowledge emerges through a reciprocal process whereby small number words are initially grounded in exact quantity representations, and learning these symbols simultaneously scaffolds attention to numerical information. As this system develops, attentional control and approximate magnitude representations support the extension of numerical meaning beyond small quantities, while the emerging verbal number system scaffolds the acquisition of Arabic digits, yielding increasingly abstract and interconnected numerical representations. This framework integrates and extends existing theoretical perspectives and generates testable predictions regarding the behavioural and neural mechanisms underlying symbolic number learning in children. Overall, this review positions symbolic number learning as a dynamic developmental process involving multiple interacting representational systems and provides an integrative theoretical framework for understanding how children develop increasingly sophisticated representations of numerical symbols.

articles_hidden.title: Day-to-day fluctuations in craving and the value of drugs and food in daily life
articles_hidden.authors: Sergej Grunevski; Emmanuel E. Alvarez; Emma M. Schweitzer; Julia Kong; Sahar Hafezi; Anna B. Konova
articles_hidden.abstract: Craving is a powerful urge for a specific target (e.g., food, drugs) that prompts decisions directed at satisfying craving. While prior laboratory studies suggest craving biases behavior by amplifying target-specific value, the real-world generalizability of this mechanism remains unknown. We validate and extend these findings in a 28-day naturalistic smartphone-enabled study in patients with opioid use disorder (N=67) and community controls (N=49) who reported on their food (savory, sweet) and drug (opioid) urges and willingness-to-pay values. Despite person-level (mean) covariation, food and drug urges fluctuated largely independently within individuals while maintaining target-specific relationships with value. Using dynamics in drug urge and value and computational modeling, we isolated a distinct, ecologically relevant craving “state” tied to drug cue exposure and drug use in daily life. This research shows craving acts on normative valuation processes in real-world decision making and offers a novel approach to infer clinically vulnerable moments for behavior change.

articles_hidden.title: Form Theory: The Conceptual Architecture of Human Thought
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Haward
articles_hidden.abstract: Human thought takes place in a world that is uncertain and constantly changing. Yet the character of human thought is often quite different. People routinely simplify complex realities and hold their beliefs with a certainty and rigidity the world itself rarely warrants. The present paper develops Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure according to which these recurring tendencies are surface signatures of a common underlying format. Form Theory proposes that each concept contains a central form: a default structure that encodes a compressed subset of the concept’s information, gives that information default influence within cognition, and activates strong default beliefs about the encoded information. On Form Theory, distortion is one natural consequence of this structure. Yet the same structure also yields benefits for cognition. By encoding selected information in a stable, certainty-generating, domain-neutral format, the central form makes rapid, complex thought possible, supports conceptual and linguistic creativity, helps establish an internal sense of identity, and provides stable conceptual structure for the frameworks through which people organize their mental worlds. Form Theory therefore characterizes the conceptual architecture of human thought as a default conceptual structure whose signatures recur throughout cognition, with both benefits and costs for cognition and for human life.

articles_hidden.title: The Climate Stance Inventory: Development and validation in a large longitudinal sample of UK adults
articles_hidden.authors: Leo Johnson; Orestis Zavlis; Laurence Wainwright; Omid V. Ebrahimi
articles_hidden.abstract: The climate attitude–behaviour gap persists, with individual variables explaining limited behavioural variance. To address this problem, we develop and validate the Climate Stance Inventory (CSI), a continuous measure of 15 recurring orientations towards climate change and climate action derived from the Norm Activation Model. In a three-wave longitudinal study, 1,503 adults from the United Kingdom completed the CSI and measures of climate appraisals and environmental behaviour over approximately 10 weeks. Across waves, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses identified a 15-factor solution that exhibited good fit (CFI = .979, RMSEA = .034), high internal consistency (α/ω = .69–.88) and test-retest correlations (r = .58–.89) and full longitudinal measurement invariance. Climate stances showed theoretically coherent associations with threat certainty, responsibility-related appraisals, efficacy, institutional trust and pro-environmental behaviour. In hierarchical regressions, they explained substantial additional variance beyond demographic characteristics and climate change anxiety in pro-environmental voting (14.2%), workplace behaviour (19.5%) and behaviour outside work (22.4%). The Bystander stance also explained unique variance beyond a conceptually adjacent established barrier measure. These findings support the CSI as a reliable, temporally stable and substantively valid measure that can distinguish different psychological routes to climate (in)action and support the development and evaluation of more targeted climate-belief interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Left Out for Too Long? Chronicity of Social Exclusion as a Key Factor in Explaining the Exclusion-Radicalism Link
articles_hidden.authors: Linda Dörr; Andrew Hales; Kipling D. Williams; Christiane Marie Büttner; Michaela Pfundmair
articles_hidden.abstract:
Chronic social exclusion has been linked to radicalization processes in real-world terrorism
cases. However, experimental research regarding this link has focused on situational
experiences of exclusion, not accounting for chronicity of exclusion. Given the differences in
the psychological consequences of chronic and short-term exclusion, across three studies, we
investigated the association between chronic social exclusion and radicalism (i.e., readiness
to engage in violent and illegal political action) as well as activism (i.e., readiness to engage
in non-violent and legal political action). We hypothesized that chronicity might act as a key
condition for the effect of social exclusion on radicalism. In a survey study (N = 370), the
frequency of different types of exclusion experiences positively predicted radical intentions.
In a quasi-experimental survey study (N = 324), participants who reported chronic exclusion
(vs. no exclusion) in their everyday lives reported higher radical intentions. Participants who
reported only short-term exclusion did not differ in radical intentions from those reporting no
exclusion. In a five-month longitudinal study with weekly assessments (N = 343, k = 5,319
assessments), average exclusion experiences across the five-month period (i.e., a chronic
assessment of exclusion) positively predicted radical intentions and behaviors. Across
studies, chronic exclusion was associated with radicalism, but not activism. Thus, chronic
experiences of social exclusion might drive radical intentions and behaviors, highlighting
chronicity as a relevant yet understudied factor of the exclusion-radicalism link. In light of
these findings, reducing chronic experiences of exclusion might represent a particularly
promising avenue for the prevention of radicalism.

articles_hidden.title: A curriculum for neural networks to process two-digit arithmetic like humans
articles_hidden.authors: Samuel Lozano; Markus Spitzer; Korbinian Moeller; Miguel Ruiz-Garcia
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding and operating on multi-digit numbers is a critical step in the development of mathematical skills and concepts. Empirical and computational modeling evidence suggest that multi-digit number magnitude is processed in a componential manner, decomposed into units, tens, hundreds, etc. However, computational models evaluating whether such componential processing generalizes to multi-digit \textit{arithmetic} have so far relied on discrete symbolic inputs rather than on noisy magnitude representations. Accordingly, we developed a hierarchical neural network model of multi-digit addition based on componential processing of noisy single-digit magnitude representations. To evaluate model performance we implemented two training curricula: (i) an all-at-once curriculum and (ii) a step-by-step curriculum, where single-digit addition is trained before progressing to multi-digit problems (following school curricula). Under the training conditions tested, only the step-by-step curriculum allowed the model to learn multi-digit addition. Once trained this way, the model reproduced the carry-over and problem-size effects observed in reaction times of children and adults, both across problem categories and across individual items. These findings generalize the idea of decomposed processing of multi-digit number magnitude to arithmetic and highlight the importance of structured, incremental learning in both cognitive modeling and education.

articles_hidden.title: Employing ventilation and mobile air cleaning in classrooms and elderly care homes for infectious disease reduction: multi-stakeholder perspectives on acceptability, feasibility and perceived effects
articles_hidden.authors: Stefanie H Meeuwis; Amy Louise de Bruijn; Jennifer Mareen Becker; Marloes Duijzings; Dieuwke S. Veldhuijzen
articles_hidden.abstract: Poor indoor air quality (IAQ) leads to increased health risks, including infectious disease and respiratory illness, and can decrease wellbeing. Poor IAQ is also associated with adverse effects on performance indicators, for instance student education. Air cleaning technologies, such as (mobile) air cleaning and mechanical ventilation, could improve IAQ but their efficacy depends on their correct use and maintenance. User perspectives on the application of these technologies are generally underexplored. User and policy maker perspectives on the acceptability, feasibility and perceived effects of (mobile) air cleaning and ventilation systems in classrooms and elderly care homes were investigated in a two-part study. First, semi-structured qualitative interviews were conducted with participants from various organizations including primary schools and elderly care. Second, focus groups were conducted to assess stakeholder perspectives on the knowledge gaps amongst primary education staff elicited from the interview study. Taken together, the findings showed that although indoor air climate is generally acknowledged to be important for health and overall performance, several factors were identified that could complicate the implementation and use of novel technologies. These importantly include knowledge gaps in end users about the technology’s relevance and usefulness. The findings indicate the significance of education for end users and the necessity of understanding behavioral factors implicated in the implementation of innovative technologies for optimal efficacy of such devices.

articles_hidden.title: The multidimensional structure of perceptual and aesthetic evaluation: Independent features, interacting feature values, and perceptual unity
articles_hidden.authors: Eline Van Geert; Nori Jacoby
articles_hidden.abstract: Subjective appearance and aesthetic appreciation are inherently multidimensional, arising from the combined influence of a variety of visual features such as color, shape, and size. Yet, how multiple feature dimensions jointly shape perceptual and aesthetic evaluations remains poorly understood. Most previous studies either employ multidimensional stimuli without precise parametric control or use parametrically controlled stimuli that vary along only one dimension, limiting our understanding of the multidimensional structure underlying subjective evaluations. To address this challenge, we combined two methodological advances: the Order & Complexity Toolbox for Aesthetics (Van Geert et al., 2023), which enables the generation of parametrically controlled multidimensional stimuli, and Gibbs Sampling with People (Harrison et al., 2020), which efficiently characterizes subjective evaluations in high-dimensional stimulus spaces. Our stimuli consisted of visual displays containing multiple elements that varied in color, shape, and size and were arranged according to different organizational structures. Across nine experiments involving more than 1,000 participants and over 125,000 evaluations, we estimated multidimensional probability distributions underlying perceptual evaluations of order and complexity and aesthetic evaluations of pleasure and interest. Three main findings emerged. First, evaluations depended on both absolute feature values and relative differences between elements for each feature dimension, indicating that observers are sensitive not only to the characteristics of individual elements but also to the relations among them. Second, the influence of these relative differences depended on the overall perceptual organization of the display. Preferences for simplicity — operationalized as small differences in feature values between elements — varied systematically across evaluation criteria and with the degree of perceptual unity within the display. Third, despite these contextual effects, different visual features (color, shape, and size) conributed largely independently to the evaluations, suggesting that their influences on subjective evaluations are relatively separable. Together, these findings provide a multidimensional account of how visual features and their relations jointly shape perceptual and aesthetic evaluations.

articles_hidden.title: A transdiagnostic computational account linking mental fatigue and cognitive effort
articles_hidden.authors: Yang Yang; Akina Umemoto; Senne Braem; Clay B. Holroyd
articles_hidden.abstract: Motivational impairments are common to many psychiatric conditions, yet associations between psychiatric symptoms and willingness to exert cognitive effort have been inconsistent. Previous studies have mostly analyzed cognitive effort at the moment when people choose to engage in an effortful task, overlooking fatigue before the choice and how the task is executed after the choice. Here we examined this process during a 75-min online experiment involving 529 adults with psychiatric profiles spanning a broad range of symptoms. Participants repeatedly chose between resting and performing a demanding working-memory task, carried out the selected activity, and reported their fatigue. We derived continuous transdiagnostic symptom dimensions and modeled fatigue, effort selection, and task performance across time. Across participants, fatigue accumulated over time, and higher pre-choice fatigue predicted effort avoidance despite high overall task accuracy. Higher anxious-depression scores were associated with greater initial fatigue, faster fatigue accumulation, and a progressively steeper decline in high-effort choices. By contrast, higher compulsivity/intrusive thought scores were associated with more frequent high-effort choices but lower accuracy after effort was selected. Motivational dysfunction therefore did not reduce to a general reluctance to exert effort, but emerged through distinct alterations in fatigue accumulation, effort selection, and task execution. A dynamic, process-based account that separates these stages may help reconcile inconsistent findings in effort-based mental health research.

articles_hidden.title: Same Effect, Different Magnitude: How the Choice of Pre- or Post-Treatment Standard Deviation Shapes Standardized Effect Sizes in Psychological Clinical Trials
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Pillny; Anika Buchholz; Anna Suling; Antonia Zapf; Tania Marie Lincoln
articles_hidden.abstract: Standardized mean differences (SMDs) are used to express treatment effects on a common metric, yet there is no consensus on whether mean differences should be standardized using the outcome standard deviation (SD) at baseline or follow-up. This study examined whether this choice systematically affects effect-size magnitude in a reproducible sample of 100 randomized psychological clinical trials. For each trial, SMDs were calculated using either the pooled baseline SD (SMDpre) or the pooled follow-up SD (SMDpost). The unweighted paired mean difference showed that |SMDpre| was, 0.11 SMD units larger than |SMDpost|, 95% CI [0.07, 0.14]. In a multilevel meta-regression |SMDpre| was 0.082 SMD units larger than |SMDpost|, equalling a 13% increase, 95% CI [0.042, 0.123]. Bland–Altman analysis indicated substantial between-study variation, 95% limits of agreement [−0.25, 0.46]. Secondary analyses including 2,228 effect sizes across all follow-ups mirrored this pattern, indicating a 7% increase of SMD magnitude associated to |SMDpre|, 95% CI [0.021, 0.044]. Moderator analyses suggested that discrepancies were larger in studies applying symptom-threshold eligibility criteria, and in secondary analyses, using the same measure both to determine eligibility and to assess the outcome and with longer follow-up. Importantly, 70% of included studies did not report how SMDs were operationalized. These findings demonstrate that the choice of standardizing SD systematically affects estimated treatment-effect magnitudes and that the discrepancy can become more pronounced under specific design conditions. Researchers should therefore carefully consider the choice of standardizer and explicitly report the time point and method used to derive the SD.

articles_hidden.title: A Longitudinal Pilot Evaluation of a Single Session Digital Mental Health Intervention to Improve Satisfaction With Life Among Autistic Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Ty B. Aller; Francesca M Knudsen; Benjamin Covington; Heather Kelley; Michael Levin
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Background: Autistic adults experience higher rates of mental health concerns and additional barriers to accessing mental health care than adults without autism.
