articles.title: Platform visibility and protest recirculation in the Cockroach Janta Party movement
articles.authors: Nitesh Kumar yadav
articles.abstract:
This paper examines how the Cockroach Janta Party connected digital communication and street
protest in India between May and July 2026. I draw on nineteen public documentary records and a
separate retrospective account of my participation. I follow calls to attend demonstrations, a
request to share protest photographs and videos, Sonam Wangchuk's involvement, and disputes
over platform access. In my early visits, I remember small gatherings, people who stayed only
briefly, and volunteers who hoped the protest would grow but were unsure how far it would spread.
These observations make it difficult to assume that online popularity leads to sustained
participation. I use a visibility-action-recirculation framework to examine how gatherings produce
material that returns to digital circulation. A limited comparison with Nepal's September 2025
protests considers how people maintain communication when services are restricted. The evidence
documents deliberate organizing and reported interruptions. It does not establish how
recommendation systems, emotional appeals or recirculated material affected attendance.

Keywords: Cockroach Janta Party; platform visibility; digital protest; recirculation; platform governance;
India; Nepal

articles.title: Exploring the Intersection of Language and Literacy in a Young Person with Autism, Learning Disability and Minimal Speech.
articles.authors: Barbara Rose Clogg
articles.abstract: It is argued that language and literacy are inseparable for users of alternative and augmentative communication, and that literacy can offer a route to the acquisition of fully functioning language for non-verbal individuals with autistic spectrum disorder. This applied linguistics project explores the intersection of language and literacy in a young person with autism, learning disability and minimal speech. By use of multimodal conversation analysis, it reveals the range of everyday literacy practices used by the young person and how these literacy practices are drawn upon to make meaning in interaction. It finds that literacy practices constitute a significant part of their multimodal communicative repertoire and offer affordances as a mode of communication that breaks the limitations posed by their disabilities and the forms of AAC available to them.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence in Agriculture: Enhancing Yield and Sustainable Farming Practices among Farmers in India
articles.authors: Seema Wankhade; Subhash Patil
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across sectors, including agriculture. In India, agriculture remains central to employment, rural livelihoods, and national food security. Rising population pressure, climate change, declining land availability, pest and disease risks, labour shortages, and resource constraints have intensified the need for more productive and sustainable farming systems. This paper uses secondary data to examine how AI can enhance agricultural yield and support sustainable farming practices among farmers in India. It reviews applications such as precision agriculture, drones, crop disease detection, digital advisory services, market information systems, and resource optimisation tools. The paper also analyses the major barriers to AI adoption, including weak rural connectivity, high initial investment, limited digital literacy, and the need for localised solutions. The study concludes that AI has strong potential to improve productivity and sustainability in Indian agriculture, provided that adoption is supported through public investment, affordable access models, local-language advisory systems, farmer training, and public- private partnerships.

articles.title: A golden era for open-ended questions? Using LLMs to scale the qualitative coding of open-ended survey responses
articles.authors: Ansgar Hudde; Shannon Taflinger
articles.abstract: Open-text questions in quantitative surveys can yield rich information from large samples, but analysing and coding these data using qualitative text analysis is resource-intensive. Large Language Models (LLMs) are a promising tool for scaling up such analyses, reducing time and costs. We first use thematic qualitative text analysis to create a typology of responses; we then let LLMs code texts based on our typology and instructions and compare their coding accuracy with that of student assistants, defining accuracy as agreement with a researcher-coded benchmark dataset. We assess performance on an interpretive coding task: applying a 15-category typology to approximately 1,400 open-ended responses from young US Americans about dating across party-political lines. We evaluate models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral, with and without training data. The most advanced models outperform student assistants, and performance further increases with training data. This study contributes by applying LLMs to a use case with great analytical potential, namely open-ended survey responses, and testing whether the resulting codes support the same substantive conclusions as hand-coded data. We offer applied social scientists practical recommendations for a division of labour in which researchers retain conceptualisation and codebook construction and delegate the standardised coding to an LLM.

articles.title: “I wouldn’t trust her with my life but...” - Exploring trust in voice-based assistants through user-generated content
articles.authors: Katharina Frehmann; Jana Peters
articles.abstract: Investigating trust in conversational AI, such as voice-based assistants (VBAs), is increasingly important for understanding their rising popularity and the tasks users entrust to them. Howev-er, since VBAs are technical devices perceived as human-like and sometimes serving as infor-mation sources, it is unclear what forms trust in them takes. Technical, interpersonal, and media trust approaches may all be relevant, yet previous studies have not fully considered this poten-tial multidimensionality of trust in AI, especially regarding the inclusion of media trust. Fur-thermore, research on VBAs lacks qualitative studies that provide insights into users’ perspec-tives. This study therefore pursues two objectives: First, to develop a more comprehensive theo-retical perspective on trust in VBAs by integrating technical, interpersonal, and media trust ap-proaches. Second, to empirically explore signs of trust in VBAs in German user-generated online content. To this end, we conducted a qualitative content analysis of 169 postings about Alexa, Siri, and Google Assistant found on marketplaces, under media coverage, and on dis-cussion platforms. The results show that users evaluate typical and new technical, interpersonal, and media trustworthiness indicators for VBAs and sometimes combine these dimensions when discussing AI capabilities. When explicitly speaking of trust, users mostly refer to the parent company in high-risk situations rather than to the VBA itself. Users also discuss aspects that may represent consequences, processes, and external factors of trust. Based on these findings, the paper proposes a preliminary model of hybrid trust in VBAs that can inform future research on trust in conversational AI.

articles.title: Measuring Students’ Attention Boundaries in GAI-Assisted Learning: Development and Validation of the GAI-Mediated Learning Boundary Scale and Latent Profile Analysis
articles.authors: XI ZHAN; Yuxiang Shi; Peiyun He
articles.abstract: The Generative AI (GAI) is reshaping the temporal and spatial organization of college learning and the perceived boundary crossing between teacher-assigned tasks and self-directed learning. This study developed and validated a scale to assess college students’ attention boundary management in GAI-mediated learning. Analyzing data from 1904 students at 3 colleges in China, the study established a five-dimensional structure: Flexibility, Fragmentation, Immersion, Positive Spillover, and Negative Spillover. Exploratory and Confirmatory Factor Analysis confirmed the scale’s psychometric properties. A Latent Profile Analysis identified four distinct student profiles, Protective, Strained, Overextended, and Engaged Permeability Management. Supplementary heterogeneity analyses examined differences across the four profiles by gender, grade level, university, purposes and duration of AI use, and other learning-related characteristics. Based on these, this study proposed profile-specific recommendations. The study provides a validated instrument for assessing students’ attention boundaries in GAI-mediated learning, identifies heterogeneous student profiles, and offers differentiated practical implications.

articles.title: Rethinking methods for studying online information and health decision-making: a participant-centred approach
articles.authors: NIHR Policy Research Unit in Reproductive Health; Elena Proffitt; Nicola Merrett; Lois Harvey-Pescott; Jennifer Hall; Abigail McNiven; Abimbola Ayorinde; Kamilla Abdullayev; Rebecca French; Kelly Dickson
articles.abstract:
Online information, accessed through social media, websites, apps and artificial intelligence, is frequently described as shaping health attitudes and decision-making.  Many methodological approaches to understanding how online information influences decisions provide important insights into online content, information exposure, or user perspectives, but often struggle to capture the personalised and algorithmically curated digital environments people encounter, how they engage with information as it appears in their everyday lives, and how such encounters intersect with wider social, cultural and personal contexts to shape decision making. New methodological approaches are needed that can generate meaningful evidence about the varied realities of navigating online health information and the role it plays in decision-making.  

Drawing on reproductive justice and feminist principles that privilege participant expertise and lived experience and informed by literature and collaboration with lived and learnt experts, we co-designed a participant-centred longitudinal content-oriented study exploring the influence of online information on contraceptive decision-making. Inspired by Photovoice approaches, participants documented in real time the online information they encountered over a one-month period, capturing content presented through their own tailored digital environments. Interviews conducted before and after the collection period explored contraceptive experiences, attitudes, decision-making and reflections on the role of online information. By combining real-time documentation with in-depth interviews, this approach enabled interpretations of participants lived encounters with online information, including algorithmic changes, emerging trends, current events, and the types of content that resonated with them. Collaborators with lived experience were involved throughout the methodological development and interpretation and analysis of findings.  

This participant-selected content-oriented longitudinal design demonstrates the value of methodologies that capture and generate evidence on lived digital and offline realities as they unfold in real time. Understanding how online information shapes health decision-making requires moving beyond approaches that treat the internet as an isolated and static influence on behaviours. Online information is not a singular, stable object of inquiry but dynamic, personalised, algorithmically mediated and embedded within broader social, cultural, and political contexts. Methodologies that recognise this complexity are essential for generating evidence capable of informing empathetic and meaningful health care and support and care for people prioritising their needs and navigating complex health decisions.

articles.title: From “Robs to Riches”: Scandal Constructivation, Democratic Ambivalence, and Pagsasaayos in the Philippines
articles.authors: Karl Patrick Regala Mendoza
articles.abstract: This research note examines Philippine corruption scandals from the dual vantage of citizen and scholar. Building on my concept of scandal constructivation, I argue that scandals are not simply signs of democratic defect but communicative events that dramatize democracy’s ambivalence. The DPWH flood control scandal illustrates this: outrage turned comic in the “robs to riches” quip, while blame extended to contractors’ children, exposing relational accountability. Local publics—through gossip, assemblies, and social media—oscillated between vigilance and cynicism. In the Global South, scandals disrupt structures yet provoke repair, serving as resources for rethinking public engagement, legitimacy, and democracy.

articles.title: Regressive Restoration: A Process Model of Belief Rigidity Under Epistemic Destabilization
articles.authors: Mitchell Sanders
articles.abstract: Beliefs do more than represent the world; they can also regulate uncertainty, affect, identity, and significance. This article introduces regressive restoration as a temporal regulatory process in which epistemic destabilization increases reliance on coherence-restoring beliefs, the immediate stabilizing effects of those beliefs reinforce commitment, and that commitment subsequently reduces epistemic flexibility. Epistemic destabilization refers to conditions in which cues for determining what is credible, coherent, or socially shared become fragmented, overloaded, unreliable, or contested. The model proposes that available integrative resources– the momentary attentional, affective, and uncertainty-tolerance resources needed to remain engaged with conflicting information– moderate whether destabilization promotes adaptive accommodation or regressive restoration. The model distinguishes short-term stabilization from maladaptive rigidity. Coherence restoration is context-sensitive and may be functional, whereas rigidity is indicated when closure-oriented responses resist correction or persist across contexts in which reflective integration is possible. Regressive restoration is defined as a process rather than a trait or latent factor, and identity consolidation is treated as an important but nonessential amplifier. Five propositions specify the model’s distinctive predictions concerning regulatory function, temporal ordering, motivational amplification, correction resistance, and cross-context generalization. A focused empirical agenda is proposed to test whether immediate coherence, affective relief, or significance restoration predicts later belief rigidity beyond established informational and motivational mechanisms.

articles.title: Are EU Kidding Me? Notes from a Poorly Drafted Social Media Ban
articles.authors: Michael Veale
articles.abstract: In September 2026, the European Commission published a proposed EU KIDS Act, responding to the demand for restrictions and further design obligations applying to digital services accessible to children, including social media. This Article argues that regardless of what one believes about the merits of this policy direction, the EU KIDS Act is not the legislative text we need. The scope and drafting are little short of chaotic, full of holes, enormous ambiguities, and unintended consequences. Recitals contradict articles. The use of scope borrowed from other pieces of legislation not designed for this purpose brings services into scope that should not be subject to the relevant provisions, like book-recommendation websites, music services, or exercise trackers. The infrastructural requirement for assurance of age and parental responsibility attestation simply omits enormous issues of complex families and childhoods. Complex design obligations are written in ways that can be plausibly interpreted as implicitly prohibiting entire swathes of products, such as voice assistants. This Article outlines these issues, and many more. The Commission should withdraw this proposal and reissue a workable and realistic text.

articles.title: El Encuadre de la Responsabilidad Ciudadana: Comunicación Digital del Servel en la Elección Presidencial y Parlamentaria 2025
articles.authors: Jaime Elorrieta
articles.abstract:
Los organismos electorales enfrentan un desafío comunicacional distinto al de los partidos o candidaturas: deben informar y movilizar al electorado sin abandonar su mandato de neutralidad. Este informe examina cómo el Servicio Electoral de Chile (Servel) resolvió ese desafío en su publicidad digital durante la elección presidencial y parlamentaria de 2025, a partir del análisis de 101 anuncios publicados en Google Ads y Meta Ads.
Los resultados muestran que la comunicación del Servel es abrumadoramente práctica: el 85,1% de los anuncios se centra en información procedimental —dónde votar, qué documentos llevar, cómo revisar el rol de vocal de mesa— por sobre la apelación emocional, cívica o sancionatoria. Contra lo esperable, el tono no escala hacia la urgencia a medida que se acerca la elección; en cambio, mensajes puntuales como el llamado al deber cívico o la alerta contra la desinformación aparecen concentrados en momentos específi cos de la campaña, no en un crescendo progresivo. La advertencia sobre multas por no votar, pese a ser un rasgo central del sistema electoral chileno, ocupa un lugar marginal (3% de la muestra) en la comunicación digital del organismo.

articles.title: Between resistance and negotiation. Intellectual property as a survival strategy for media facing AI and digital platforms
articles.authors: Javier Díaz-Noci; Javier Odriozola-Chéné; Rosa Pérez Arozamena; Koldobika Meso-Ayerdi; Simón Peña-Fernández
articles.abstract:
Introduction. Generative AI has intensified tensions between news organisations and technology platforms over intellectual property, audience traffic and journalism’s economic sustainability. The report examines how leading Spanish digital media have framed AI since ChatGPT’s emergence, while considering the subsequent disruption caused by Google AI Overviews and AI Mode.

Methods. The study combines quantitative content analysis with legal and industry analysis. It examines 242 AI-related articles published between January 2022 and December 2024 by leading Spanish digital-native and legacy outlets, selected according to GfK DAM audience data. Frequency distributions and contingency tables assess thematic frames and editorial positions.

Results. Intellectual property emerges as the central underlying conflict. Coverage concentrates on authorship (68%), ethics and legal liability (45%), business models and licensing (32%), and employment (21%). Legacy media generally frame AI as a threat to journalistic assets, whereas digital-native outlets emphasise efficiency and commercial opportunities. Civil society and journalists themselves remain marginal in the debate. Google’s AI-generated summaries further intensify concerns by retaining users within the platform and reducing referral traffic.

Discussion. Intellectual property is becoming both a defensive right and a bargaining asset. The sector is consequently shifting from litigation towards licensing, collective negotiation and technological adaptation, although confidential agreements may strengthen major publishers while marginalising smaller outlets.

articles.title: Citizens’ Support for EU AI Sovereignty Policy
articles.authors: Pascal König; B.J.A. Leidorf-Tidå
articles.abstract: This article examines EU citizens’ support for EU policy to attain digital sovereignty regarding Artificial intelligence (AI). Promoting domestic industries in AI is crucially important for attaining AI sovereignty. Yet, AI sovereignty policy ultimately hinges on support by the European public, and protective policy intervening in the EU AI market may be felt directly – and negatively – by citizens. Using survey data from Lithuania, the Netherlands, Romania, and Sweden, we examine how much citizens support AI sovereignty policy even if this comes with costs and study how political and AI attitudes are associated with this trade-off evaluation. The analysis shows that EU-centrism is positively associated with support for AI sovereignty policy whereas positive attitudes toward AI and higher trust in US and Chinese tech companies show negative associations. The results have important consequences for the EU’s possibilities to garner public support for an AI sovereignty policy agenda.

articles.title: Citizen Trust in AI Regulatory Regimes in Four EU Countries
articles.authors: B.J.A. Leidorf-Tidå; Pascal König
articles.abstract: Trust in artificial intelligence (AI) applications is deemed crucial for uptake of the technology and the development of an AI market. In the present article, we argue that the institutional design of regulatory regimes matters for whether citizens trust AI systems. We study how trust in AI systems depends on who the responsible regulator is, the scope of the regulator’s scrutiny of AI systems, and the involvement of external stakeholders in regulatory oversight. Based on a conjoint design, we examine how respondents value these institutional design choices for the case of high-risk AI systems used in health care. Using samples from Lithuania, Romania, Sweden, and the Netherlands, with 4001 respondents overall, the pre-registered experiment shows that citizens have more trust in AI systems if vendors, civil society and especially independent researchers are involved in oversight, and if regulators actively scrutinize AI systems rather than relying solely on self-reporting. At least in two countries, citizens also seem to have more trust in AI systems if the sectoral health care regulator is the responsible regulator instead of a cross-sectoral regulator such as the national Data Protection Authority or a specific AI regulator.

articles.title: Digital Civic Activism and Configurations of Social-Identity Factors: Protest Campaigns in Gaming Communities on Reddit
articles.authors: Gudzenko Vladislav; Anastasia Poretskova
articles.abstract:
This study examines the conditions associated with successful digital protest campaigns in online video-game consumer communities. The theoretical framework combines the Social Identity Model of Collective Action (SIMCA) with research on digital political consumerism. The analysis covers 20 campaigns coordinated on Reddit between 2019 and 2024 and includes five conditions: discursive indicators of collective efficacy (EFFIC), group identification (IDENT), and group-based anger (ANGER), as well as the share of new/low-karma accounts (ANON) and the concentration of activity among the most active participants (LEAD). The empirical corpus contains 312,816 comments; an additional 8,055 comments were manually coded for validation and comparison with automated annotation. Fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) is used to identify configurations associated with outcomes.
None of the five conditions is necessary for a concession by the campaign target. The parsimonious solution contains three alternative configurations, but the most robust result is the combination of high group-based anger and low concentration of activity among the most active participants (ANGER × ~LEAD). This path survives most sensitivity checks and indicates that concessions in this sample are associated with mass, emotionally salient, and relatively decentralized mobilization. At the same time, cases of intense mobilization without concessions show that community-level characteristics are insufficient to explain outcomes without considering the cost of concession, the type of demand, and the position of the target organization.
Artificial-intelligence tools were used in the research process and in preparing this manuscript. A pretrained CardiffNLP model was used for emotion classification; Gemini was used for automated EFFIC and IDENT annotation; Claude models assisted with the development and checking of replication code; and ChatGPT was used to translate the manuscript. The research question, case selection, operationalization, calibration decisions, result validation, and substantive interpretation were performed by the researcher.

articles.title: Data Report:   Anchoring International Law’s Dynamism (ANCHOR)  project
articles.authors: MOBILE - Center of Excellence for Global Mobility Law; Anouk Lamé; Sarah Scott Ford; Nora Stappert
articles.abstract:
How are interpretive shifts at international courts accepted or resisted within the day-to-day work of domestic legal systems? Over the past few years, several international courts have faced critique by policymakers for developing international law too dynamically. Consequently, scholarly literature has argued that we are entering a period of backlash, with states actively trying to hedge against the domestic impact of international rulings. Yet, little is known about how – and under what conditions – interpretive shifts are received within the day-to-day work of domestic legal systems, especially at lower and specialized courts. 

This data report describes the data used for the research conducted as part of the research project entitled “Anchoring International Law’s Dynamism: Tracing Denmark’s Reception of International Rulings” (ANCHOR). Focusing on international refugee and migration law as a critical test case, the project analyses case data from the Danish Refugee Appeals Board (RAB) to examine the domestic reception of international rulings. The data report begins by describing the data collection process across its different data sources, after which it turns to data processing. The report then outlines the extraction and qualitative coding of citations to international rulings, ending with a brief discussion of the choices made for the data analysis.

articles.title: From Berberism to Kabyle-Nationalism. Historical Analysis of Berberism in Algeria between 1930 and  2005.
articles.authors: Christoph Novak
articles.abstract: This article examines the historical development of Berberism in Algeria from the emergence of Algerian nationalist movements in the 1930s to the aftermath of the Black Spring of 2001. It argues that Berberism should not be understood as a stable political ideology with a fixed substantive meaning, but rather as a changing political practice through which the idea of a distinctive Berber identity has been mobilised in response to particular political contexts. The analysis distinguishes three phases in the development of Berber activism. The first, exemplified by the Berber Crisis of 1948–49, was largely an elite struggle within the Algerian nationalist movement over the definition of the Algerian nation and the recognition of its linguistic and cultural plurality. The second, crystallised in the Berber Spring of 1980, transformed Berberism into a broader social movement centred on cultural recognition, linguistic rights and opposition to state Arabisation. During the subsequent period of political liberalisation and civil war, Berber activism became increasingly institutionalised through political parties, social movements and transnational networks. The third phase, associated with the Black Spring of 2001, marked a significant reorientation. The declining legitimacy of established Berberist parties and the emergence of the Citizens’ Movement shifted political mobilisation toward territorial, socio-economic and increasingly Kabylia-centred claims. Drawing on concepts of political identity, recognition, nationalism and imagined communities, the article argues that this development contributed to the emergence of a specifically Kabyle nationalism. Whereas Berberism provided a broader cultural and transnational identity, it lacked a clearly defined territorial project capable of consolidating a common political community. The post-2001 mobilisation in Kabylia, by contrast, increasingly linked cultural identity to a specific homeland, territorial political structures and demands for autonomy. The article therefore conceptualises the transition from Berberism to Kabyle nationalism not as a linear transformation, but as a reconfiguration of political actors, strategies, territorial imaginaries and claims to collective self-determination. The article was written in 2012.

articles.title: The distinctive nature of non-partisanship: How independents pursue and prioritize political information
articles.authors: Stuart Perrett; Delia Baldassarri
articles.abstract: The two major parties present American voters with increasingly stark electoral alternatives. How do independents make political decisions in this era of heightened partisanship? Prevailing accounts portray independents either as inattentive, low-information voters or as "undercover" partisans whose behavior mirrors that of Democrats and Republicans. We challenge both characterizations. Drawing on novel survey experiments, we compare the information-seeking behavior of independents and partisans by examining the importance they attach to different candidate attributes and the quantity of information they seek before choosing between candidates. We find that independents and partisans rank candidate attributes in similar ways, with both groups prioritizing issue positions over socio-demographic characteristics. Yet, independents rely less on candidate partisanship and acquire more information than partisans across a variety of hypothetical electoral conditions. These differences persist across levels of political knowledge, suggesting that independents and partisans use distinct decision rules when evaluating political candidates.

articles.title: Contagion or substitution? Experimental evidence on spillovers in trust between legislative and judicial institutions
articles.authors: Michal Ovadek; Stuart Perrett
articles.abstract: Does information about one branch of government affect trust in another? We show that institutional trust is neither institution-specific nor uniformly system-wide. In a survey experiment embedded in the British Election Study Internet Panel, respondents received information about the UK Parliament, the UK Supreme Court, and the European Court of Human Rights that varied the policy content of decisions, party framing of these decisions, and the conduct of individual officeholders. Policy decisions conflicting with respondents' preferences reduce trust well beyond the institution responsible, while congruent decisions leave trust unchanged. Spillovers are strongly asymmetric: parliamentary decisions depress trust in the courts more than in Parliament itself, whereas court decisions produce little spillover beyond the judicial domain. Criticism from parties offsets rather than deepens the penalty, regardless of how much respondents like the cueing party. Information about conduct of officeholders moves trust neither within nor across institutions. We conclude that institutional trust is selectively contagious, shaped above all by the policy decisions institutions make.

articles.title: Distributional Validity of a Korean Synthetic Persona Panel: Evidence From the Korea Media Panel Survey
articles.authors: Howard Kim; Keun Tae Cho
articles.abstract: Large language model (LLM) personas are proposed as survey respondents, yet validation outside English-speaking contexts is scarce. We evaluate how well a Korean synthetic persona panel used to condition Gemini 3.5 Flash and EXAONE reproduces digital and artificial intelligence (AI) service-use distributions of the Korea Media Panel Survey. About 8,000 personas per model answered eight service-use items and eight attitudinal constructs; responses were compared with weighted survey estimates. The overall mean absolute error (MAE) was 14-19 percentage points (pp), with binary item-mean correlations of 0.70-0.91 across waves. Segment error across five axes was 14-18 pp, with between-group signed-error ranges of 49.6/34.7 pp (Gemini/EXAONE; 39.5/31.2 without the non-comparable teen cells). Errors were model-specific: an age stereotype (Gemini) versus an acquiescence-consistent level bias (EXAONE). Generative-AI overestimation was consistent with temporal misalignment; short-form underestimation was framing-sensitive and persisted under randomized order (both shown for Gemini). Post-hoc holdout calibration on 30% of the real data, with the correction form selected inside the calibration set, cut cell MAE from 18.3/15.1 to 4.9/4.4 pp, yet direct estimation from that subsample was more accurate than the calibrated panel (3.6 pp), a synthetic-informed shrinkage estimator beat its real-only counterpart by at most 0.7 pp, and the correction did not transfer competitively across waves. The calibrated panel kept an advantage only below roughly 250-860 real responses (at most 2.3 pp over a real-only shrinkage estimator) or, for one model, on unobserved segments. In this setting, synthetic panels are not survey substitutes; their value is diagnostic.

articles.title: Beyond compensation: Climate politics, mobilization, and transformative statecraft
articles.authors: Benjamin Braun; Leah Downey
articles.abstract: Governments have pursued decarbonization through a combination of subsidies for capital and compensation for people. Political scientists have identified the compensation of those who incur losses from climate policies as the the central challenge in building green coalitions and achieving a just transition. However, a decarbonization path aimed at limiting global warming to 2 degrees Celsius entails transformative change for virtually everyone. We argue that, under such conditions, a compensation-based approach reduces green backlash to pocketbook concerns; citizens to bundles of fixed preferences; and evaluation to policy-by-policy assessment. Proposing to move beyond compensating existing preferences, we contend that transformative statecraft reshapes preferences through political mobilization. From this perspective, a technocratic approach—focused on calculation and compensation—constitutes a binding constraint on green statecraft. We defend this mobilization-based approach against the objections of manipulation and deprivation of freedom and suggest that a democratic version of transformative statecraft is possible.

articles.title: From volume to care: an ethic of aver cura for tourism and host-community well-being
articles.authors: Christian Josef Wiedermann; Patrick Rina; Harald Pechlaner; Fulvio Longato
articles.abstract:
Purpose. This paper proposes an ethic of care — aver cura — as an integrative concept for destination development that connects two disconnected uses of "care" in tourism scholarship and specifies how the concept can be observed and measured.
Design/methodology/approach. The paper is conceptual. It synthesizes tourism studies, public health and the ethics of care, and illustrates the argument through the single case of Meran, South Tyrol, a historic alpine health resort.
Findings. Tourism research invokes care as an ethos, while public health and health tourism treat care as provision; the two seldom meet. An ethic of aver cura, built on caring for self, others and place, integrates them and reframes success from volume to sustaining visitor, resident, worker and landscape together. Civic trust, distinct from commercial destination trust, is the operational core through which care becomes measurable.
Research limitations/implications. The six propositions are conceptual and untested; they set a future agenda for comparative and longitudinal research.
Practical implications. Destinations would shift from volume metrics to civic-trust and community indicators and to recurring deliberative governance.
Social implications. The approach foregrounds the well-being of residents and tourism workers alongside that of visitors.
Originality/value. The paper offers an integrative concept of care that bridges ethical and public-health registers, distinguishes civic from commercial trust as its measurable core, and grounds care in a destination's own formative logic rather than importing it from outside.

Preprint of a manuscript currently under review at the Journal of Tourism Futures (Emerald). This is the submitted version and has not been peer-reviewed.

articles.title: Efficiency, Elasticity, and Disruption: A Mechanistic Framework for Socio-Technical System Transitions
articles.authors: Vitor Miranda de Souza; Diogo Figueirinhas; Brian D. Fath; Fredrik Nilsson
articles.abstract: Efficiency improvements are persistently accompanied by demand expansion and increased resource throughput, systematically undermining sustainability strategies in operations and supply chain management. While existing explanations rely on behavioural assumptions or empirical correction factors rather than structural accounts, this paper develops a first-order mechanistic formulation of efficiency-induced demand expansion, introducing system elasticity εsys as a structural property of socio-technical configuration. Building on and generalising Ayres and Warr’s framework, we derive the service relationship S ∝ η^(ε_sys−1) and its resource corollary R ∝ η^(ε_sys−2), establishing two sustainability thresholds: ε_sys > 1 for service expansion and ε_sys > 2 for absolute resource growth. Two independent empirical cases – the 19th-century steam engine and contemporary computing – yield ε_sys ≈ 3.5, consistent with the backfire condition. The formulation reframes the operational challenge from governing resource efficiency to governing service elasticity.

articles.title: When Red Is - and Is Not - Blood: A Corpus-Assisted Cognitive-Semantic Analysis of Five Settler Australian Texts (1874-1907)
articles.authors: Nguyen Huynh Si Tan
articles.abstract: This study investigates when the colour term RED is conceptually connected with BLOOD and when the two domains remain independent in settler Australian literary discourse. The data comprise five complete public-domain texts published between 1874 and 1907 by Marcus Clarke, Henry Lawson, Miles Franklin, Joseph Furphy, and Jeannie Gunn. The study adopts a corpus-assisted qualitative design combining full-text lexical retrieval, paragraph-level concordance reading, cognitive-semantic annotation, and counterexample analysis. A verified analytical set of 30 concordance contexts was assembled across the five texts to test explicit BLOOD-RED bridges against competing RED and BLOOD pathways; the set is deliberately criterion-based and is not treated as a frequency sample. Three direct bridge types are attested: blood-red compounding, blood as a colour comparator, and bodily circulation as a causal basis for visible redness. The same texts also provide systematic counterevidence to any general RED IS BLOOD equation. RED occurs independently in landscape, fire, flora, atmospheric description, and conventional idioms, while BLOOD extends independently to violence, personhood, descent, temperament, inheritance, vitality, and exploitation. The findings support an asymmetrical partial-overlap model: BLOOD can motivate RED, but RED does not entail BLOOD, and many figurative BLOOD constructions have no chromatic component. The analysis further shows that red soil, red gum, and comparable Australian landscape expressions cannot be classified as blood imagery without local lexical or causal co-activation. Methodologically, the study demonstrates the value of separating lexical semantics, metonymic motivation, metaphorical extension, and literary symbolism before cross-linguistic comparison.

articles.title: Informing Instruction During Educational Disruptions: A UTAUT-Informed Mixed-Methods Study of Grade 11 Students' Evaluations of YouTube for Oral Communication Learning
articles.authors: Jo Michael Llamelo
articles.abstract: Educational disruptions can require students to rely on supplementary digital resources when ordinary classroom interaction is restricted. This study examined how 26 Grade 11 students enrolled in Oral Communication at a private senior high school in Legazpi City, Philippines, evaluated YouTube during emergency remote teaching in Academic Year 2020-2021. A convergent, cross-sectional mixed-methods survey used 17 six-point Likert-type items organized through UTAUT-informed domains, each paired with an open-ended prompt. Quantitative responses were summarized descriptively, while 442 written explanations were analyzed through deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis and integrated with their corresponding ratings. Domain means were generally favorable, ranging from 4.48 for behavioral intention to 5.08 for facilitating conditions. Internal consistency was strong for performance expectancy (α = .82) but weaker for the other domains (α = .37-.65), so domain-level results were interpreted cautiously and alongside item-level and qualitative evidence. The qualitative analysis produced 28 substantive codes synthesized into five cross-domain patterns: controllable multimodal explanation supported comprehension; YouTube expanded explanatory options but required active selection; educational value depended on content and presenter quality; access was flexible but infrastructure-dependent; and acceptance was pragmatic and supplementary rather than substitutive. Across 442 rating-explanation pairs, 75.3% were congruent positive and 15.4% were qualified or mixed. The findings suggest that students valued YouTube primarily as a flexible supplementary resource for clarification, review, and continuity rather than as a replacement for teacher-led instruction. Notably, connectivity and infrastructure concerns remained visible even among participants selected for online readiness, underscoring the distinction between nominal readiness and reliable access.

articles.title: Adolescent Online Leisure, Media Literacy, and Emotional Distress from Online Victimization: Evidence Across Fifty Countries and Economies
articles.authors: Yunqi Wang; Yan Ruth Xia; James A. Bovaird; Maria Rosario T. de Guzman; Paul Springer; Xiaoran Sun
articles.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has accelerated adolescents’ engagement in online activities. However, research on adolescents’ technology use and mental health often overlooks the complexity of online behaviors and the role of media literacy without examining specific mechanisms. This study addresses the gap by analyzing survey data from 295,843 adolescents aged 15-16 years across 50 countries and economies from Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) collected in 2022, examining the relations among adolescent online leisure, media literacy, and emotional distress from online victimization. Structural equation modeling results revealed that both adolescents’ online leisure and media literacy are positively associated with their emotional distress from online victimization experiences, such as exposure to unwanted content. Findings provide important implications for research, theories, and practices, highlighting an urgent need for parenting practices and interventions to promote adolescents’ media literacy and digital skills to navigate the online environment and mitigate online risks.

articles.title: Captured by the Ballot: Non-Partisan Judicial Elections and Democratic Erosion in Mexico
articles.authors: Brett Ryan Bessen
articles.abstract: Public tolerance for democratic erosion is often attributed to voter partisanship. Voters are thought to overlook undemocratic maneuvers to support the partisan in-group. Yet, backsliders  often disavow traditional parties and frame their reforms as non-partisan. I examine the role of voter partisanship in non-partisan elections, showing how elite manipulation of the information environment can generate partisan outcomes that facilitate backsliding—even when citizens prefer non-partisan outcomes on average. I examine Mexico’s 2025 judicial elections, pairing a conjoint experiment with an analysis of the electoral results. While the conjoint indicates that voters preferred independent judges, the electoral results indicate that government-aligned candidates on illicitly circulated voter guides (acordeones) received the most support, contributing to the partisan capture of the Supreme Court. Elite manipulation of the information environment and electoral incentives—rather than partisan preferences among the eligible electorate—were primary contributors to the court’s partisan capture.

articles.title: Empirical Reasoning About FOI Request Delays in the European Union
articles.authors: Jukka Ruohonen
articles.abstract: Freedom of information (FOI) is a human right and an important concept for the transparency and accountability of governments and public administrations. It is also essential for democracy. Despite a long research lineage on FOI laws and their use by citizens, existing empirical knowledge is still limited regarding the inner workings of FOI requests. This limitation applies particularly to the European Union (EU) and the documents possessed by its various institutions. To help at addressing this limitation, the paper presents a few empirical observations about FOI requests in the EU context. By using a dataset containing 500 requests made between 2022 and early 2023, the insight presented cover the EU institutions targeted, the requesters making FOI requests, and particularly the bureaucratic delays in handling of FOI requests. According to results based on a regression analysis, the bureaucratic delays vary according to both the EU institutions and the individual requesters.

articles.title: Responsibility to Prepare: From Individual Security to Collective Resilience
articles.authors: Paulus Damgaard; Jonas Toubøl; Lærke Høgenhaven
articles.abstract: In the context of heightened geopolitical tensions, European societies increasingly frame private crisis preparedness as integral to societal resilience. Once viewed as antisocial survivalists, preppers now offer insight into civil society’s role in prepar-edness. Drawing on a netnographic study of one of Denmark’s largest Facebook prepper groups (2015-2024), this article examines how the group members per-ceive responsibility for crisis preparedness across four periods: before COVID-19, during the pandemic, after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and following the Danish government’s 2024 appeal for household preparedness. Findings reveal a dominant individualistic framing in stable times, but a shift towards collective understandings of responsibility following official communication during crises. The article con-tributes to sociological research on crisis preparedness by demonstrating how per-ceptions of crisis contexts and state communication shape preppers’ responsibility frames, challenging static portrayals of preppers as antisocial and highlighting how individualised practices of preparedness can evolve into collective orientations that complement state capacity.

articles.title: Localized Multimodal Interfaces in English-Default Mobile Apps: A Multimodal Discourse Analysis of Non-Native Users' Perception
articles.authors: Hanieh Hatefi Yousefi
articles.abstract:
The purpose of this research project is to examine how English-default and localized multimodal mobile interfaces affect user perception across six constructs: comprehension, cognitive load, motivation, inclusivity, tonal reception, and credibility. Onboarding and upgrade screens from three globally used applications (Duolingo, Spotify, and Notion) were analyzed as experienced by Italian-locale users whose devices were set to Italian, but whose interfaces remained predominantly in English. 
A mixed-methods design was used, combining qualitative multimodal discourse analysis of 24 application screenshots with quantitative descriptive statistics from a Likert-scale perception survey (n = 56). The multimodal analysis utilized a visual grammar framework, whereas the survey constructs were based on cognitive load theory, Self-Determination Theory (SDT), and digital credibility research. 
Results show moderately positive comprehension and tonal reception across all three applications, largely supported by visual elements such as mascots, icons, and color-coded calls to action. Inclusivity scored lowest overall. Italian L1 participants reported higher perceived effort and lower credibility than non-Italian participants, with the sharpest differences observed in upgrade flows.
The findings are examined in the context of linguistic justice, English as a lingua franca, and discursive legitimation. The findings support biphasic localization strategies and suggest avenues for future research employing behavioural metrics and expanded participant samples.
Keywords: multimodal discourse analysis, localization, English-default interfaces, cognitive load, linguistic justice, user experience, mobile applications

articles.title: What the Balkan Barometer Can and Cannot Rank: A Measurement Audit of the Western Balkans' Flagship Survey
articles.authors: Milos Kankaras
articles.abstract: The Balkan Barometer, annual since 2015 with roughly 1,000 face-to-face interviews in each of six Western Balkan economies, is cited across the region as what its citizens think. We evaluate it as a measuring instrument from the Regional Cooperation Council's own released microdata for 2023 to 2025, within a total survey error frame. The published percentages reproduce from the microdata (440 of 444 cells within one point). Of the fifteen pairwise economy differences on each of thirty 2025 headline items, 71 percent are resolvable at a design effect of 2.0, but only 40 percent of adjacent-rank pairs are: six points is the least difference at which two economies of 1,000 can be told apart. The WB6 figure is an unweighted mean of six economies whose populations differ tenfold; under population weights it moves by 6 to 12 points on the most-quoted items, including EU membership (64 versus 58 percent in 2025). Of twenty-three headline series present in all three editions, four are comparable throughout; between 2024 and 2025 the changed series moved by 14 points on average against 6 for the stable ones. The 2025 institutional battery is scalar invariant once two cells are freed, police in Kosovo* and courts in North Macedonia; with them freed, Kosovo*'s raw-score lead disappears and the top three economies cannot be separated. The two published editions score 16 of 32 on a documentation checklist built from what the ESS, the Eurobarometer and the AAPOR Transparency Initiative publish routinely; precision, comparability and limitations score zero. We report two database errors and a file anomaly for correction, and close with the four things a technical report would need to contain.

articles.title: An Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK: a fine-grained typology of economic activities from open, large-scale web archive data
articles.authors: Leonardo Castro Gonzalez; Emmanouil Tranos; Levi John Wolf; Rui Zhu; Emerald Dilworth
articles.abstract: We present the Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK, a granular and dynamic typology of economic activities. Built using large-scale web data from Common Crawl, the Atlas captures how UK businesses describe their economic activities, creates an activity typology and geolocates them at the postcode level. The Atlas provides a complementary source to established industrial classifications, which are static and insensitive to the evolution of economic activities. It is designed to support research and policy analysis requiring fine-grained information about economic activities over space and time. The Atlas is developed transparently using open tools and web archive data, so that it can be replicated and adapted to different research and policy contexts.

articles.title: Blaming Across the Aisle: Political Contrasting and Blame Attribution in the Danish Parliament
articles.authors: Markus Lundsfryd Jensen; Rune Egeskov Trust; Kenneth C. Enevoldsen; Sara Kolding
articles.abstract: Political discourse is widely perceived to be growing more hostile, yet robust evidence remains scarce. This study examines blame attribution in the Danish Parliament from 1997 to 2026, combining a purpose-built classifier, BlameBERT (F1: 0.80), with multilevel statistical modeling. The classifier is constructed using an annotation-efficient pipeline for blame attribution in low-to-mid resource languages. The results reveal a banana-shaped trajectory, with blame declining until around 2016 before entering a significant and sustained increase in recent years (2019-2026). Government status consistently influenced blame attribution - an effect we term political contrasting - with opposition parties blaming substantially more than governing parties. This effect was moderated by ideology: The blame-dampening effect of governing was less pronounced among right-wing parties, and ideological extremity amplified blame more strongly on the right. In recent years, the interaction between political wing and ideological extremity intensified, suggesting an ideological hardening of the blame rhetoric concentrated on the right of the political spectrum. Taken together, these patterns suggest that the perceived rise in harsh political language reflects not merely a general rhetorical drift, but an ideologically asymmetric hardening of political discourse. A sensitivity analysis showed that the conclusions were robust to varying classification thresholds.

articles.title: Organising the Social Layer: How Organisational Paradoxes Shape Engagement in Cryptocurrency Communities
articles.authors: Annika Aebli; Fabienne Silberstein-Bamford; Joshua Silberstein Bamford
articles.abstract: Cryptocurrencies (crypto) and their underlying blockchain technologies are designed around the promise of collective organising without reliance on centralised authority, intermediaries, and hierarchical coordination. Yet sustaining collective participation in decentralised networks without conventional forms of coordination remains an organisational challenge. This study demonstrates that keeping participants engaged in crypto communities depends on continuous work within crypto’s social layer. Drawing on the organisational paradox lens and 26 semi-structured interviews with developers, team members, and regular users across four crypto communities, we show that sustained engagement depends on balancing organisational paradoxes rooted in communication, decision-making, and community development: technical discourse versus social-media-style interaction, decentralised participation versus centralised guidance, and scaling versus a sense of authentic community. Our findings suggest that continually balancing, rather than resolving these tensions is essential for engagement and community cohesion. This research contributes to the theoretical understanding of decentralised organising by showing how collective participation can be maintained in organisational arrangements that seek to reduce reliance on conventional centralised structures. More broadly, we show that decentralisation does not eliminate the need for organising but relocates much of this work to the social layer of interaction, coordination, and community building, where contradictory demands must be continually negotiated to keep participation workable and sustainable.

articles.title: The Electoral Costs of Exclusion: Women’s Candidate Placement and Party Performance
articles.authors: Iris E. Acquarone; Alba Huidobro
articles.abstract: Political elites continue to behave as if including women in electable positions is electorally risky, despite growing evidence of voter support for gender-inclusive representation. This paper advances a theory of the electoral costs of exclusion, arguing that continued exclusion can become electorally costly when parties fail to adapt to changing electoral responses to women's representation. Using data from Spanish local elections (2003-2019) and a difference-in-differences design, we show that parties increasing women's representation in electable list positions gain votes and seats relative to parties that do not; this divergence coincides with gains among parties increasing women's representation and losses among those maintaining or reducing it. These consequences grow over time and are strongest where inclusion is voluntary rather than quota-mandated. Our findings challenge the idea that underrepresentation persists because inclusion fails electorally, pointing instead to a changing electoral constraint some elites may fail to recognize: exclusion has become costly.

articles.title: Still Secularizing: Cohort Replacement, Rebound, Overreporting, and Gender Convergence in a Pooled Analysis of Eight National Surveys
articles.authors: David Eagle; Joshua Gaghan
articles.abstract: Recent reports claim young men in the United States are becoming more religious. This would signal an end to the longstanding pattern of cohort-driven declines in religiosity. Pooling young-adult trends within eight national surveys measuring affiliation, attendance, salience, prayer, and biblical literalism, we find no measure shows a credible increase among young men, and the youngest cohort is no more religious than its predecessor was at the same age. The gender gap is narrowing because women are secularizing faster, not because men are returning, which likely reflects gender-based ideological realignment. Religiosity has rebounded from its pandemic trough, but not credibly past pre-pandemic levels, and the gap between self-reported attendance and time-use diaries has widened. Intense religious identity is also declining across cohorts. Variability between surveys, a post-pandemic rebound, and growing measurement drift are all confounding patterns of religious change. Cutting through the noise, cohort replacement continues to organize American religion.

articles.title: The Promise: A Breakthrough for Social Science
articles.authors: Bruno Sérgio Dias Oliveira
articles.abstract:
[SSRN has the latest version of this preprint at https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=4982428 ] 

Sociology has long wrestled with theoretical fragmentation, hindering a unified understanding of social life. This paper unveils the General Social Theory of Compromises (G-STOC), a bold framework that reimagines social phenomena through the lens of promises and their reciprocal arrangements, termed compromises. G-STOC posits that all social interactions — whether mundane exchanges or transformative societal shifts — hinge on promises, broadly defined to include not just explicit pledges but also tacit expectations, norms, and imposed duties. These promises knit together into compromises, forming the essential fabric of social relationships. The theory advances several key insights: (1) social behavior springs from actual and virtual agency, with virtual agency rooted in anticipated promises; (2) emotions like anger and disappointment reveal breaches of these promises, highlighting their omnipresence; (3) compromises unify individual actions with broader social influences; and (4) sociological insight arises from tracing these compromises across time. Emphasizing the future-oriented nature of social action, G-STOC sidesteps perennial debates like agency versus structure, offering a potent, streamlined tool to decode human interactions. This paper urges scholars to engage with G-STOC, testing its potential to revitalize social science and deepen our grasp of society’s complexities.

articles.title: Health system and hospital utilization in Chile, 1952–2020: trends, reforms, and inflection points
articles.authors: Mauricio Matus-Lopez
articles.abstract: Objective. To collect and analyze longitudinal data on hospital discharges in Chile between 1952 and 2020, both at the national level and within the public subsystem. Patterns of change were identified in relation to the following key institutional milestones: the Curative Medicine Act of 1968, the creation of the National Health Services System in 1979, and the implementation of the Universal and Guaranteed Access Reform in 2005. Methods. A first-of-its-kind time series was constructed using official sources from the Ministry of Health and institutional documents. Indicators were calculated for the total number of discharges, discharge rates per thousand population, and comparisons with the United States. The analysis included exploratory graphics and construction of segmented regression models. Results. Hospital discharges rose steadily, with two periods mirroring robust expansion of the private sector: between 1982 and 1987 and between 2006 and 2019. Public provision of hospital services slowed or decreased with the 1979 reform and with the 2005 reform, although not with the 1968 reform. Conclusion. This study provides empirical evidence on the long-term trajectory of Chilean hospital services and confirms a structural contrast between the country's major health system models and the differences in their reforms. It also underscores the need for long-term information to analyze the impact of health reforms.

articles.title: Agreeing in Principle, Disagreeing on Policy: How Beliefs About the Gender Pay Gap Shape Fairness Concerns and Policy Preferences
articles.authors: Fabian Kalleitner; Jule Adriaans; Ole Brüggemann; Cristóbal Moya; Sandra Bohmann
articles.abstract: Willingness to reduce gender inequalities partly depends on whether people are aware of them and consider them unfair. Extending scholarship centered on inequality misperceptions, we focus on beliefs about the sources of the gender pay gap (GPG), experimentally varying people's ability to attribute pay disparities to women's choices. Preregistered survey experiments in the U.S. and Germany show that information about larger (vs. smaller) and within-job (vs. overall) GPGs independently increases awareness, raises perceived unfairness, and translates into general support for government action. Initially less-supportive groups (conservatives, men) showed some of the largest increases in general support. Yet, updated beliefs did not increase support for specific policies, such as pay transparency laws or gender quotas. These findings suggest that information campaigns can affect beliefs about GPG's size and sources, but even perceiving GPGs as unfair does not bridge the gap between abstract commitment to gender equality and concrete policy support.

articles.title: Algorithms of Fabrication: Generative AI and the Reshaping of Democratic Resilience and Regime Stability
articles.authors: Guy Schleffer
articles.abstract:
The 2024 election cycle marked a strategic turning point in digital influence. While previous interference relied on algorithmic distribution, Generative AI (GenAI) has introduced a paradigm of automated fabrication, fundamentally reshaping the mechanics of political stability. This article examines GenAI as a strategic amplifier whose impact is filtered through the institutional structures of four distinct regime types.
In Strong Democracies, synthetic content accelerates epistemic erosion, dissolving the shared factual reality necessary for deliberation. In Weak Democracies, it fuels precision radicalization, enabling populist actors to bypass institutional gatekeepers and dismantle oversight from within. Conversely, Strong Autocracies co-opt GenAI for digital fortification and automated narrative control, while Weak Autocracies face synthetic volatility, where low-cost deepfakes bypass porous censorship, triggering rapid destabilization. The article concludes by proposing a four-pillar policy framework including standardized content provenance, liability reform, strategic hardware controls, and transnational enforcement to restore information integrity in an increasingly deregulated global environment.

articles.title: Rethinking methods for studying online information and health decision-making: a participant-centred approach
articles.authors: NIHR Policy Research Unit in Reproductive Health; Elena Proffitt; Nicola Merrett; Lois Harvey-Pescott; Jennifer Hall; Abigail McNiven; Abimbola Ayorinde; Kamilla Abdullayev; Rebecca French; Kelly Dickson
articles.abstract:
Online information, accessed through social media, websites, apps and artificial intelligence, is frequently described as shaping health attitudes and decision-making.  Many methodological approaches to understanding how online information influences decisions provide important insights into online content, information exposure, or user perspectives, but often struggle to capture the personalised and algorithmically curated digital environments people encounter, how they engage with information as it appears in their everyday lives, and how such encounters intersect with wider social, cultural and personal contexts to shape decision making. New methodological approaches are needed that can generate meaningful evidence about the varied realities of navigating online health information and the role it plays in decision-making.  

Drawing on reproductive justice and feminist principles that privilege participant expertise and lived experience and informed by literature and collaboration with lived and learnt experts, we co-designed a participant-centred longitudinal content-oriented study exploring the influence of online information on contraceptive decision-making. Inspired by Photovoice approaches, participants documented in real time the online information they encountered over a one-month period, capturing content presented through their own tailored digital environments. Interviews conducted before and after the collection period explored contraceptive experiences, attitudes, decision-making and reflections on the role of online information. By combining real-time documentation with in-depth interviews, this approach enabled interpretations of participants lived encounters with online information, including algorithmic changes, emerging trends, current events, and the types of content that resonated with them. Collaborators with lived experience were involved throughout the methodological development and interpretation and analysis of findings.  

This participant-selected content-oriented longitudinal design demonstrates the value of methodologies that capture and generate evidence on lived digital and offline realities as they unfold in real time. Understanding how online information shapes health decision-making requires moving beyond approaches that treat the internet as an isolated and static influence on behaviours. Online information is not a singular, stable object of inquiry but dynamic, personalised, algorithmically mediated and embedded within broader social, cultural, and political contexts. Methodologies that recognise this complexity are essential for generating evidence capable of informing empathetic and meaningful health care and support and care for people prioritising their needs and navigating complex health decisions.

articles.title: Detecting Inequality in Noisy Communication: Promises and Pitfalls of Large Language Models
articles.authors: Susanne Reinhardt; Jonathan J.B. Mijs; David Schieferdecker; Michael Vaughan
articles.abstract: How inequality is communicated shapes how it is explained, understood, and legitimated or contested. Yet studying these communicative processes at scale is challenging because inequality is multidimensional, often expressed implicitly and relationally, and context dependent. We argue that large language models (LLMs) shift, but do not eliminate, these methodological challenges. We trace the development from manual content analysis to rule-based computational approaches and machine learning to LLMs and assess how these methods combine conceptual alignment, semantic sensitivity, contextual sensitivity, and scalability. LLMs help relax some longstanding trade-offs between semantic sensitivity to meaning and scalability, thus promising more comprehensive analyses of established research questions and opening possibilities for comparative research across contexts. Yet untapping their full potential for research on inequality communication depends on addressing problems concerning conceptual validity, representation, comparative measurement, and substantive inference. We conclude by outlining a research agenda for rigorous LLM-based inequality communication research.

articles.title: L’IA dans les élections municipales 2026 : Des usages qui appellent un regard nuancé
articles.authors: Antoine Marie
articles.abstract:
The municipal elections of March 15 and 22, 2026 constitute the first
French local election in which generative artificial intelligence has
massively entered campaign practices. This research brief offers a
balanced analysis of documented uses, distinguishing legitimate
applications (poster generation, programmatic chatbots, content
synthesis) from confirmed abuses (defamatory deepfakes, misleading
images, astroturfing). While these new technological capabilities raise
legitimate concerns for the integrity of democratic debate, we argue that
their impact must be put in perspective in light of the literature on the
limited effects of mass political communication and the actual
determinants of disinformation consumption. Rather than a
catastrophism that risks fueling generalized distrust, we advocate for an
approach grounded in media literacy and the strengthening of
professional journalism.

articles.title: An Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK: a fine-grained typology of economic activities from open, large-scale web archive data
articles.authors: Leonardo Castro Gonzalez; Emmanouil Tranos; Levi John Wolf; Rui Zhu; Emerald Dilworth
articles.abstract: We present the Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK, a granular and dynamic typology of economic activities. Built using large-scale web data from Common Crawl, the Atlas captures how UK businesses describe their economic activities, creates an activity typology and geolocates them at the postcode level. The Atlas provides a complementary source to established industrial classifications, which are static and insensitive to the evolution of economic activities. It is designed to support research and policy analysis requiring fine-grained information about economic activities over space and time. The Atlas is developed transparently using open tools and web archive data, so that it can be replicated and adapted to different research and policy contexts.

articles.title: A New Era of Political Socialization? The Interplay Between Political Social Media Exposure, Conspiracy Thinking, and Political Distrust Among Dutch Younger vs. Older Generations
articles.authors: Tamar Montagne; Anouk Smeekes
articles.abstract: In recent years, populist radical-right parties (PRRP) have gained substantial electoral support in European countries, especially among younger voters. However, few studies have focused on the generational divide in PRRP voting behavior and the factors that explain why current younger generations are more likely to vote for PRRP. The current study addresses this research gap by examining whether generational differences in PRRP voting can be explained by variations in political social media exposure (PSME) and its indirect pathways through conspiracy thinking and political distrust, while accounting for the moderating role of anti-immigrant attitudes. Drawing on insights from developmental psychology, political psychology, and political science, we developed an interdisciplinary framework. We tested our expectations in the context of the Netherlands using data from the Dutch Parliamentary Election Study 2023, drawing on a sample of Dutch eligible voters. Results showed that current younger generations (Generations Y and Z) were more likely to vote for PRRP compared to older generations, partly explained by their higher PSME and subsequently, stronger conspiracy thinking and political distrust. Results further showed that the effect of conspiracy thinking on PRRP voting was particularly pronounced for respondents with low levels of anti-immigrant attitudes.

articles.title: Health-Related AI Information Seeking, Anxiety, and Professional Mental Health Service Use Among U.S. College Students
articles.authors: Tania Akter
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are becoming more widely used in students’ daily lives, yet little is known about how anxiety relates to college students’ use of generative AI for health-related information seeking. This exploratory study examined associations between anxiety, health-related generative AI information seeking, and professional mental health service use among U.S. college students. Survey-weighted logistic regression models were used to assess these associations. Results showed that higher anxiety scores were associated with greater odds of reporting health-related AI use. Among students who reported health-related AI use, higher anxiety was also associated with greater odds of professional mental health service use. Findings suggest that health-related generative AI use is an emerging behavior modestly associated with anxiety and may coexist with professional mental health help-seeking among college students.

articles.title: DE LA MAREA ROSA A SOMOS
articles.authors: RICARDO DE LA PEÑA MENA
articles.abstract: El texto analiza el surgimiento de la organización política Somos (derivada de la Marea Rosa y opositora a la autodenominada Cuarta Transformación). Examina el contexto histórico de las reformas electorales impulsadas por Andrés Manuel López Obrador (Planes A, B y C) y el proceso de obtención de su registro como partido político nacional ante el INE en 2026, enfrentando impugnaciones jurídicas y observaciones sobre su denominación y emblema.

articles.title: What is edtech for? A cross-national popularity index of educational apps
articles.authors: Lulu Shi; Basak Bozkurt
articles.abstract: Digitalisation in education is so far described through broad indicators such as market growth, venture capital investment, infrastructure provision, or device availability in schools and homes. While useful, these measures reveal little about for what purposes digital technologies are used in education, and how these purposes vary across national contexts and time. This article addresses these gaps by developing an education app popularity index based on daily top-200 education app rankings across twelve countries between 2017 and 2023: Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Norway, Poland, Spain, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Drawing on app metadata, education apps are categorised according to the services and functions they offer to understand for what purpose they serve. The ranking is then aggregated to analyse category prominence over time and across countries to understand popularity of education apps by category. The study makes three contributions. First, it provides a granular account of what educational apps offer, showing that the educational app landscape is not dominated by a single type of service but consists of a heterogeneous mixture of tutoring tools, management platforms, parent-facing communication apps and a range of apps supporting infomal learning. Second, it shows the popularity of different types of digital education services and how and their popularity shift over time. Third, it shows that these patterns vary across country contexts. Differences across countries point to that edtech usage is not only driven by individual preferences but by distinct institutional arrangements and cultures. Lastly, this study also advances a methodological approach for understanding the realities of edtech deployment by using Google Play Store data, the world’s largest app market in terms of content volume.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Constructed Recovery from Cognitive Collapse: An analytic autoethnography
articles_hidden.authors: Xin Sun
articles_hidden.abstract: Severe childhood maltreatment is known to impair brain development. However, this retrospective single-case autoethnography illustrates that an individual with extreme developmental trauma can achieve functional recovery without formal intervention. This study covers the participant’s life from birth to age 28, and the core recovery period begins with cognitive collapse at age 14 and ends with high functional recovery at age 28. This recovery is marked by the participant‑researcher’s ability to produce this manuscript. Consequently, this case shapes a distinct recovery trajectory that existing models do not capture.

articles_hidden.title: Fertility, Affiliation Transmission, and Religious Reproduction in Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Gordey Yastrebov
articles_hidden.abstract: Religious groups reproduce across generations through childbearing and the transmission of affiliation. I examine how these processes jointly shape religious composition in Germany. A pseudo-prospective design combines repeated cross-sectional surveys of women’s affiliation and fertility with retrospective information on maternal affiliation and adult offspring affiliations from the German Socio-Economic Panel. I reconstruct five-group distributions for women born in 1931-1950 and their offspring, including childless women in the starting population. Under the assumptions linking these sources, fertility differences modify but do not reverse the generational redistribution associated with affiliation transmission. Catholic point estimates indicate partial fertility compensation for transmission losses, whereas Protestant fertility provides little compensation. Lower fertility moderates but does not eliminate unaffiliated gains. Across maternal cohorts, the unaffiliated generational gap narrows as the maternal share rises toward a comparatively stable reconstructed offspring share. Unaffiliated mothers also account for a growing share of unaffiliated offspring. A conditional reconstruction for women born in 1951-1970 yields the same directions in the point estimates under fixed transmission probabilities. The findings quantify the limited extent of fertility compensation in the reconstructed religious reproduction of these cohorts.

articles_hidden.title: Empathy-Related Traits and Domain-Specific Self-Rated Creativity: Indirect Associations Through Five C-PETS Dimensions
articles_hidden.authors: Masahiro Yoshida
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examined statistical indirect associations between empathy-related traits and domain-specific self-rated creativity through five dimensions of the Creative Personality and Thinking Styles Scale (C-PETS). An online survey of 359 North American adults assessed Perspective Taking (PT), Fantasy (FS), and Empathic Concern (EC), the five C-PETS dimensions, and five domains of the Kaufman Domains of Creativity Scale (K-DOCS). Parallel multiple mediation models were estimated using 10,000 bootstrap samples and Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction. Significant total indirect effects were found for PT across all five K-DOCS domains, for FS across four domains, and for EC only for Self/Everyday creativity. After correction, significant specific indirect effects were limited to Challenge-Seeking (CS) pathways from PT and FS to all five K-DOCS domains. Because the data were cross-sectional and based on self-report, these results do not establish causal mediation. Instead, they indicate that challenge-seeking is a robust conditional statistical link between perspective-related empathy traits and domain-specific self-rated creativity.
