articles_hidden.title: Immigrant wages are lower in immigrant-dense areas, and the limited-English differential is mostly occupational: metropolitan Philadelphia, 2012–2024
articles_hidden.authors: Haobing Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Immigrants who speak limited English earn less than those who speak it well. On the protective view of residential concentration, that differential should be smaller where immigrants are concentrated, because concentration supplies employers and customers who do not require English. On the isolation view it should be larger. This study tests both views in metropolitan Philadelphia, a former gateway whose immigrant population has grown again, with American Community Survey microdata for 2012 to 2024 and a two-level model of 7,355 foreign-born workers in 48 Public Use Microdata Areas. Hourly wages are about 8 percent lower per standard deviation of area immigrant density for foreign-born workers who speak English well and about 3 percent lower, an estimate not distinguishable from zero, for those who speak it poorly. Native-born workers in the same areas show a gradient of 2 percent, so most of the difference is specific to immigrants. The interaction between density and limited English is 0.049 (standard error 0.029) and disappears once occupation is held constant. The limited-English differential is 21 percent overall and 9 percent within an occupation, so most of it is associated with the occupations limited-English workers hold. An exploratory measure of the density of the worker’s own home language gives a positive interaction of 0.046 (0.022), driven by lower wages for proficient workers rather than higher wages for limited-English workers, and the same specification in the New York metropolitan area gives 0.045 (0.009). Higher earners move from the city to the suburbs.

articles_hidden.title: List and Sequential Attention
articles_hidden.authors: Yunhao Yang
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper studies stochastic choice when both availability and presentation order may vary across choice problems. We characterize a fixed-list sequential attention model for menu choice and a sequential attention model with a common continuation profile for list choice. In the list domain, we further show that, holding preferences fixed, more persistent attention shifts choice probability toward more preferred alternatives.

articles_hidden.title: The shape of NSF openness to newcomers: same share, fewer doors
articles_hidden.authors: Jingwen Zhang; Hengyi Fu; Haining Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: Openness to new investigators is often judged by the share of awards to principal investigators (PIs) without recent funding. We examine it in fiscal year (FY) 2026, when the US National Science Foundation (NSF) made the fewest new grants in four decades. NSF made 30% fewer new research projects than in FY2025, and the number of funded PIs with no NSF award as PI in the previous decade (newcomers) fell nearly as much, yet their share of new projects barely moved (34.5% to 34.3%). CAREER, NSF's main early-career award, added 3.3 percentage points to the newcomer share, offsetting the closure of three early-career programs reserved for institutions outside the Carnegie R1 tier (−3.0 points). The stable share hid a narrowing of reach. Where those programs closed, newcomers fell by 13% at R1 universities and by 66% at institutions below R2, whereas in engineering, which kept its program, newcomers below R2 rose. CAREER's growth went to institutions with more prior NSF projects, and NSF's grant obligations to institutions below R2 fell by 44%, twice the fall at R1 universities, with no offset from other federal research agencies. Per dollar, the closed programs had produced more papers than CAREER or standard grants.

articles_hidden.title: Cruelty Across Substrates: From Animal Cruelty to Embodied AI and the Coming Detection Gap
articles_hidden.authors: Travis Gilly
articles_hidden.abstract:
Childhood cruelty to animals is among the most durable behavioral warning signs of later interpersonal
violence in the forensic and clinical literature. The predictive mechanism does not rest on any settled
answer about the moral status of the target. It rests on what the perpetrator practices, rehearses, and
trains in themselves: desensitization, dominance affect, and the social learning of cruelty as pleasure.
This paper offers a conceptual continuity argument and research agenda. We argue that the substrate
of the target is incidental to that training, with one critical qualification: the configuration of the target
matters. Routine digital destruction in static media (the static video game target, the scripted non player
character) is a categorically different case from the closed loop, contingent emotional response systems
on which the argument turns. As world models, embodied robotics, and closed loop emotional voice
systems converge toward agents that perform distress in ways a user cannot reliably distinguish from a
being in pain, we argue that the dispositional consequences of practiced cruelty against those agents are
likely to recruit sufficiently similar mechanisms to warrant clinical and forensic attention. The paper does
not claim that synthetic agents are moral patients. It claims that the warning signal forensic and clinical
fields have relied upon for fifty years risks migrating to a venue with substantially diminished detection
infrastructure. Existing human robot interaction research already shows that users do not need to believe
a synthetic agent is conscious to respond to it through social, emotional, or dominance based scripts. The
Kantian observation that cruelty corrupts the cruel is sufficient to ground the argument. Conduct disorder
assessment, character evidence frameworks, school counseling protocols, and pre employment screening
for sensitive roles will need to adapt or lose one of the more durable early behavioral indicators available
to forensic and clinical assessment. The paper is offered as agenda setting; the operational protocols it
identifies as necessary are deliberately scoped to a planned companion paper.

articles_hidden.title: Researcher well-being as a leading indicator in research-funding governance: A system dynamics exploration of top-down versus bottom-up allocation
articles_hidden.authors: Tomoko Sakai; Satoshi Sano
articles_hidden.abstract: Governments face a recurring dilemma in dividing public research funding between top-down, competitive, mission-oriented programmes and bottom-up, investigator-led institutional grants. This research note presents an exploratory system dynamics model that endogenizes researcher motivation, conceived following self-determination theory as a slow-moving stock of psychological capital, within the feedback structure linking funding allocation, research outputs, and societal returns. Simulation experiments across three policy scenarios reveal a consistent time-asymmetric pattern. First, accelerating the shift toward competitive funding produces an earlier but lower peak in societal returns, followed by sustained decline. Second, shifting toward bottom-up funding restores motivation but opens a transition valley in returns whose depth grows with transition speed. Third, delayed corrective reallocation exhibits hysteresis: once motivation is depleted, even aggressive reallocation requires roughly two decades before returns recover. One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis indicates that these qualitative patterns persist across the tested parameter ranges, while the level of long-run returns proves highly sensitive to the weight placed on discretionary research time, around which the baseline system undergoes a regime shift. The model implies that researcher well-being functions as a leading indicator of research-system health, preceding declines in publication-based lagging indicators. We derive three testable propositions and outline an agenda for empirical calibration, beginning with a national baseline survey of researchers being launched in Japan. For funding governance, the results imply that monitoring leading indicators and pacing allocation transitions matter as much as choosing the allocation ratio itself.

articles_hidden.title: Lexical, Syntactic, and Semantic Distances Across Five Languages: A Reproducible Framework Integrating Python NLP and R Statistical Modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Shunxin Yao
articles_hidden.abstract: Quantitative comparisons across languages have traditionally relied on manually curated typological features, while recent advances in multilingual language models provide new opportunities for large-scale cross-linguistic research. This paper presents a reproducible framework that integrates natural language processing and statistical modeling to examine lexical, syntactic, and semantic variation across English, Chinese, Spanish, French, and German. Drawing on a corpus of 1,860 Wikipedia articles, the study combines traditional linguistic indicators with LaBSE-based semantic representations. The results show that language differences dominate the observed variation, with Chinese forming a distinct outlier and English and Spanish exhibiting the greatest similarity. Moreover, lexical-syntactic distances are significantly correlated with semantic distances derived from Transformer embeddings. These findings suggest that traditional quantitative measures and modern representation-learning approaches capture complementary aspects of language structure and meaning. The framework offers a scalable methodology for multilingual corpus linguistics and quantitative typology.

articles_hidden.title: Position: A Score Should Travel With Its Repair History
articles_hidden.authors: Louis Yiven Zhu
articles_hidden.abstract: Machine learning settles many capability claims with scores on accepted benchmarks, and a venue reviews a benchmark once, when it accepts the paper that introduces it. We call this arrangement review once, use forever. We argue that it leaves without stewardship the instruments that, on the literature's account, carry much of the field's adjudication. Reforms of peer review in AI research should therefore extend to them. In the public record of MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding), five projects sharing no author with one another or with the original repaired four defects in 2024. Language model agents coded 194 passages in 26 documents under written rules. In the 170 reporting events, the passages that report a model's score, we test whether six qualifications accompany the score. Model reports attach 1.05 of six qualifications per event (95% interval [0.85, 1.32]) against 1.70 in the repair papers ([1.47, 2.08]). Of their 77 events, 21% carry no qualification ([10%, 31%]) and none carries an item-error qualification. After MMLU-Pro and MMLU-Redux appeared in June 2024, 19 of 28 model-report events on the original MMLU print a repaired variant beside it without its reason. On a second benchmark, Humanity's Last Exam, none of 14 events in nine 2026 model releases carries an item-error qualification. We propose three norms, with the cost of each to the actor who enforces it, and answer six alternative views.

articles_hidden.title: Single Family Schoolyards: Residential Zoning and School Segregation
articles_hidden.authors: Stan Nguyen Oklobdzija; Nicholas Marantz; Carolina Reid
articles_hidden.abstract: Though the Supreme Court's 1954 decision in Brown v. Board of Education outlawed explicit segregation of public schools, segregation has remained stubbornly persistent in the intervening decades. What explains continuous racial segregation in the absence of explicit policy? One possible driver is America's built environment designed with similar segregationist impulses but not subject to the same corrective legal action. Zoning and land use policy influence where households of different means can live, thereby sorting their children across schools. We investigate this link drawing on housing unit counts from the American Community Survey, apportioned to 923 school district boundaries and 13,002 school attendance zones with 27 million residential parcels. We find that districts where single-family and multifamily housing is spread unevenly across attendance zones are more segregated by race and income. Schools with attendance zones that contain a higher proportion of single-family detached residences enroll a disproportionately high share of Asian and White students, as compared with their districts. When an attendance zone boundary is redrawn to encompass a higher share of single-family housing, its Asian and White share increases further. These findings help illuminate how land use policy influences educational segregation and contributes to literature on how policies that regulate the built environment affect racial sorting.

articles_hidden.title: Machine-Learning Geographic Sampling Frames Underrepresent People on the Move in Fragile Settings
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Carlomaria Caflisch; Daniel Masterson; Stephen Daniel O'Connell; Ettan Patel; Julia Smith Omomo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Political science research often studies difficult-to-locate populations: internally displaced persons (IDPs), returnees, migrants, and others who move during war, disaster,
or crisis. We compare machine-learning (ML)-generated building footprints against high-resolution satellite imagery for constructing sampling frames. In displacement-
affected communities in Iraq, 15.5% of ML points were invalid or duplicated, and manual additions constituted 19% of the final hybrid frame. Manual additions reached
10.2 percentage points more IDPs in rural communities and 10.1 more returnees in urban areas. We attribute differences to two mechanisms: temporary and informal
shelters are harder for ML algorithms to detect, while post-bombardment reconstruction can create structures absent from the imagery underlying ML frames. ML-only
frames produce systematic coverage error, and targeted satellite validation can reduce it.

articles_hidden.title: MAGA Republicans as  “Particularistic Authoritarians” on the Welfare State:  Parallels with the European Populist Right
articles_hidden.authors: Jake Haselswerdt; Hang Qi; Suhyun Cho
articles_hidden.abstract: Has MAGA remade the Republican politics of the welfare state? While Republican voters have traditionally favored retrenchment, the so-called “populism” of the MAGA movement suggests that the social policy preferences of right-leaning Americans are due for reexamination. Drawing from the “particularistic authoritarian model” of European populist radical-right voters, we expect MAGA Republicans to favor benefits for deserving groups, stronger “workfare” policies, less social investment, and more restrictive deservingness criteria. We test these expectations using a 1,000-respondent module of the 2025 Cooperative Election Study. Factor analysis and regressions show that MAGA Republicans are substantially more supportive than non-MAGA Republicans of policies benefiting seniors and express levels of support comparable to those of Democrats and other respondents. MAGA Republicans also show somewhat stronger endorsement of restrictive deservingness criteria than other Republicans, while differences between the two Republican groups are less pronounced for social investment. Overall, the results indicate that MAGA Republicans do not simply favor either welfare state expansion or retrenchment. Instead, they distinguish among forms of social protection according to their beneficiaries and perceived deservingness.

articles_hidden.title: Are the children of homeowners increasingly advantaged? Trends in relative and absolute mobility of homeownership in Europe
articles_hidden.authors: Selçuk Bedük; Enrico Benassi; Philipp M. Lersch
articles_hidden.abstract: Homeownership is declining among younger generations across Europe. A common assumption is that this decline has been increasingly stratified by parental homeownership, due to rising house prices and the growing importance of parental financial support. We show that this assumption does not hold for the average European (and for most countries). Using data from EU-SILC 2011 and 2019 covering 24 European countries, we examine trends in relative and absolute mobility of homeownership for birth cohorts 1951 to 1984. On average, relative mobility remained largely stable across cohorts, while absolute mobility increased. The apparent stability of relative mobility masks a deeper structural cohort shift: downward mobility increased from 14 per cent to 38 per cent, while upward mobility declined from 23 per cent to 8 per cent between cohorts born in the early 1950s and early 1980s. Therefore, homeownership has declined significantly for both children of homeowners and renters. We also compare absolute and relative mobility trends across countries and show that they often diverge for two reasons. First, a mechanical effect of the origin distribution: in countries with widespread parental homeownership, relative mobility largely reflects changes in upward mobility. Second, the source of mobility: using two novel counterfactual simulations, we show that observed absolute mobility changes mainly stem from structural shifts in homeownership chances, rather than strengthening parent-child associations.

articles_hidden.title: The Space Headright System: A Diachronic Analysis of First-Mover Elite Formation Mechanisms from Colonial Virginia to Twenty-First-Century Space Resource Law
articles_hidden.authors: Shungo Arai
articles_hidden.abstract:
This study examines how first-mover advantage was converted into durable elite dominance in seventeenth-century colonial Virginia, using this structural logic to critically evaluate twenty-first-century space resource law. Drawing on a Multilayered Frontier Capital Accumulation Model (MFCAM) that integrates frontier theory, world-systems theory, and institutional path dependence, the study addresses four research questions (RQ1–RQ4). Historical analysis shows how the First Families of Virginia (FFV), preempting land under the 1618 headright system, monopolized power through mutually reinforcing mechanisms of institutional pre-emption, marital closure, and symbolic capital accumulation, thereby converting land capital into political and cultural capital to maintain that dominance. At the same time, the study traces the formation of a lower-white stratum through indentured servitude, post-release landlessness, and racial divide-and-rule policies after Bacon's Rebellion (1676) and shows that elite and lower-class formation were two sides of the same institutional design. A comparison with the Massachusetts Bay Colony suggests these outcomes depended on early institutional choices.

Based on these findings, the study conceptualizes a "Space Headright System" (SHS) comprising priority access to institutional design, revolving-door relations between regulators and industry, and the accumulation of legal precedent. By examining Section 402 of the 2015 U.S. Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act, the Artemis Accords, and national space resource laws, it assesses risks of lower-class formation such as space indentured servitude and space company towns. The study advances a conditional warning: if current legal trajectories continue, they suggest convergence toward a Virginia-type stratified order. To avert this, three policy recommendations (primary rules)—an international space cadastre, a Space Commons Fund, and treaty-based protections for later settlers—are proposed, alongside secondary design requirements to guard the implementing institutions against regulatory capture.

articles_hidden.title: The Relationship between China's One-Child Policy and Female Empowerment
articles_hidden.authors: Wendi Wang; Qing Guan; Natalie Nitsche
articles_hidden.abstract: Vanessa Fong (2002) theorised that China's One-Child Policy (OCP; 1979–2016) enhanced female empowerment by removing competition from sons and allowing daughters to obtain resources traditionally reserved for sons. However, no systematic review has comprehensively assessed the available evidence on this issue. Drawing on Fong’s framework, we examined the relationship between the OCP and female empowerment across seven subfields: family investment and parental support, education, employment and career development, gender attitudes and norms, intergenerational relationships, reproductive rights and autonomy, and other social dynamics. We searched six scientific databases, yielding 1265 sources and, after applying exclusion criteria, analyzed 32 studies published between 2002 and 2024. The majority (21 of 32) report a positive relationship between the OCP and female empowerment. Resource concentration driven by reduced sibling size emerges as a central mechanism, benefiting only-daughters in family investment, education, and career development. In contrast, impacts on mothers are more mixed; while the OCP reduced childbirth burdens and enhanced life autonomy, it also violated reproductive rights and imposed disproportionate contraceptive burdens on women. Moreover, it emerges the OCP's empowering effects were contingent on external conditions, such as local educational and economic resources or place of residence. We point out various research gaps in the existing literature, amongst other the consistent failure to distinguish the OCP’s effects from concurrent socio-economic transformations. Nonetheless, the evidence suggests that the OCP, together with broader social changes, has shaped women's lives and promoted female empowerment, although its impacts were neither uniform nor inherent, but rather shaped by contextual factors.

articles_hidden.title: A comment on “A Mother's Voice: Impacts of Spousal Communication Training on Child Health Investments”
articles_hidden.authors: Evan Veer; Lenka Fiala
articles_hidden.abstract: Björkman Nyqvist et al. (2024) evaluate a randomized experiment in rural Uganda that studies whether strengthening women’s communication skills within marriage can shift household decisions toward greater investment in child health. All treatments provide health and nutrition training, varying whether mothers or fathers are involved, while one additional treatment incorporates a communication skills curriculum for mothers, allowing the authors to isolate the effect of communication. The authors report five core findings: First, women offered communication training report improved relationship quality. Second, the communication treatment increases the frequency of discussions between spouses about health and finances, but does not improve men’s health knowledge, indicating limited information transmission. Third, communication training does not increase the adoption of health-promoting behaviors beyond the gains from women’s health training alone. Fourth, the communication training shifts household spending, particularly on meat and fish. Fifth, none of the treatments improves the study's primary child health outcomes. We successfully computationally reproduce the paper's main claims, and show that the results are robust to corrections for multiple hypothesis testing, inclusion of control variables in analyses, and an alternative definition of relationship quality measure.

articles_hidden.title: Recordable participation and the construction of student engagement in UK higher education
articles_hidden.authors: Xinqi Yu
articles_hidden.abstract: Student engagement is widely invoked as evidence of educational quality, yet its meanings are contested. This article examines how the concept is constructed and mobilised in UK higher education research, policy and institutional documentation. Drawing on Bacchi’s problematisation approach and Fairclough’s critical discourse analysis, it analyses a purposive corpus of 36 texts: 23 conceptual and research texts, two policy documents and 11 institutional documents from three West Midlands universities. Iterative close reading identifies three connected patterns. Multidimensional accounts of engagement are narrowed into visible proxies; evaluative infrastructures privilege meanings that can be documented and compared; and these constructions redistribute responsibility in ways that obscure unequal conditions of participation. Worked coding examples show how support, attendance, digital traces and regular logging become linked in institutional procedures. The article argues that recordable participation acquires authority because it can serve as evidence of both student conduct and institutional quality. This does not eliminate relational or participatory meanings, but places them at a disadvantage within systems organised around demonstrable performance. The contribution is to explain how the demand for evidence connects conceptual narrowing to unequal recognition, and why institutions should distinguish the visibility of participation from the conditions that make participation possible.

articles_hidden.title: Resilience by Design: Adhocracy, Collaborative Governance, and Public-Private-Nonprofit Partnerships in Bergamo’s COVID-19 Economic Recovery
articles_hidden.authors: Paolo Valter Caroli; Francesco Longo
articles_hidden.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic revealed the vulnerabilities of traditional bureaucratic governance structures in responding effectively to rapid, large-scale crises. This paper presents a detailed case study of Rinascimento, an innovative urban recovery program launched in Bergamo, Italy—one of the epicenters of the early pandemic. It explores how an adhocratic governance model, characterized by :lexibility, decentralization, and cross-sector collaboration, was employed to mitigate the economic impact of the crisis. The program was implemented through a public-private-nonpro:it partnership involving the Municipality of Bergamo, Intesa Sanpaolo Bank, and CESVI, a local humanitarian NGO. Drawing on collaborative governance and network theories, the Rinascimento initiative combined emergency grants and impact investment loans to support nearly 4,500 small businesses and professionals. The paper analyzes the design and operational mechanisms of the adhocracy, its rapid decision-making capabilities, and its emphasis on real-time learning and adaptation. Empirical evaluation using key performance indicators demonstrates the program’s effectiveness in enhancing business resilience, reducing business mortality rates, and fostering economic regeneration. The :indings underscore the potential of adhocratic models in municipal crisis management and offer scalable insights for future governance frameworks addressing systemic shocks.

articles_hidden.title: From Governance to Government? The European Commission and the three faces of politicisation
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Nicoli; Lorenzo Lombardi
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on the politicisation of the European Union has concentrated on reactive, bottom-up contestation of existing EU action. This article argues that such an understanding is incomplete because it conflates politicisation of issues with politicisation of institutions. We distinguish three faces of politicisation. Reactive politicisation refers to the public contestation of existing EU competences. Proactive politicisation occurs when supranational actors claim a political mandate in order to justify wider discretion. Induced politicisation emerges when intergovernmental conflict over already politicized state functions creates a vacuum that the Commission can try to fill, thereby inheriting the political character of the function itself. The empirical sections focus on induced politicisation. They reconstruct three episodes: Jean-Claude Juncker's attempt to use EMU deadlock to place the Commission at the centre of euro-area reform; the failed institutionalisation of an EU Finance Minister, a euro-area fiscal capacity, and a more political treasury function; and Ursula von der Leyen's attempts to centralise foreign-policy initiative during successive geopolitical crises. The argument is that politicisation does not only constrain supranational action. Under specific institutional conditions it can also widen supranational authority by transforming the Commission from guardian of the Treaties into a proto-governmental executive.

articles_hidden.title: Sectoral Credit Reallocation and Consumer Credit Expansion: A Difference-in-Differences and Decomposition Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Gudzenko Vladislav
articles_hidden.abstract: This article examines sectoral bank-credit reallocation in Kyrgyzstan by combining a difference in differences (DiD) comparison around 2015 with a detailed accounting analysis for 2019–2025. The research question is how conclusions about reallocation depend on the comparison period, portfolio denominator and distinction between shares and real balances. Four focal lending categories are compared with a residual category in a historical series extended through 2025. The full-portfolio DiD contrast is +1.28 percentage points for 2010–2025, but −0.17 points when the window begins in 2012; the group gap already changes substantially before 2015. In the recent period, consumer loans rise from 11.8% to 33.6% of bank credit and account for 42.5% of the nominal increase in the outstanding portfolio. CPI-deflated non-consumer credit grows by 49.3%. Agriculture loses portfolio share while its real balance grows by 12.3%; industry and construction experience real declines of 34.7% and 17.5%. A symmetric decomposition separates the changing consumer-credit mix from redistribution within non-consumer lending. The integrated findings show why positive period-average sectoral contrasts can coexist with recent share losses and uneven real growth. DiD remains descriptive, and the decomposition is an accounting identity. Neither identifies the effect of accession or consumer-credit crowding out. Independent verification of the historical inputs remains incomplete.

articles_hidden.title: Workplace Mental Health and Psychological Safety: A Systematic Review of Interventions and Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Khairunnisa Budiyanto
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Workplace mental health and psychological safety are critical determinants of employee wellbeing, organizational performance, and public health. Despite growing recognition of their importance, evidence on effective interventions across occupational sectors remains fragmented, and the moderating role of psychosocial safety climate (PSC) is underexplored in existing syntheses.
Objective. This systematic review synthesizes global evidence on individual- and organizational-level workplace mental health interventions, with particular attention to psychological safety climate as a moderating construct and the differential effectiveness of universal versus targeted delivery models.
Methods. A comprehensive, PRISMA 2020-compliant search was conducted across  PubMed and Google Scholar databases, covering publications from 2011 to 2026. Ninety-seven records were identified; following removal of four duplicates, 93 deduplicated records were retained, encompassing systematic reviews, meta-analyses, umbrella reviews, and qualitative syntheses. Quality appraisal employed ROBINS-I, QATQS, AXIS, Downs and Black, GRADE, and EPHPP tools.
Results. Individual-level digital interventions demonstrated the strongest measurable short-term effects: mindfulness-based eHealth programs (Hedge’s g = 0.60) outperformed cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT; g = 0.15) and stress management programs (g = 0.17). Web-based interventions improved psychological wellbeing (g = 0.37) and work effectiveness (g = 0.25), with effects sustained at follow-up (g = 0.23). Targeted delivery yielded markedly larger effects for stress management (g = 0.64–0.69) compared to universal delivery (g = 0.00). Universal CBT reduced depression across the general workforce (SMD = 0.16). Manager training significantly increased mental health knowledge (SMD = 0.73). Among healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic, pooled disorder prevalence reached 36% for depression, 37% for PTSD, 27% for stress, 47% for anxiety, and 49% for insomnia. Organizational-level interventions showed mixed results with high heterogeneity.
Conclusions. Effective workplace mental health promotion requires multi-layered strategies that combine scalable digital tools with organizational structural changes and manager capability building. Future research should prioritize longitudinal designs, under-represented worker populations, cost-effectiveness analyses, and the integration of PSC measurement into intervention frameworks.

articles_hidden.title: Analisis Value Chain Upgrading Komoditas Kakao melalui Strategi Branding dan Diferensiasi Produk di Sabang
articles_hidden.authors: Daudy Sukma; Sofia Keumalasari; Azlina; Zahriatul Aini; Aulia Hafizah Nazwa
articles_hidden.abstract:
Kakao Sabang memiliki potensi terroir — rasa dan aroma khas — namun
produksi dan luas lahan menurun dalam lima tahun terakhir, dengan mayoritas
biji masih dijual non-fermentasi bernilai rendah. Penelitian kualitatif ini
memetakan rantai nilai (value chain analysis atau VCA) dan mengidentifikasi peluang peningkatan nilai (value chain upgrading atau VCU) kakao Sabang
melalui wawancara mendalam terhadap petani, pengumpul, UMKM pengolah,
dan Dinas Pertanian Kota Sabang, dilengkapi triangulasi sumber. Hasil
menunjukkan premi harga fermentasi mencapai 200 persen, namun hanya
terealisasi pada jalur petani–UMKM, belum pada jalur pengumpul umum.
Ditemukan pola functional upgrading organik berupa UMKM yang berperan
sebagai pengumpul mutu. Penelitian ini merumuskan strategi branding berbasis
marketing mix 7-P dengan perspektif consumer agency, merekomendasikan
perluasan insentif fermentasi dan formalisasi Indikasi Geografis sebagai
instrumen branding jangka panjang.

articles_hidden.title: A Middle Way proposal towards an equitable open access publishing model
articles_hidden.authors: Diogo Provete
articles_hidden.abstract: Open access promised to widen participation in science, but the article-processing charge (APC) that funds much of gold open access has shifted the cost of publishing onto authors, reproducing rather than removing exclusion for the Global South. Writing as a journal editor based in Brazil, I argue that the instruments now relied upon, namely fee waivers, purchasing-power-parity pricing and transformative agreements, are each useful but insufficient, because each treats a structural problem as a matter of discounting. Latin America's non-commercial diamond model, exemplified by SciELO, has shown that affordable open access is achievable at roughly a tenth of the cost of a commercial APC, yet it remains constrained by limited global visibility. I propose a “Middle Way”: a public–private model in which national governments fund and own the core publishing infrastructure as a public good, as Brazil is now doing through the nationalisation of SciELO, while commercial firms are contracted, on transparent and unbundled terms, for the services they perform better, chiefly discoverability and global distribution. Ownership stays public, and the commercial sector becomes a contracted supplier rather than the owner of the venue. The proposal's scope condition is ownership: it fits systems where the publishing venue is, or can become, publicly or institutionally owned.

articles_hidden.title: Youth physical activity in transitioning subsistence societies varies by biological maturity and market integration
articles_hidden.authors: Lee Gettler; Vidrige Kandza; Jessica K. Hlay; Haneul Jang; Rahul C. Oka; Francy Kiabiya Ntamboudila; Derlan Brenez Bihoundou Mouketou; Chelvin Destin Siassia Vindou; Evrahd Ngalekandza; Brel Koubemba
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Physical activity patterns across childhood and adolescence help shape long-term health and contribute to the allocation of limited resources among growth, maintenance, and reproduction during maturation. The vast majority of data on youth physical activity comes from post/industrial societies. We know relatively little about youth physical activity in smaller-scale subsistence contexts where youth routinely contribute to production and household tasks under energetically demanding conditions. Methods: Using wearable technology, we measured moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) and sedentary behavior among BaYaka forager and Bantu fisher-farmer youth (N=206; obs. days=798) in the Congo Basin. These communities live under energetically-demanding conditions and varying degrees of early market integration. Results: Youth were highly physically active, averaging 4.07 hours of daily MVPA. Forager females had the highest routine MVPA, although foragers were more sedentary than farmers. Developmentally, youth who were more pubertally advanced engaged in a lower percentage of daily MVPA, and older youth were more sedentary. Youth residing in the most market-integrated village engaged in a lower percentage of daily MVPA compared to the least-integrated village. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that youth facultatively adjust their activity levels as they biologically mature and that physical activity is lower with incipient market integration. The routinely high levels of youth physical activity in these communities underscore the gap between subsistence lifestyles in energetically-demanding environments and physical activity in post/industrialized societies. From a global public health perspective, our findings highlight a crucial window during early economic transitions for public health interventions aimed at preventing physical inactivity and the chronic disease burden associated with lifestyle shifts.

articles_hidden.title: Insights into the scale, organisation, implementation and motivations behind dog culling in a rabies-endemic setting
articles_hidden.authors: tasmin alexander; Kennedy Lushasi; Lwitiko Sikana; Anna Czupryna; Elaine Ferguson; Mirava Yuson; Deborah Nadal; Nicholas Hanley; Nai Rui Chng; Sarah Cleaveland
articles_hidden.abstract: Culling is recognised as ineffective and potentially counterproductive for sustainable dog population management and rabies control, yet the practice persists in many countries. Empirical data on the scale, organisation, implementation and motivations behind culling remain sparse, limiting understanding of its persistence, and implications. Focusing on Tanzania, a rabies-endemic country where culling has been documented, this study uses a mixed-methods approach, combining two structured surveys (survey of occurrence, n = 51; survey of practice in districts reporting culling, n = 16) and in-depth interviews with district and field-based veterinary and livestock officers (n = 8). Culling was reported in 45% of surveyed districts (23/51). Culling events were reportedly led by veterinary departments, often with involvement of other sectors and communities, with officers also describing communities as carrying out some culling independently. Culling was motivated by complaints, requests and orders about the number of and harms attributed to free-roaming dogs. Roaming dogs were culled regardless of ownership, sterilisation and vaccination status, using methods inconsistent with humane killing standards. Extrapolating from the survey data, using a stochastic simulation, we estimate approximately 26,000 dogs (95% CI 20,000-33,000) are culled annually nationwide. Culling was difficult to reconcile with evidence-based international guidance on dog population management and rabies control, national animal welfare legislation, and One Health principles, underscoring the need to understand and address the factors sustaining it. Addressing culling will require engaging with the wider concerns motivating the practice, and with the sectors and communities involved.

articles_hidden.title: Accountability Among Allies: Intra-Party Competition and the Electoral Cost of Scandal
articles_hidden.authors: Stefano Sangiovanni; Giovanna Maria Invernizzi; Andrea Ceron
articles_hidden.abstract: When do voters electorally punish politicians for scandals? We argue that a scandal changes votes only when it can tip voters who are near indifference between candidates, and that intra-party contests place far more voters in that position than inter-party contests. We formalize this argument in a model of electoral sanctioning and test it in a pre-registered conjoint experiment on 3,000 U.S. adults. The scandal penalty is about 57% larger in intra-party contests, and, as the model predicts, the amplification appears even when both candidates come from the party the voter opposes. Inter-party choice settings may therefore understate how strongly voters punish misconduct when credible co-partisan alternatives are available.

articles_hidden.title: Industrializing Eastern Slovakia and Its Post- Socialist Legacy: The Cases of the East Slovak Ironworks in Košice and the Metal Working Factory in Medzev
articles_hidden.authors: Tereza Juhászová
articles_hidden.abstract:
This article explores patterns of post-socialist reindustrialization in Eastern Slovakia—a region
deeply shaped by heavy socialist industrialization and subsequently exposed to the tumultuous
“manager’s privatization” of the 1990s. Bridging social and economic history, it argues that
inherited industrial legacies—in know-how, infrastructure, workforce, and export orientation—
persisted even after a sharp decline in the first decade following the fall of socialism. Through
two case studies—the “giant” East Slovak Ironworks near the regional capital Košice and a
smaller metalworking factory in the nearby town of Medzev—the article shows how foreign
investment, limited state intervention, and local agency jointly enabled the partial revitalization
of regionally significant industries, despite the absence of a coherent industrial policy and the
dismantling of state coordination after 1989. Drawing on archival records, contemporary press,
and biographical interviews, the study traces the long-term trajectories of these sites within both
socialist development agendas and post-socialist restructuring. By demonstrating how
industrial continuity and reactivation emerged largely in the absence of strategic governance
and industrial policy, the article contributes to broader debates on post-socialist varieties of
capitalism, state capacity, and the uneven geography of industrial transformation. By
foregrounding continuity and reinvention, this nuanced perspective challenges binary accounts
of post-socialist change.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Employment in Mothers’ Careers After First Birth: A Comparison of South Korea and the United States
articles_hidden.authors: Wonjeong Jeong
articles_hidden.abstract: Upon parenthood, women face pressure to reorganize their paid work and careers. In this process, self-employment can offer a distinct option, with a different set of risks and benefits than wage work. Yet research on mothers’ employment trajectories rarely examines self-employment as a distinct option. This paper examines how self-employment fits into mothers’ careers after their first birth and how this pattern differs between two institutional contexts: South Korea and the United States. Using the Korean Labor and Income Panel Study and the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, I track mothers’ employment history from their first birth through the following ten years. Descriptive and sequence analyses show that one in five mothers experiences self-employment at least once, but the way they leverage it differs by institutional context. In South Korea, self-employment more often follows nonemployment, is primarily full-time, and occurs within trajectories leading back to paid work. In the United States, mothers more often enter self-employment from wage work, while part-time self-employment appears intermittently in wage-centered trajectories. Thus, self-employment occupies different positions across these two contexts, where mothers’ counterfactual career options vary. As technology shifts, the potential importance of diverse forms of self-employment, including contract-based gig work, may increase, raising the need for future research to examine how self-employment fits into one’s career.

articles_hidden.title: “It’s Hard to See It Through Clinical Eyes When It’s Yourself”:    General Practice and Community Healthcare Professionals’ Experiences of Domestic Abuse, Disclosure, & Help-Seeking
articles_hidden.authors: Sandi Dheensa; Rebecca Cox; Judith Worthington; Paula Whittaker; Gene Feder; Alison Gregory
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Domestic abuse is highly prevalent and causes wide-ranging harms. Healthcare professionals are especially likely to receive disclosures and international policies call for a robust healthcare response to abuse.  But the needs of affected healthcare professionals (HCPs) have been sidelined. Globally, 42% of female HCPs report lifetime experience of domestic abuse. Our study aimed to explore how experiencing domestic abuse affects HCPs to understand the safety and support interventions needed. 
Methods
We used semi-structured interviews with 18 National Health Service primary and community HCPs and used Framework Analysis, drawing on four interrelated concepts: problem recognition, stigma, candidacy, and professional identity.  
Results
Perpetrators used HCP-survivors’ roles against them and domestic abuse had wide-ranging consequences for work. Remaining themes mapped onto HCP-survivors’ trajectory towards support, including problems with recognising and/or naming domestic abuse, the impact of recognising and naming it, reflections on different support options, consequences of workplace disclosure, support experiences, and reflections on what needs to change. Professional identity and profession-related factors affected each aspect of this trajectory, delaying recognition of domestic abuse and making help-seeking and positive support experiences less likely.  
Conclusion
Building an effective and compassionate healthcare response to domestic abuse will be impossible without attending to HCP-survivors’ needs and the inadequate responses of fellow HCPs. HCP-survivors are likely assets in improving responses to patients, colleagues, and students; but without support may experience trauma symptoms. We recommend improved first-line responses to HCP-survivors in workplaces and a move towards a recognition of HCPs as potential survivors in domestic abuse education, funding, and interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Closure without Resolution in European Prison Oversight
articles_hidden.authors: Nasrul Ismail
articles_hidden.abstract: Compliance with judgments of the European Court of Human Rights is conventionally recorded as a terminal status: a case is open or closed, a judgment executed or pending, an obligation met or unmet. These measures enable scholarly comparison, but they cannot show how a state engages with the supervision of a judgment or whether reform of prison conditions endures. As such, this article treats compliance as conduct and asks whether the closure of supervision reflects durable improvement in the conditions a judgment addressed. Drawing on the documentary record of Committee of Ministers supervision in three pilot-judgment jurisdictions (i.e., Italy, Romania, and Hungary), with two contextual comparators (i.e., Spain and England and Wales), it codes state disclosures for opacity and stance and reconstructs responsiveness descriptively from the dated supervisory sequence. Two independent coders reached strong agreement (Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.88 for stance and 0.90 for opacity, on small, well-specified eligible data sets). The cases did not form a single compliance scale but displayed distinct configurations. Specifically, Italy was transparent but shifted in its stated position before closure in 2016; Romania combined continuing engagement with capacity explanations; and Hungary combined formal but insubstantial engagement with selective disclosure. Set against current prison occupancy, the state that had completed supervision was the most overcrowded: Italy recorded 120.7 occupants per 100 places, exceeding Hungary's 114.5 and Romania's 111.2. Because the occupancy snapshot postdated Italy's closure, it could not reveal whether closure caused the later overcrowding, but it did manifest that closure did not secure lasting improvement in reforms. The article frames this durability gap as a problem of means-ends decoupling and offers a reproducible method for distinguishing compliance conduct from the substantive conditions oversight exists to change.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Good and Bad Controls: Endogenous Legal Factors in Sentencing Research
articles_hidden.authors: Jose Pina-Sánchez; Andrzej Uhl
articles_hidden.abstract: Observational studies of institutional decision-making often rely on explanatory variables that are themselves partly constructed through the process under investigation. In sentencing research, many legal factors are defined by the judge and may therefore act simultaneously as confounders and mediators. Controlling for them may introduce post-treatment bias, whereas omitting them may reintroduce confounding bias. We propose overcoming this impasse by conceptualising judicially-defined legal factors as variables affected by measurement error. Using a typical regression model of racial disparities in the U.S. Federal Courts, we demonstrate how sensitivity analyses based on SIMEX and Monte Carlo simulations can be used to assess the bias arising from judicial disagreement and judicial prejudice. We show that even modest levels of uncertainty in discretionary legal factors can generate substantial and unpredictable bias, affecting estimates of racial disparities even when measurement error is entirely random and therefore unrelated to race.

articles_hidden.title: The Self-Destruction Hypothesis of Consumerism: The Inflation of Consumption Standards and the Mismatch with Household Income
articles_hidden.authors: ZY Liu; Di Yuan
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper proposes and develops a theoretical proposition concerning the endogenous evolution of consumerism: consumerism may not necessarily come to an end because of “excessive consumption”; rather, by continuously raising the consumption standards associated with “normal life,” it may make an increasing number of ordinary workers unable to participate in the consumption patterns it has itself constructed, thereby eroding the demand base on which it depends. Consumer demand has a positive expansionary effect during the early stages of economic development. The paper then explains why social consumption standards may continue to rise through three channels: firm competition; positional goods and social comparison; and the diffusion and amplification of cultural products and social media. On this basis, it argues that under conditions of market competition, firms simultaneously need to expand effective demand on the consumer side and have an inherent incentive to control labor costs, creating a structural mismatch between the growth of workers’ incomes and the rise of consumption standards. When consumption standards grow persistently faster than the actual disposable incomes of ordinary workers, consumption behavior may shift from “keeping up with the standard” toward “reducing, postponing, or even exiting consumption,” with particularly concentrated effects in marriage and family formation. Using the decline in China’s marriage and birth rates, the rising consumption standards associated with wedding photography and housing, and the adjustment of the real-estate sector as illustrative empirical cases, the paper distinguishes two post-turning-point adjustment paths—“structural consumption downgrading” and “aggregate-demand-driven consumption contraction”—and discusses the possibilities and limits of external trade as a substitute for domestic demand. The paper further constructs a conceptual income–consumption-standard mismatch model to characterize the pressure generated by the divergence between income and consumption standards and its transmission to consumption behavior, family formation, and future demand. Finally, it proposes four policy directions: optimizing social-media algorithms, establishing a Departmental Employment Quality Index (DEQI) for higher education, reducing the minimum cost of basic living, and limited government intervention in consumption externalities.

articles_hidden.title: Language Replacement and Individualism: Linguicide as a Measurable Cultural Variable
articles_hidden.authors: Isha Sarah Snow
articles_hidden.abstract: Cross-cultural research has linked grammatical features, especially the obligatory use of subject pronouns, to national individualism, but such links are hard to separate from language family, wealth and history. This study treats colonial language replacement as a measurable variable and asks whether colonized countries whose majority home language became a European colonizer's language are more individualist than colonized countries that kept their own. Using a 55-country dataset and a validated individualism index (Akaliyski et al., 2025), I compare 10 replaced-language and 9 retained-language countries, controlling for GDP and diagnostic infrastructure. Replacement was associated with 12.1 points higher individualism (95% CI [8.0, 16.2]). The association was larger where English, which requires overt subject pronouns, did the replacing (17.5 points) than where Spanish or Portuguese, which allow pronoun drop, did so (11.4 points), though the difference between the two was not statistically significant (p = .10). The replacement association persisted when census-based settler population share was controlled, and settler share showed no independent association. This test rests largely on a single case: Ireland, where the population remained and the language shifted, scored with the English-speaking settler states. Within Ireland (N = 3,057), residents of areas where more Irish was spoken in 1911 placed less weight on self-direction values today, while present-day daily use of Irish showed no association. Within Latin America, Indigenous language retention was inversely associated with individualism, but this could not be separated from national wealth. Replacement was not associated with autism prevalence once diagnostic capacity was controlled. I argue that language replacement offers a direct, measurable proxy for linguicide and a route for testing claims about language and selfhood.

articles_hidden.title: Making Place for Health and Good Life: Tourism at the Intersection of Philosophy and Public Health
articles_hidden.authors: Fulvio Longato; Patrick Rina; Christian Josef Wiedermann
articles_hidden.abstract: Tourism is increasingly promoted as a resource for health, and destinations market the well-being their landscapes are said to afford; yet the notion of well-being invoked where tourism and public health meet requires further specification, as the fields that converge there do not necessarily use the term in the same sense. The conceptual analysis clarifies well-being by distinguishing its psychological dimensions from its philosophical characterisation in terms of human flourishing, and frames health from a salutogenic perspective. Human flourishing and salutogenesis intersect particularly through meaningfulness and the ways persons engage with what places make possible. Drawing on the phenomenology of the tourist experience and on the literatures of therapeutic landscapes and restorative environments, the paper argues that places contribute to health through multiple and potentially interacting pathways involving characteristics of settings, activities and experiences, and their social and environmental contexts. Embodied pathways further show the interconnection of experiential and bodily dimensions of health. The paper draws out implications for public health and participatory destination design. Alpine tourism destinations provide a suitable context in which these relationships can be examined empirically.

articles_hidden.title: Linking Basic Psychological Needs Satisfaction to Motivation and Professional Knowledge Development in Dual Vocational Education and Training (VET)
articles_hidden.authors: Jennifer Schauer; Julian M. Etzel; Stephan Abele
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examined the relationships between basic psychological need satisfaction (BPNS), self-determined learning motivation, and intraindividual changes in professional knowledge (PK) in dual vocational education and training (VET) which combines learning in vocational schools and workplace learning in companies. Longitudinal data from N = 473 automotive technician apprentices were analyzed across both contexts using SEM. Results showed that overall BPNS in both contexts predicted stronger self-determined motivation in the respective context. Motivation, in turn, was positively associated with prior PK but not with subsequent changes in PK. Exploratory analyses indicated indirect associations between BPNS and prior PK through motivation in both contexts, and a small indirect association with PK change in the company context. Need-specific sensitivity analyses largely supported the conclusions of the primary models. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of BPNS for fostering self-determined learning motivation in dual VET, while suggesting that its role for PK outcomes may involve cumulative processes integrating prior knowledge.

articles_hidden.title: "How do I survive the next 12 hours?": Disability and lived experiences of extreme heat in the UK
articles_hidden.authors: Hollye Kirkcaldy; Annayah Miranda Beatrice Prosser; Keren MacLennan; Christina Demski
articles_hidden.abstract: As extreme heat becomes a more frequent consequence of climate change, understanding how marginalised populations experience it is critical for adaptation. Disabled people are routinely categorised as ‘at-risk’, yet research largely quantifies heat risk at population level, leaving lived dimensions of heat experience for Disabled people under-explored, particularly in the UK. Drawing on theories of ableism and psycho-emotional disablism, this qualitative study asks how Disabled people in the UK experience extreme heat and what shapes their capacity to adapt. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 27 self-identified Disabled adults across the UK between July and September 2025 and analysed data using Reflexive Thematic Analysis. Across three main themes, participants depict heat as an actively disabling environmental condition which erodes capacity, diminishes identity, exposes ableist assumptions in adaptation and is mediated by material and structural conditions across housing, care and urban infrastructure. Current adaptation frameworks contain significant blind spots, including the temporal and psycho-emotional dimensions of heat harm, and are, in some respects, actively harmful for Disabled people. Addressing this requires a fundamental interrogation of whose knowledge informs the design of heat adaptation policy in the UK.

articles_hidden.title: Moral Load and Moral Strain: Situational Demands and the Experience of Carrying Them
articles_hidden.authors: Chase Crossno
articles_hidden.abstract: People often recognize that something morally significant is happening before they can name what they are experiencing. Existing vocabulary, including moral distress, moral injury, moral residue, and moral resilience, describes important forms and consequences of moral difficulty. This paper develops an analytic distinction among moral demands, moral load, and moral strain. Moral demands are the morally significant claims, obligations, risks, or consequences present in a situation. Moral load names how those demands bear on a particular person through roles, relationships, commitments, foreseeable consequences, and available agency; moral strain names the internal experience of carrying that load. Load is therefore neither a property of the situation alone nor a subjective reaction to it. Prior uses of moral load have addressed moral sensitivity, clinical decision-making, and moral deliberation. The contribution here is a relational architecture that separates situation-level demands, person-specific load, and internal strain. Demands, tasks, authority, resources, and support may be redistributed, thereby changing the load borne by particular people; support may also alter strain even when underlying load remains. Consequences including moral residue and moral injury can generate new obligations and shape later load and strain, making the relationship recursive rather than linear. Implications for education, team practice, and research are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: A Reader’s Guide to the Rubin Report
articles_hidden.authors: John Levi Martin
articles_hidden.abstract: This was written for those readers of the Rubin report who are outsiders to the discipline of sociology, and look to this report as a guide to the state of this field.  Given the publicity this report has received, it would be reasonable for them to imagine that there is warrant for its claims.  There have been many responses to this report, but (as far as I know) none that have simply focused on whether she actually marshaled evidence to support her arguments, and whether she correctly represents her sources.

articles_hidden.title: Observed Shifts in the Health Equity Research Landscape: Results of a National Survey of Health Equity Researchers April-July, 2025
articles_hidden.authors: Clair Kronk; Sima Rabinowitz; Denise Milstein; Devin Madden; Nita Vangeepuram; Dinushika Mohottige; Timnit Berhane; Andrew Maroko
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives. To assess changes health equity researchers have made or anticipate making to their research in the context of the current federal administration’s policies on diversity, equity, and inclusion. 
Methods. We shared an electronic survey link with health equity researchers at academic, non-academic non-profit, non-academic for-profit, and governmental institutions in the U.S. between April and July 2025. 634 responses were received; 381 completed. The survey assessed demographics, occupational and institutional characteristics, perceptions of job security, experiences of stress, collaborations, censorship, and funding sources. 
Results. A large majority of respondents (96.6%) reported having made or anticipated making changes to their health equity research. Changes included: using different language (83.7.%), adapting or altering research questions (56.4%), pivoting to new health equity topics (49.6%), developing new health equity projects (50.4%), seeking new collaborators (31.0%), stopping health equity research activities (18.9%), and withdrawing from existing collaborations (8.9%).
Conclusions. A significant number of health equity researchers have made or anticipate making fundamental changes to their research. These changes have critical implications for health equity research, public health, research teams, and the communities most impacted by this work.

articles_hidden.title: Patient-reported experience as audit evidence: a new perspective on governance in integrated care
articles_hidden.authors: Ilona Ogurcova
articles_hidden.abstract:
Patient-reported experience can identify problems in integrated care, yet feedback alone does not show whether organisations address them. This Perspective argues that experience data can inform internal audit evidence and person-centred healthcare governance when their quality, context and interpretive limits are examined. Developed within the author's doctoral research programme, the argument draws on a purposively selected set of scientific publications and official documents; it does not report a literature review or analyse the programme's empirical datasets. The conceptual method compares the purposes and units of patient-experience measurement, SCIROCCO integration maturity assessment, value-based healthcare implementation assessment and professional internal audit. An illustrative crosswalk then connects five coordination and participation concerns with contextual domains, candidate audit questions, corroborating information and management follow-up. The proposed cycle moves from patient-defined priorities through evidence evaluation to accountable action and repeated assessment of experience. It preserves management ownership of controls and distinguishes a reported concern from a demonstrated organisational failure. Neither the crosswalk nor the combined framework has been empirically validated. Patient involvement, feasibility assessment and comparative evaluation are needed to establish usefulness, burden and effects. The contribution is a testable governance proposition, not evidence of improved clinical outcomes or economic value.
Keywords: patient-reported experience data, internal audit, audit evidence, integrated care, SCIROCCO maturity model, healthcare governance, person-centred care

articles_hidden.title: Post-growth policies and business transformation: A mixed-methods expert assessment of perceived relevance
articles_hidden.authors: Josefine Henman; Manuel Suter
articles_hidden.abstract: This article examines how different policies are perceived by researchers regarding their relevance in supporting the transformation of traditional businesses toward reducing ecological footprints, securing well-being, and increasing social equity. While post-growth scholarship has discussed a wide range of policy proposals, their implications for business transformations remain underexplored. To address this gap, the study combines a quantitative survey of 1,734 sustainability policy researchers with qualitative focus group discussions with post-growth business scholars. The survey results indicate that the majority of policy instruments are perceived as at least moderately relevant for supporting a business transformation towards post-growth. Descriptive analyses show that respondents with a degrowth work-orientation tend to perceive the instruments as more relevant than growth-indifferent or green growth-oriented respondents, with differences particularly pronounced for more structurally disruptive interventions. The qualitative analysis explores how post-growth business scholars perceive key tensions, barriers, and enabling conditions associated with three previously highly ranked policies: transitioning ownership structures, banning planned obsolescence, and introducing declining resource caps. Two central topics emerge from these discussions: the role of businesses’ profit orientation as a structural factor that may shape responses to policy interventions, and the importance of combining policies in order to address anticipated tensions and wider societal implications. The article bridges post-growth policy and business research by suggesting how different policy instruments and mixes may support business transformations in line with post-growth objectives.

articles_hidden.title: Geopolitical Influence & Peace: Tracking the trends shaping international relations
articles_hidden.authors: Sascha Nanlohy; Paulina Pijacka
articles_hidden.abstract:
This report asks whether the world has entered a "new Cold War" and what intensifying great power competition means for peace, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Using datasets including SIPRI, ICEWS, UCDP/PRIO, the Correlates of War and the Foreign Bilateral Influence Capability (FBIC) dataset, it compares today's international system with the Cold War and post-Cold War periods.

Geopolitical risk now exceeds Cold War levels and is nearing the peaks seen after 9/11. Global military expenditure reached a record US$2.43 trillion in 2023, the largest annual rise since 2009. Nuclear disarmament has stalled, and the UN Security Council has become less effective, with fewer resolutions passed and more vetoes since the 2010s. Bilateral sentiment between the US, Russia and China has deteriorated since 1995.

The current system nonetheless differs from the Cold War. It is multipolar and economically interdependent, although trade has plateaued at around 60 per cent of global GDP. It is also shaped by technological competition and global challenges such as climate change. The number of countries holding more than 10 per cent influence in five or more other states has almost tripled, from 13 at the end of the Cold War to 34 in 2024. This reflects the rise of middle powers such as Türkiye, the United Arab Emirates, Brazil, South Africa, Vietnam and Indonesia, alongside China and India.

For LMICs, competition for influence is intensifying, notably in the Sahel, West Africa, South Asia and South America. The US holds more than 10 per cent influence in 74 LMICs and China in 65. China is dominant in sub-Saharan Africa and the US in Latin America. Internationalised intrastate conflicts have increased nearly threefold since 2010. The Sudan and Syria case studies show how external backing for warring parties can prolong conflict and raise the risk of mass atrocities. Proxy wars also drove many of the Cold War's deadliest conflicts.

Economic pressures compound these risks. In 2024, 3.3 billion people lived in countries where debt interest payments exceeded spending on health and education. Aid is also shifting from multilateral to bilateral channels, which further constrains development and Positive Peace.

The report concludes that competition for influence can undermine local governance and divert attention from climate change, food insecurity and peacebuilding. A nuanced understanding of these dynamics is needed to support long-term stability and development in the developing world.

articles_hidden.title: No King, and Other Matters—America’s Perspectives in Mid-2026 on Democracy, Authoritarianism, and Election-Related Violence:  Findings from a Nationally Representative Survey
articles_hidden.authors: Garen J. Wintemute; Bradley Velasquez; Sonia Robinson; Krista Neumann; Shaina Sta Cruz; Aaron Shev; Daniel Joseph Tancredi; Elizabeth A. Tomsich; Mona A. Wright; Veronica Pear
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Political violence and the rise of authoritarianism are emerging threats to the nation’s health, stability, and future as a representative democracy. To inform and facilitate prevention efforts, we present new and updated findings on the public’s views on authoritarianism and its support for and willingness to engage in election-related and pro- or anti-government violence. 

Methods: Findings are from Wave 5, conducted May 15-June 15, 2026, of a nationally representative annual longitudinal survey of adult members of the Ipsos KnowledgePanel that was initiated in 2022. Findings are for the cohort as a whole and for subgroups defined by political party/Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement affiliation. Year-to-year change for items included in 2025 and 2026 is estimated using mean change scores. Cross-sectional findings for 2026 are presented as weighted prevalences and item scores.

Results: The completion rate was 90.7%; there were 7,552 respondents. Nearly 90% of respondents continued to consider it very or extremely important that the US remain a democracy (change 0.01, 95% CI -0.00, 0.03). Agreement with expressions of authoritarianism was much less common; it decreased for the statement, “having a strong leader for America is more important than having a democracy” (change -0.04, 95% CI -0.07, -0.02) and others. In 2026, 2.1% (95% CI 1.6%, 2.7%) of respondents agreed strongly or very strongly that President Trump should be made king, but nearly half (47.7%, 95% CI 46.2%, 49.2%) agreed strongly or very strongly that he should be impeached and removed from office. 

There was little agreement with 5 actions the federal government might take in 2026 that employed violence to enforce its policies or suppress its critics in the US; the prevalence of strong or very strong agreement ranged between 4.4% and 9.6%. Across 12 items, there was very little agreement with actions—including violence—the federal government might take to subvert elections; strong or very strong agreement ranged between 2% and 4%. Willingness to commit violence was rare. For example, only 1.6% (95% CI 1.2%, 2.1%) were very or completely willing to use violence “to make sure that President Trump remains in office after his term ends.” Decreases from 2025 to 2026 in support for expressions of authoritarianism and for government-initiated violence were common across the spectrum of party/MAGA movement affiliations.

Conclusions: With national elections a few months away, Americans remained strongly supportive of democracy, did not endorse authoritarianism, and rejected the use of force by the current federal government to enforce its policies or subvert elections. They were deeply unwilling to engage in violence. These hopeful findings can inform and guide efforts to preserve democracy and prevent political violence.

articles_hidden.title: The Darkside of Collegiality: From Audit Culture to Participatory Taylorism
articles_hidden.authors: Abe Walker
articles_hidden.abstract: Cultures of shared governance in academia may appear as a noble tradition to be upheld and defended against the steady encroachment of audit culture. However, building upon recent interest in the ‘dark side’ of collegiality, this theoretically-motivated article proposes that the collegial ideal of collective and participatory decision-making now co-exist alongside performance metrics in an uneasy alliance that softens their surface-level opposition. Invoking the paradoxical concept of ‘participatory Taylorism,’ this study demonstrates that faculty engagement is essential to audit culture’s apparent staying power. Performance metrics survive by opening themselves to the demos, inviting robust debates about their composition and legitimacy – provided these dialogues stop short of contesting audit culture itself. In this sense, permissible modes of shared governance perform a type of ‘collegiality-washing,’ substituting a simulacra of participation for the real thing.  Moreover, because ‘participation’ is precisely the lever through which performance measures exert their influence, conventional oppositional strategies risk co-optation. In a university setting that demands constant engagement and actively recuperates dissent, resistance may take the form of withdrawal, silence, or even a more recent trend, ‘quiet quitting.’

articles_hidden.title: Effective Anti-Corruption Strategies for Public Organizations: Insights from Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression
articles_hidden.authors: Kristina Sabrina Weißmüller
articles_hidden.abstract: Fighting corruption remains one of the most pressing management challenges in public organizations worldwide. While different organizational approaches to anti‑corruption exist, evidence of their effectiveness and the conditions under which they reduce different forms of administrative corruption remains limited. Drawing on a meta analysis and meta regression of 174 effect sizes from 34 empirical studies, this study shows that both integrity based and compliance based anti corruption strategies have a significant, positive, small to moderate effect on public organizations’ ethical performance, although their effectiveness varies across contexts. Compliance based strategies, particularly formalization and accountability mechanisms, are more effective in addressing multiple forms of administrative corruption, whereas integrity‑based strategies, such as ethical leadership, primarily reduce collusion, demonstrating that ‘one-size-fits-all’ approaches are ineffective. The findings highlight the conditional effectiveness of organizational anti‑corruption strategies and the importance of context‑sensitive ethics management. These findings carry important implications for public administration theory, research, and practice.

articles_hidden.title: Digitalización de la información política y Democracia: Paradojas, contradicciones y desafíos. Una propuesta inter-transdisciplinar de análisis conceptual
articles_hidden.authors: Ángel Gutiérrez Escobedo
articles_hidden.abstract: Resumen: Tomando un punto de partida interdisciplinario (Thompson, 1996), presentamos una propuesta de análisis para la información política en las democracias para la época de lo virtual; que trabaja con los principios de la teoría general de sistemas sociales (Luhmann, 2022; 1981) y la teoría de la información (Shannon, 1948). Algunos intentos contemporáneos para entender dicho escenario de información y democracia (Huang, 2026) ponen especial énfasis en la paradoja que surge entre libertad de expresión e información para la democracia. Partiendo de la teoría general de sistemas sociales, entendemos que la comunicación política no produce información para sus observantes sino que se relaciona con la continuidad, adaptación o reproducción de la misma comunicación; es decir, mediante la comunicación digital, los actores políticos han acoplado sus comunicaciones en la exageración o el escándalo, desarticulando la racionalidad tradicional en la política donde la calidad y alternativas de información suele ser necesaria (Dahl, 2009) desplazándola por una inmaterialidad que va un poco más allá del espectáculo (Debord, 1995), pero que reincide en la misma realidad política. Esto es importante para entornos como México porque atraviesa el derecho a la libertad de expresión en tanto que la comunicación de opiniones extremistas puede ser utilizado por diversos actores para deslegitimar otras formas de comunicación (Russo, 2025) como también un mecanismo para limitar derechos. Finalmente, sus efectos ocultos, la información política virtual/digital permite facilitar el entendimiento o aceptación de decisiones materiales que de otra forma podrían parecer aberrantes mediante estiramientos de la verdad, es decir, discusiones o debates en torno a tópicos que se podrían considerar fundamentales (Vössing, 2024). Termina con una serie de consideraciones para el análisis político contemporáneo puesto que la situación global de las democracias mantiene tendencias de erosión (Stokes, 2025) y se emplea la ironía por lideres políticos para consolidar el poder o des-presupuestar instituciones. Se necesitan estudios que visibilicen y permitan combatir esta contradicción.

articles_hidden.title: Adverse Outcomes Among Youths Admitted to Compulsory Institutional Care: A Swedish Matched Cohort Study
articles_hidden.authors: Amber L. Beckley; Fredrik Sivertsson; Sofi Oskarsson; Catherine Tuvblad; Peter Larm
articles_hidden.abstract: Youths admitted to compulsory institutional care represent a particularly vulnerable population with substantial behavioral, social, and health-related needs. However, evidence on their long-term outcomes relative to other high-risk youths, and on when adverse outcomes emerge following discharge, remains limited. We examined the characteristics of youths admitted to compulsory institutional care in Sweden, compared their overall and adulthood outcomes with matched youths from the general population and compulsory social care, and examined the timing of adverse outcomes following discharge. The Swedish Longitudinal Compulsory Care Study (SLCCS) includes all youths admitted to compulsory institutional care (CIC) in Sweden between 2000 and 2020 (n = 14,677), matched to youths from the general population (14,349 pairs) and compulsory social care (8,879 pairs).
