Analyses were stratified by sex and included descriptive statistics, fixed-effects regression, Cox proportional hazards models, and Kaplan–Meier analyses. Criminal behavior and substance use were the most common reasons for placement. The CIC group experienced poorer outcomes than both comparison groups overall and in adulthood. Compared with matched women from the general population, adjusted hazards of substance use disorder (HR = 7.83, 95% CI 6.07–10.10) and all-cause mortality (HR = 8.42, 95% CI 3.01–23.54) were nearly eightfold higher among women admitted to compulsory institutional care. Corresponding hazards among men were fivefold higher for substance use disorder (HR = 5.11, 95% CI 4.26–6.12) and threefold higher for all-cause mortality (HR = 3.11, 95% CI 2.02–4.77). Kaplan–Meier analyses indicated that mental health and substance use diagnoses were concentrated within the first five years following discharge. Youths admitted to compulsory institutional care face an elevated risk of adverse outcomes extending into adulthood, and the first five years following discharge may represent an important period for aftercare and support.

articles_hidden.title: Maternal Solidarity: Unconditional Cash Prescriptions and a Moral Economy of Motherhood in Flint, Michigan
articles_hidden.authors: Caroline Doenmez; Jenny LaChance; Mallory Goldsworthy; Mona Hanna
articles_hidden.abstract: How do mothers make meaning out of the experience of being “prescribed” no-strings-attached cash to improve their family’s health and life chances? This paper explores the impact of Rx Kids, the first community-wide cash transfer program for mothers and newborns in the United States. Launched in Flint, Michigan, in January 2024, the program seeks to “prescribe away” child poverty by providing cash transfers to mothers during and after their pregnancies. The program design stands apart from other cash transfer programs due to its universal and unconditional features: it ensures that all pregnant mothers in a participating community can receive the cash and does not impose any spending restrictions or reporting requirements on them. This paper is interested in Rx Kids’ cultural impact as ascertained through mothers’ narratives of their involvement with the program. Drawing on 46 interviews conducted with mothers in Flint, we ask: What did the unconditionality and universality of the program mean to them? Through their narratives, we identify how the transfer of monetary resources to the mothers elicited profound moral considerations. As mothers moved through the process of encountering, applying to, participating in, and advocating for the program, they narrated grappling continuously with the question of maternal worth and worthiness. Through their affective experiences of disbelief, astonishment, mistrust, anxiety, gratitude, and compassion for other mothers, we argue that the participants give voice to a moral economy of motherhood in Flint, circulating and contesting cultural values regarding reproductive labor and maternal worth. Ultimately, we show how through participating in the program, the mothers were actualized as both the recipients and providers of what we term “maternal solidarity,” an unconditional mode of care premised on a shared understanding of the pronounced and ubiquitous challenges of contemporary motherhood.

articles_hidden.title: Co-creating change in agriculture and food systems: A systematic review of co-creation processes and approaches for evaluating their contributions to sustainability transformation
articles_hidden.authors: Sara Delaney; Sophia Alami; Maria Busse; Bonnie Averbuch; Fanny Boeraeve; Pauline Cassart; Valéria Csonka; Graeme Dean; Cedric Gossart; Bienvenu Kambashi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Co-creation is widely proposed to address complex sustainability challenges by bringing together diverse forms of experience and expertise. Yet practical, evidence-based guidance on how co-creation processes can support sustainability transformation remains fragmented and insufficient, including for agriculture and food systems. We conducted a systematic literature review to characterize scholarly work on co-creation for environmental sustainability and to identify process insights relevant to Living Labs and related participatory initiatives. Following a four-stage screening procedure, we reviewed 5,291 articles and retained 266 studies describing multi-stakeholder, action-oriented, experimental processes; 51 agriculture- and food-focused articles were subjected to in-depth qualitative analysis. We combined bibliometric and descriptive analyses, including co-authorship network mapping, with framework-guided qualitative coding of co-creation inputs, processes, outcomes, impacts, and evaluation practices.
Publications on this topic increased substantially over the past decade, but relatively few studies documented action and experimentation in sufficient methodological detail. Agriculture and food studies constituted a moderately self-contained segment of the broader literature. Across the qualitative sample, five enabling factors were most consistently associated with productive co-creation: participant alignment, institutional support, strong facilitation, inclusive participation and trust, and sufficient time for iteration. Studies also identified recurring trade-offs between diversity and alignment, resource-intensive engagement and scalability, and place specificity and transferability. Frequently reported outcomes were new knowledge, communication and networks, empowerment or efficacy, and skills. However, evidence of longer-term sustainability impacts was limited: most articles described intermediate outcomes rather than demonstrated transformation. Only sixteen articles evaluated the co-creation process itself, and participatory development of evaluation criteria was rare. Co-creation efforts can build the practical and relational capacities, and “social infrastructure” needed for sustainability transitions, but stronger methodological reporting and participatory, longitudinal evaluation are needed for validation of criteria and proxies for impact and establishment of how these processes contribute to lasting transformation.

articles_hidden.title: От «светоча нации» до «педагога-тирана»: как русскоязычные Telegram-медиа конструируют образ учителя, 2020–2025
articles_hidden.authors: Munira Vassilova
articles_hidden.abstract: Исследование анализирует, как профессия учителя конструируется в русскоязычном новостном Telegram-корпусе за 2020–2025 гг. Исходный архив был получен из открытого набора ResearchData.kz (dataset 233) и включал 653 170 публикаций; после ограничения периода осталось 551 880 сообщений. Лексический поиск по основам «учител*», «педагог*» и «преподавател*» дал 5 721 кандидата, после скрининга сформирован рабочий корпус из 5 256 размещений в 19 каналах. Семантическое кодирование выявило 4 440 содержательно валидных упоминаний и 816 нерелевантных совпадений. Кодбук, сформированный абдуктивно из литературы и повторяющихся паттернов корпуса, различает F0 — присутствие учителя без самостоятельного профессионального фрейма — и семь содержательных фреймов. F0 составляет 32,2% валидных публикаций. Среди содержательных фреймов наиболее распространены поддержка/инвестиции и уязвимость — по 15,1%; экспертность/агентность составляет лишь 6,2%. Это показывает, что медиа чаще говорят об учителе как об объекте поддержки, ограничений, регулирования или оценки, чем как о самостоятельном производителе профессионального знания. Временные различия невелики: доля экспертности/агентности возрастает с 3,8% в 2020 г. до 7,3% в 2025 г., а уязвимости — с 11,6% до 17,6%. Среди казахстанских источников медиа регионального охвата значительно чаще используют фрейм экспертности, а государственные — признание и поддержку; негосударственные чаще проблематизируют профессию и показывают уязвимость. Работа показывает, почему для анализа статуса профессии важно различать простую видимость, профессиональную репрезентацию и распределение символической агентности.

articles_hidden.title: Resistance to Backsliding: The Role of Democratic Conceptions
articles_hidden.authors: Noam Gidron; Yotam Margalit; Lior Sheffer; Itamar Yakir
articles_hidden.abstract: We examine who mobilizes against democratic backsliding, focusing on mass protests against the judicial overhaul advanced by the Israeli government in 2023. As contemporary subversion of democracy is often driven by governments that won an electoral majority, we posit that protesting against the government's actions requires people to have a thick conception of democracy that goes beyond majority rule. Drawing on panel data collected before and after the overhaul's announcement, we show that citizens vary substantially in their conception of democracy, and that a thick conception not only predicts protesting against backsliding but also moderates the role of other key factors in mobilizing against democratic erosion. The findings highlight the role of small-d democrats in safeguarding democracy.

articles_hidden.title: Your AI Knows Your Story. Should It Die With You?
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Seifert
articles_hidden.abstract: Personal conversations with AI assistants increasingly contain memories, reflections, and records of changing judgment that may outlive their users. This commentary argues that selected exchanges could form a digital legacy: not a posthumous replica, but a personal testimony curated while the person is still able to correct it. Such legacies may be especially meaningful for people who wish to pass on their experience beyond their immediate family. Their creation, however, requires explicit consent, designated recipients, durable access, and a clear separation between the user's own words, the system's contributions, and any interpretations generated later. Whether such archives transmit wisdom or support bereavement remains an open question.

articles_hidden.title: Social Networks and Unequal Income Returns to Education: Gender Differences and Cross-National Context
articles_hidden.authors: INVEST Flagship; Emmi Mäkeläinen; Aki Koivula
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines how social networks are associated with unequal income returns to education and whether these associations vary by gender and across national contexts. Using data from the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) 2017 from representative samples in 15 countries, the study analyses the interrelations between educational attainment, social ties, and personal income. The analyses distinguish both the status of social contacts and the type of ties to the upper middle class, while also examining variation by gender and country-level income inequality. The results show that access to upper-middle-class contacts is associated with wider educational differences in income, and that close ties, especially family members, relatives, and close friends, are more strongly associated with income than weaker ties. These patterns also vary by gender, with educated men’s income more strongly associated with upper-middle-class ties than educated women’s. In addition, educational differences in the association between social networks and income are more pronounced in countries with higher levels of income inequality. The study contributes to research on social stratification by showing that income returns to education are socially embedded and also vary by gender and national context.

articles_hidden.title: Daily Dynamics of Urban Racial Segregation in the United States
articles_hidden.authors: Cody Arlie Reed
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines racial segregation changes across the day and week to assess three perspectives in urban sociology: social isolation, compelled mobility, and cosmopolitanism. I link mobile phone tracking data collected on 18 days in January 2020 to 2020 Census data on the racial composition of estimated home tracts. Using the Theil multigroup segregation index, I estimate hourly racial segregation in 18 large U.S. commuting zones. Racial segregation is highest overnight, declines during weekday work hours, and is generally higher on weekends than weekdays. These patterns are most consistent with the compelled mobility perspective, under which lower racial segregation is expected when residents travel beyond their neighborhoods to access employment and other resources. Relatively high weekend racial segregation offers only weak support for social isolation. Friday and Saturday nights and the following early mornings have lower racial segregation than Wednesday at the same hours, offering clearer partial support for cosmopolitanism. Although the data do not identify why people travel, they show that the clearest declines in racial segregation coincide with the workday. Measuring racial segregation across hours and days thus helps distinguish theoretical accounts of how racial segregation persists or diminishes beyond residential neighborhoods.

articles_hidden.title: Mind the Gap: Elite Preferences for Redistribution and How they Differ from the Mass Public
articles_hidden.authors: Mogens K. Justesen; Marko Klašnja; Sara B. Hobolt; Robert Klemmensen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Increasing inequality has raised concerns over the disproportionate influence of the rich on public policies. Central to such concerns is the assumption that elite policy preferences are unified and differ significantly from the general public. We theorize economic elites as fiscal constituencies, highlighting intra-elite differences in policy preferences based on elite sources of affluence and therefore fiscal claims they face from the state. 
Employing high-quality administrative and survey data, including conjoint experiments, from Denmark, we compare tax and spending preferences in the general population with the largest samples to date of the top 1% by income and wealth. While elites are more economically conservative, they are not uniformly anti-redistribution; the asset-rich are less conservative than the income-rich; and their preferences often differ over tax policy. These findings highlight elite group differences based on their relation to the fiscal structure of the state and offer new insights into the micro-foundations of unequal representation in advanced democracies.

articles_hidden.title: Ranking Data in Political Science
articles_hidden.authors: Yuki Atsusaka; Shubhangi Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Across scientific disciplines, researchers have used ranking data to study people's comparative judgments, preferences, and decision-making over a range of items. While existing data-sharing infrastructures in statistics and machine learning, such as PrefLib, offer a rich collection of ranking datasets, including those related to politics, they are not necessarily designed specifically to support cumulative research in social science. In this work, we introduce the first large-scale database of political rankings based on various studies from leading political science journals. Our first release covers 52 datasets from 27 original studies published between 2005 and 2025. Our database demonstrates notable variation in substantive topics and forms of ranking data that go well beyond canonical examples of candidate evaluations and value orientations, enabling researchers to perform comparative analyses, replication, reanalysis, methodological evaluation, and new substantive research with real-world political rankings. Along with validating our database, we illustrate it by replicating key findings in four selected studies, including those of multiple identities in American politics, the representation of Muslims in India, factional leaning in the Syrian civil war, and legislative accountability for affordable health care.

articles_hidden.title: Causal Inference in the CLS Cohort Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Liam Wright; Georgia D Tomova; Martin Nejedly; George Ploubidis; Richard J. Silverwood
articles_hidden.abstract: Correlations between variables in cohort and other observational studies do not necessarily indicate causal effects and may instead reflect bias due to confounding, sample selection processes, or measurement issues. Thankfully, multiple statistical methods, frameworks, and research designs have been developed that – when used judiciously – can aid making causal inferences with observational data. This is especially the case with CLS’s cohorts, which have several properties (e.g., longitudinal assessment and rich and varied data collection) that that can make the assumptions of these methods more plausible or provide ample opportunities for each method’s use. In this guide, we provide an overview of the possibilities for causal inference in CLS’s cohorts. Specifically, we: (1) provide background on the problem of causal inference in observational data, (2) detail the attributes of CLS’s cohorts that can support causal inference, and (3) outline an extensive set of methods and research designs that – assumptions permitting – can be used to estimate causal effects in CLS’s cohort data, illustrating each with existing applications and highlighting opportunities for further work.

articles_hidden.title: FRAGMENTED GOVERNANCE AND THE FAILURE TO EXECUTE URBAN PROJECTS: THE LARGO DA BATATA COMPETITION (2001-2022)
articles_hidden.authors: Leticia Takeda Lodi
articles_hidden.abstract: Architecture and urban design competitions are often defended as democratic selection mechanisms, yet many fail during implementation. This article argues the failure stems from fragmented governance: semi-autonomous sectoral authorities operating without a coordinating hierarchy. Through a 21-year documentary analysis of the National Competition for the Urban Reconversion of Largo da Batata (São Paulo), comparing the winning, basic and executed projects (2001-2022), we show each authority discharged its mandate competently, yet the absence of coordination fragmented the outcome. This mechanism, pockets of micro-regulation practices, moves the debate from describing competition failure to explaining it, with implications for governance research.

articles_hidden.title: Heed the warning: how NATO can find and fill the gaps in its warning systems
articles_hidden.authors: Nikki Ikani
articles_hidden.abstract: Intelligence warning failures are too often viewed in binary: Either intelligence succeeded or it failed. In reality, often only segments of the warning chain collapse while others operate well. This Outlook paper treats warning success as a spectrum rather than as a pass/fail test in a new framework for warning performance. It illustrates the use through three recent case studies: the fall of Kabul (2021), Russia’s invasion of Ukraine (2022) and the Niger coup (2023). The decisive shortfall across all three cases was the failure to reconcile divergent NATO member state views into an operational consensus within NATO. There are practical solutions for integrating NATO capabilities to institutionalize rapid after-action reviews, conduct periodic divergence drill exercises, prepare contingency packages and further embed red team analyses.

articles_hidden.title: What influences the time to reach a tenured university professorship? Insights from machine-learning
articles_hidden.authors: Jasmin M. Kizilirmak; Frauke Peter
articles_hidden.abstract: The race to professorship is influenced by many factors, ranging from individual achievements to systemic structures. Prior research has underscored the significance of aspects such as academic productivity, institutional affiliations, and personal choices in shaping academic careers, but comprehensive analyses in specific contexts remain limited. The last two decades have seen strategic shifts within the German academic system, most notably with the introduction of junior and tenure-track professorships intended to offer a more secure career path. Yet, uncertainties persist regarding the determinants of career trajectories to tenured university professorship. Addressing this gap, this paper uses unique and novel longitudinal data of German professors to elucidate the various pathways to professorship. Based on a sample of individuals who successfully secured full university professorship, we estimate comprehensive models using machine learning to determine relevant factors that predict the time needed to reach this position. Key correlates are obtaining a habilitation, having held positions with leadership responsibilities, and disciplinary fields.

articles_hidden.title: Women and AI: A Large-Scale, Validated Mapping of Women’s Under-Represented and Under-Recognized Contributions to AI Research
articles_hidden.authors: Chiara Binelli; Elena Cossu
articles_hidden.abstract: Participation in AI research shapes which type of AI is built, whose societal needs it addresses, and how it is used in society. Despite increasing attention to gender diversity in AI, we lacksystematic evidence on the research topics, methods used, and collaboration structures associated with female AI researchers. This paper addresses this significant gap by developing the first large-scale, validated mapping of women’s contributions to both generative and non-generative AI research across data science and the main social science disciplines (economics, political science, and sociology). Using a sample of over 500,000 papers published between 2023 and 2026, we document three key findings. First, women are under-represented among academic AI authors across all four disciplines and recent years, and least represented in data science. Second, conditional on participating, women’s AI research is thematically distinctive: it is more applied, social and purpose-driven, concentrated in health, education and fairness, and, in data science, oriented towards using rather than building AI. Third, this distinctive work is heard less: conditional on working on the same AI topic women and men are cited equally, but the topics women disproportionately work on are themselves cited less, so women’s ideas receive systematically fewer citations. This voice gap is therefore a topic-composition penalty rather than a same-topic penalty, and it reduces efficiency by giving a distinctive, society-oriented research agenda too little voice in how AI develops.

articles_hidden.title: Social Exclusion, Institutional Support and the Perceived Criminal Involvement of Waste Pickers: Evidence from a Stakeholder Survey in Rawalpindi–Islamabad, Pakistan
articles_hidden.authors: rabail ghazanfar
articles_hidden.abstract: Informal waste pickers (rag-pickers) are among the most marginalised urban groups in Pakistan, yet they are often linked in public debate to petty crime, substance use and sex work. This study surveys 300 frontline stakeholders (78 police personnel, 175 NGO staff and 47 other residents) in Rawalpindi and Islamabad to examine which offences they attribute to waste pickers and how these perceptions relate to perceived social exclusion and perceived support from government and NGOs. Substance use (80%) and prostitution (79%) were the offences most often attributed; murder rarely (5%). Perceived social exclusion was strongly associated with perceived criminal involvement (r = .73, p < .001), while perceived institutional support showed a weak negative association (r = -.17, p = .004). In a regression model (R2 = .53), exclusion was the only significant predictor (beta = .75); the association of support with criminal involvement operated indirectly through lower exclusion (indirect effect = -.23, Sobel z = -5.27, p < .001). The findings suggest that support reduces perceived criminality only insofar as it reduces exclusion, and argue for inclusion-oriented policy: integrating waste pickers into municipal waste systems, making social protection reachable, and protective rather than extractive policing. Based on the author's MPhil thesis (National Defence University, Islamabad, 2020).
